docs.title: What is SRv6 (IPv6 Segment Routing) and How Does It Work?
docs.text:
SRv6 (Segment Routing over IPv6) — also written Segment Routing v6, SR v6 or IPv6 Segment Routing — is the IPv6 data plane of the Segment Routing architecture (RFC 8402). It encodes forwarding instructions directly in IPv6 packet headers. Instead of relying on MPLS labels and signaling protocols like LDP or RSVP-TE, SRv6 uses native 128-bit IPv6 addresses as Segment Identifiers (SIDs) to program network paths and behaviors.

The source node builds an ordered list of segments that defines the packet's path and the processing at each hop. The active segment sits in the IPv6 destination address; when there is more than one, the rest travel in a Segment Routing Header (SRH) — and with uSID compression a whole path often fits in the destination address with no SRH at all. Transit routers simply forward on the destination address. This enables traffic engineering, VPN services, fast reroute and service function chaining on a plain IPv6 network.

Why choose SRv6 over traditional MPLS?

  • Simplified operations — No more MPLS label management, LDP, or RSVP
  • Native IPv6 — Uses the existing IPv6 data plane with no overlays
  • Network programmability — Define custom network behaviors with SRv6 functions (End, End.DT4, End.DX6, etc.)
  • Scalability — 128-bit SID space supports massive networks and micro-segmentation
  • Unified data plane — Single protocol stack for transport, VPN, and TE services

docs.title: ¿Qué es SRv6 (IPv6 Segment Routing) y cómo funciona?
docs.text:
SRv6 (Segment Routing over IPv6, o Segment Routing sobre IPv6), también escrito Segment Routing v6, SR v6 o IPv6 Segment Routing, es el plano de datos IPv6 de la arquitectura Segment Routing (RFC 8402). Codifica las instrucciones de reenvío directamente en la cabecera de los paquetes IPv6. En lugar de depender de etiquetas MPLS y de protocolos de señalización como LDP o RSVP-TE, SRv6 usa direcciones IPv6 nativas de 128 bits como identificadores de segmento (SID) para programar las rutas y los comportamientos de la red.

El nodo de origen arma una lista ordenada de segmentos que define la ruta del paquete y lo que debe hacer cada nodo. El segmento activo va en la dirección IPv6 de destino; cuando hay más de uno, el resto viaja en una Segment Routing Header (SRH), y con uSID muchas veces la ruta completa cabe en la dirección de destino sin necesidad de SRH. Los routers de tránsito simplemente reenvían según la dirección de destino. Esto habilita ingeniería de tráfico, servicios VPN, fast reroute y encadenamiento de funciones de servicio sobre una red IPv6 normal.

¿Por qué SRv6 en lugar de MPLS tradicional?

  • Operación más simple: sin gestión de etiquetas MPLS, LDP ni RSVP
  • IPv6 nativo: usa el plano de datos IPv6 existente, sin overlays
  • Programabilidad de red: comportamientos definidos con funciones SRv6 (End, End.DT4, End.DX6…)
  • Escalabilidad: el espacio de SID de 128 bits soporta redes de gran escala
  • Un solo plano de datos: un único stack para transporte, VPN e ingeniería de tráfico

docs.title: Cabecera SRH: recorrido del paquete
docs.text:
Read in English · 日本語で読む

Entender cómo funciona la Segment Routing Header (SRH) a nivel de paquete es esencial para diseñar y diagnosticar redes SRv6. Esta página recorre la mecánica paso a paso.

docs.title: Campos principales
docs.text:
Campo Tamaño Descripción Next Header 8 bits Tipo de la siguiente cabecera (por ejemplo, 41 = IPv6, 4 = IPv4) Hdr Ext Len 8 bits Longitud de la SRH en unidades de 8 octetos, sin contar los primeros 8 Routing Type 8 bits Siempre 4 para la SRH Segments Left (SL) 8 bits Índice en la lista de segmentos que apunta al segmento activo Last Entry 8 bits Índice del último elemento de la lista (empieza en 0) Flags 8 bits Banderas; el RFC 8754 no define ninguna Tag 16 bits Agrupación o marcado de paquetes Segment List 128 bits cada uno Lista ordenada de SIDs, en orden inverso

¡Orden inverso!

La lista de segmentos se codifica en orden inverso: Segment List[0] es el último SID que se procesa y Segment List[n] es el primero. El puntero Segments Left empieza en n y va bajando hasta 0.

docs.title: Recorrido completo de un paquete
docs.text:
Sigamos un paquete a través de una red SRv6 de 3 nodos:

Origen (A) → Nodo B → Nodo C → Destino (D)

SIDs SRv6:
  B::100  = comportamiento End en el Nodo B
  C::200  = comportamiento End.DT4 en el Nodo C (desencapsula a IPv4)

docs.title: Paso 1: entrada (Origen A)
docs.text:
El origen A recibe un paquete IPv4 con destino 10.0.0.2 y tiene que dirigirlo por B y luego por C.

Paquete original:
  [IPv4: 10.0.0.1 → 10.0.0.2][Payload]

Tras la encapsulación SRv6:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Cabecera IPv6 externa                     │
  │   Origen:  A::1                           │
  │   Destino: B::100  ← SID activo           │
  │   Next Header: 43 (Routing)               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ SRH                                       │
  │   Segments Left: 1                        │
  │   Last Entry:    1                        │
  │   Segment List[0]: C::200  (último SID)   │
  │   Segment List[1]: B::100  (primer SID)   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Cabecera IPv4 interna                     │
  │   10.0.0.1 → 10.0.0.2                    │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Payload                                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

DA = SID activo

La dirección IPv6 de destino siempre es igual al SID activo (Segment List[Segments Left]).

docs.title: Paso 2: tránsito (Nodo B, comportamiento End)
docs.text:
El Nodo B recibe el paquete. La dirección de destino coincide con su SID local B::100, que tiene el comportamiento End:

  1. Decrementa Segments Left: 1 → 0
  2. Copia Segment List[0] en la dirección de destino IPv6: DA = C::200
  3. Reenvía según la nueva dirección de destino
Tras el procesamiento en el Nodo B:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Cabecera IPv6 externa                     │
  │   Origen:  A::1                           │
  │   Destino: C::200  ← ¡Actualizado!       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ SRH                                       │
  │   Segments Left: 0     ← ¡Decrementado!  │
  │   Last Entry:    1                        │
  │   Segment List[0]: C::200                 │
  │   Segment List[1]: B::100                 │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ IPv4 interna: 10.0.0.1 → 10.0.0.2        │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Payload                                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Paso 3: salida (Nodo C, comportamiento End.DT4)
docs.text:
El Nodo C recibe el paquete. La dirección de destino coincide con su SID local C::200, que tiene el comportamiento End.DT4:

  1. SL = 0, así que es el último segmento
  2. Desencapsula: quita la cabecera IPv6 externa y la SRH
  3. Busca la dirección de destino IPv4 interna en la tabla de la VRF indicada
  4. Reenvía el paquete IPv4 original
Tras el procesamiento en el Nodo C:
  [IPv4: 10.0.0.1 → 10.0.0.2][Payload]  ← ¡Paquete original restaurado!

docs.title: Paso 4: entrega
docs.text: El paquete IPv4 original llega al destino 10.0.0.2 como si SRv6 nunca hubiera intervenido.

docs.title: Diagrama de secuencia
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Origen A
    participant B as Nodo B (End)
    participant C as Nodo C (End.DT4)
    participant D as Destino

    A->>A: Recibe paquete IPv4 para 10.0.0.2
    A->>A: Encap: IPv6(DA=B::100) + SRH[C::200, B::100] + IPv4
    A->>B: Reenvía a B::100 (SL=1)

    B->>B: B::100 coincide → comportamiento End
    B->>B: SL: 1→0, DA: B::100→C::200
    B->>C: Reenvía a C::200 (SL=0)

    C->>C: C::200 coincide → comportamiento End.DT4
    C->>C: Desencapsula y busca IPv4 en la VRF
    C->>D: Reenvía el paquete IPv4 original

docs.title: Sabores PSP, USP y USD
docs.text:
Los endpoints SRv6 pueden soportar distintos sabores (flavors) que optimizan cómo se maneja la SRH:

Sabor Nombre completo Descripción PSP Penultimate Segment Pop El penúltimo nodo (SL=1) quita la SRH antes de reenviar al último segmento. Reduce la carga en el nodo de salida. USP Ultimate Segment Pop El último nodo quita la SRH él mismo. USD Ultimate Segment Decap El último nodo desencapsula toda la cabecera IPv6 externa y la SRH. Se usa con End.DT4/DT6.

PSP es el más común

PSP está muy desplegado porque libera al PE de salida de quitar la SRH. La mayoría de las implementaciones modernas anuncian End with PSP o End with PSP-USP-USD.

docs.title: SRH con TLVs
docs.text:
La SRH puede llevar objetos TLV (Type-Length-Value) opcionales después de la lista de segmentos:

TLV Descripción HMAC TLV Autenticación criptográfica de la SRH Padding TLV Relleno para alineación NSH Carrier TLV Transporta metadatos NSH para encadenamiento de servicios

docs.title: Encapsulación reducida
docs.text:
H.Encaps.Red (Reduced Encapsulation, RFC 8986) optimiza la SRH omitiendo de la lista de segmentos el primer SID de la ruta, porque el nodo de entrada ya lo coloca en la dirección IPv6 de destino. Así se ahorran 16 bytes por paquete, y con una ruta de un solo SID la SRH desaparece por completo.

Ruta: SID-1 → SID-2 → SID-3   (la lista se guarda en orden inverso)

H.Encaps:      SRH [SID-3, SID-2, SID-1], SL=2, DA = SID-1
H.Encaps.Red:  SRH [SID-3, SID-2],        SL=2, DA = SID-1  ← SID-1 solo va en la DA

docs.title: Estructura del SID
docs.text:
Read in English · 日本語で読む

Un Segment Identifier (SID) de SRv6 es un valor de 128 bits con formato de dirección IPv6 estándar. Codifica a la vez la ubicación de un nodo y el comportamiento que se debe ejecutar.

docs.title: Anatomía de un SID de SRv6
docs.text:
|<------------ 128 bits ------------->|
|  Locator      | Function | Arguments|
|<-- L bits --->|<-F bits->|<-A bits->|
Campo Descripción Tamaño típico Locator Prefijo enrutable que identifica al nodo 40-64 bits Function Identifica el comportamiento local (End, End.DT4, etc.) 16-24 bits Arguments Parámetros opcionales para la función 0-48 bits

docs.title: Ejemplo
docs.text:
SID:  5f00:0:1::100

Desglose:
  Locator:  5f00:0:1::/48   (identifica al nodo)
  Function: ::100            (End.DT4 - desencapsula y busca en la tabla IPv4)
  Args:     (ninguno)

El Locator es una ruta del IGP

El bloque del Locator se anuncia como una ruta IPv6 normal en el IGP (IS-IS u OSPFv3). Así se garantiza la alcanzabilidad de cualquier nodo con SRv6 en la red.

docs.title: Bloque de SIDs SRv6 asignado por IANA (5f00::/16)
docs.text:
El RFC 9602 (octubre de 2024) asigna un prefijo IPv6 dedicado para los identificadores de segmento SRv6. IANA tomó el bloque del registro de direcciones unicast IPv6 y lo registró en el IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry.

Propiedad Valor Bloque de direcciones 5f00::/16 Nombre Segment Routing (SRv6) SIDs RFC RFC 9602 Fecha de asignación 2024-04 Source True Destination True Forwardable True Globally Reachable False Reserved-by-Protocol False

El bloque 5f00::/16 se puede reenviar dentro de los dominios SR, pero está marcado explícitamente como no alcanzable globalmente: los paquetes con estas direcciones como destino no deben atravesar Internet.

Una jerarquía de asignación típica dentro del bloque:

5f00::/16                          <- Bloque SRv6 de IANA
  5f00:<dominio>::/32              <- Operador / dominio SR
    5f00:<dominio>:<nodo>::/48     <- Locator del nodo
      5f00:<dominio>:<nodo>:<func>::/64  <- SID (Locator + función)

docs.title: Prefijos GUA del operador vs 5f00::/16
docs.text:
El RFC 9602 no obliga a usar 5f00::/16. Los operadores pueden seguir usando sus propios prefijos globales (GUA) como Locators SRv6. Ambos enfoques son válidos:

Enfoque Origen del prefijo Ventajas Desventajas Bloque SRv6 de IANA 5f00::/16 Se reconoce al instante en capturas y ACLs; fácil de filtrar; no consume espacio GUA No es enrutable globalmente; requiere anunciarlo explícitamente por IGP/BGP dentro del dominio SR GUA del operador /32 o /48 del proveedor Ya es enrutable en la red del operador; sirve también para la alcanzabilidad IPv6 Consume espacio GUA; es más difícil distinguir el tráfico SRv6 del IPv6 normal

La mayoría de los primeros despliegues de SRv6 (China Mobile, SoftBank y otros) usan prefijos GUA del operador. El RFC 9602 ofrece una opción complementaria, especialmente útil en redes nuevas y en SRv6 entre dominios, donde un prefijo común y reconocible simplifica el filtrado.

docs.title: Filtrar 5f00::/16 en los bordes del dominio
docs.text:
Uses 5f00::/16 o tu propio GUA, debes evitar que los SIDs SRv6 se filtren fuera del dominio SR.

Cisco IOS-XRJuniper JunosLinux (ip6tables) 
prefix-set DENY-SRV6
  5f00::/16 le 128
end-set

route-policy EBGP-IN
  if destination in DENY-SRV6 then
    drop
  endif
end-policy

policy-options {
    prefix-list SRV6-SID-SPACE {
        5f00::/16;
    }
    policy-statement REJECT-SRV6 {
        term deny-srv6 {
            from prefix-list SRV6-SID-SPACE;
            then reject;
        }
    }
}

ip6tables -A FORWARD -d 5f00::/16 -j DROP

Si usas prefijos GUA del operador, aplica el mismo principio con el rango de tus Locators (ver también la sección 5.1 del RFC 8754).

docs.title: ¿Qué es SRv6?
docs.text:
Read in English · 日本語で読む

SRv6 (Segment Routing over IPv6, o Segment Routing sobre IPv6) es una arquitectura de red que usa el plano de datos de IPv6 para implementar enrutamiento de origen (source routing) y programación de red. También lo verás como IPv6 Segment Routing o Segment Routing v6: los tres nombres se refieren a la misma tecnología del IETF.

docs.title: IPv6 Segment Routing, Segment Routing v6, SRv6: una sola tecnología
docs.text:
Segment Routing (RFC 8402) es una arquitectura de enrutamiento de origen con dos planos de datos:

Nombre que verás Qué significa SRv6, Segment Routing over IPv6, IPv6 Segment Routing, Segment Routing v6, SR v6 Los segmentos son direcciones IPv6; la lista viaja en la dirección de destino y, cuando hace falta, en la Segment Routing Header (RFC 8754) SR-MPLS, Segment Routing MPLS Los segmentos son etiquetas MPLS en una pila de etiquetas (RFC 8660)

El "v6" de "Segment Routing v6" indica la versión de IP del plano de datos, no una sexta versión de Segment Routing. Las funciones del plano de control (extensiones de IS-IS/OSPFv3, Flex-Algo, TI-LFA, SR Policy) se comparten entre ambos, por eso la documentación de los fabricantes suele cubrirlos en una sola guía de "Segment Routing". La comparación lado a lado está en SRv6 vs SR-MPLS.

docs.title: Visión general
docs.text:
SRv6 codifica una lista de instrucciones, llamadas segmentos, en la cabecera del paquete IPv6. Cada segmento es una dirección IPv6 de 128 bits que representa una instrucción o un comportamiento específico de la red.

graph LR
    A[Origen] -->|Ruta SRv6| B[Nodo 1]
    B -->|Lista de segmentos| C[Nodo 2]
    C -->|End.DT4| D[Destino]

docs.title: Segmentos
docs.text:
Un segmento es una dirección IPv6 que codifica:

  • Locator (localizador): identifica al nodo dentro de la red
  • Function (función): especifica el comportamiento que se debe aplicar
  • Arguments (argumentos): parámetros opcionales para la función

Cada una de estas partes se explica en detalle en Estructura del SID.

docs.title: Enrutamiento de origen
docs.text: En SRv6, el nodo de origen (el nodo de entrada o ingress) define toda la ruta a través de la red al llenar la lista de segmentos. Los nodos intermedios solo procesan el segmento activo y reenvían el paquete.

docs.title: Ventajas
docs.text: Característica Descripción IPv6 nativo No necesita protocolos de overlay: usa IPv6 de forma nativa Programabilidad Los comportamientos de la red se definen mediante funciones SRv6 Simplificación Elimina los protocolos de señalización de MPLS (LDP, RSVP) Escalabilidad El espacio de SID de 128 bits soporta redes de gran escala Seguridad La SRH admite el TLV HMAC para autenticación

docs.title: Cómo funciona (versión simplificada)
docs.text:
1. El nodo de entrada recibe un paquete y determina la política SRv6 que le corresponde
  2. Encapsula el paquete con una cabecera IPv6 externa más una SRH
  3. Llena la lista de segmentos con la ruta deseada
  4. Los nodos de tránsito reenvían según la dirección IPv6 de destino
  5. Los nodos endpoint procesan el SID activo y ejecutan el comportamiento asociado
  6. El nodo de salida (egress) desencapsula y entrega el paquete original

Flujo simple de un paquete SRv6

Original:  [IPv4: 10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.0.2][Payload]

SRv6:      [IPv6: A::1 -> B::100]             <- IPv6 externa (DA = SID activo)
           [SRH: SL=1, [C::100, B::100]]       <- Lista de segmentos
           [IPv4: 10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.0.2]        <- Paquete original
           [Payload]

docs.title: SRv6 vs MPLS
docs.text: SRv6 cambia de fondo la forma de programar redes frente al MPLS tradicional. MPLS usa etiquetas de 20 bits con protocolos de señalización (LDP, RSVP-TE); SRv6 usa direcciones IPv6 de 128 bits como identificadores de segmento, lo que permite una red programable sin la complejidad de los overlays. La comparación completa está en SRv6 vs SR-MPLS.

docs.title: SRv6 vs SR-MPLS
docs.text:
Read in English · 日本語で読む

SRv6 y SR-MPLS implementan Segment Routing, pero usan planos de datos distintos. Esta es una comparación práctica.

docs.title: Tabla comparativa
docs.text:
Aspecto SR-MPLS SRv6 Plano de datos MPLS IPv6 Identificador de segmento Etiqueta de 20 bits Dirección IPv6 de 128 bits Espacio de SID ~1M de etiquetas Prácticamente ilimitado Encapsulación Pila de etiquetas MPLS SRH de SRv6 (cabecera de extensión IPv6) Programación de red Limitada Amplia (End, End.X, End.DT4…) Impacto en la MTU 4 bytes por etiqueta 40 B de IPv6 + 8 B + 16 B por SID Infraestructura existente Requiere reenvío MPLS Usa IPv6 nativo Señalización Ninguna (igual que SRv6) Ninguna Madurez Ampliamente desplegado En rápido crecimiento

La sobrecarga de SRv6 ya no es lo que era

La cifra de 16 bytes por SID corresponde a SRv6 clásico. Con uSID (RFC 9800) caben hasta 6 instrucciones en un solo contenedor de 16 bytes, lo que deja a SRv6 a la par o mejor que una pila de etiquetas MPLS. Ver uSID.

docs.title: Cuándo elegir cada uno
docs.text:
Elige SR-MPLS cuando...

  • Ya tienes infraestructura MPLS
  • La sobrecarga de MTU es una preocupación
  • Tu caso de uso es principalmente ingeniería de tráfico o VPN

Elige SRv6 cuando...

  • Estás construyendo una red nueva, nativa en IPv6
  • Necesitas programabilidad de red avanzada
  • La simplificación y la preparación para el futuro son prioridad
  • Quieres eliminar MPLS por completo

docs.title: uSID: compresión de SIDs en SRv6
docs.text:
Read in English · 日本語で読む

Una de las primeras críticas a SRv6 fue la sobrecarga: cada SID ocupa 128 bits (16 bytes), y una lista de 5 SIDs suma 80 bytes a cada paquete. El Micro-SID (uSID) lo resuelve empaquetando varias instrucciones de segmento en un solo SID de 128 bits.

docs.title: El problema
docs.text:
Con SRv6 clásico, cada salto de la lista de segmentos cuesta 16 bytes:

SRv6 clásico (5 SIDs = 80 bytes de sobrecarga):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SRH: lista de segmentos                       │
│   [0]: fc00:0:5::1  (16 bytes)               │
│   [1]: fc00:0:4::1  (16 bytes)               │
│   [2]: fc00:0:3::1  (16 bytes)               │
│   [3]: fc00:0:2::1  (16 bytes)               │
│   [4]: fc00:0:1::1  (16 bytes)               │
│                          Total: 80 bytes      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Para paquetes pequeños o tráfico sensible a la latencia, esta sobrecarga es importante.

docs.title: La solución: Micro-SID (uSID)
docs.text:
uSID (RFC 9800) empaqueta hasta 6 microinstrucciones en un solo contenedor de 128 bits:

Contenedor uSID (6 micro-SIDs = 16 bytes en total):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Una sola dirección IPv6 de 128 bits:          │
│                                               │
│  fcbb:bbbb:0001:0002:0003:0004:0005:0006    │
│  ├──┬────┤├──┤├──┤├──┤├──┤├──┤├──┤          │
│  │Bloque ││uS1││uS2││uS3││uS4││uS5││uS6│    │
│  │(32bit)││16b││16b││16b││16b││16b││16b│     │
│                          Total: 16 bytes      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Estructura
docs.text: Componente Tamaño Descripción Bloque uSID 32 bits Prefijo común a todos los uSIDs del dominio (por ejemplo, fcbb:bbbb) uSID 16 bits cada uno Microinstrucción individual que identifica un nodo y un comportamiento Fin de contenedor 16 bits (0000) Marca el final de los uSIDs activos en el contenedor

docs.title: Cómo funciona
docs.text:
Procesar un contenedor uSID es una operación sencilla de desplazar y buscar (shift-and-lookup):

Paso 1 - El ingress recibe:
  DA = fcbb:bbbb:0001:0002:0003:0000:0000:0000
                  ^^^^
                  uSID activo → Nodo 1

Paso 2 - El Nodo 1 procesa el uSID 0001 y desplaza a la izquierda:
  DA = fcbb:bbbb:0002:0003:0000:0000:0000:0000
                  ^^^^
                  uSID activo → Nodo 2

Paso 3 - El Nodo 2 procesa el uSID 0002 y desplaza a la izquierda:
  DA = fcbb:bbbb:0003:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000
                  ^^^^
                  uSID activo → Nodo 3

Paso 4 - El Nodo 3 procesa el uSID 0003 y desplaza a la izquierda:
  DA = fcbb:bbbb:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000
                  ^^^^
                  Fin de contenedor (0000) → pasar a la siguiente entrada de la SRH

docs.title: Comparación de sobrecarga
docs.text:
Escenario SRv6 clásico uSID Ahorro 3 SIDs 48 bytes 16 bytes 67% 6 SIDs 96 bytes 16 bytes 83% 10 SIDs 160 bytes 32 bytes (2 contenedores) 80% 12 SIDs 192 bytes 32 bytes (2 contenedores) 83%

6 saltos en 16 bytes

Un solo contenedor uSID codifica hasta 6 instrucciones de segmento en el mismo espacio que SRv6 clásico usa para 1 solo SID. Con esto, la sobrecarga de SRv6 queda a la par o por debajo de una pila de etiquetas MPLS.

docs.title: uSID vs G-SRv6
docs.text:
Surgieron dos enfoques de compresión, hoy unificados en el RFC 9800:

Aspecto uSID (NEXT-C-SID) G-SRv6 (REPLACE-C-SID) Origen Cisco, Bell Canada China Mobile, Huawei Procesamiento Desplazar y buscar Reemplazar y buscar Tamaño del uSID 16 o 32 bits 16 o 32 bits RFC RFC 9800 RFC 9800 Adopción Varios operadores globales Varios operadores globales

Ambos están estandarizados en el RFC 9800 (compresión de SIDs SRv6), lo que garantiza la interoperabilidad.

docs.title: Ejemplos de configuración
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRLinux (iproute2) 
segment-routing
 srv6
  locators
   locator uSID-MAIN
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fcbb:bb01::/48
   !
  !
 !
!

# Encapsular con un contenedor uSID
ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 encap seg6 mode encap \
  segs fcbb:bbbb:0001:0002:0003:: dev eth0

docs.title: Conformance Testing: IPv6 Ready SRv6 Logo
docs.text:
The IPv6 Forum's IPv6 Ready Logo program added SRv6 as a test category for routers (Logo ID letter "R"). It tests conformance against RFC 8402, RFC 8754 and RFC 8986 — SRv6 only, not SR-MPLS.

Logo Scope Launched SRv6 Silver Conformance (SRH flags/TLVs, HMAC, Segments Left and Hop Limit handling, PMTU, SID arguments, End.X/End.T, ...) March 2025 SRv6 Gold Conformance + multi-vendor interoperability September 2025

The test specifications (developed by UNH-IOL, CNLabs and BII) are public on the IPv6 Ready SRv6 resources page. When comparing platforms, an SRv6 logo is useful evidence of baseline RFC compliance, but it does not cover uSID/C-SID, control-plane extensions, or service behaviors beyond the specs.

Contribute your experience

Running SRv6 on a platform not listed here? We'd love your contribution!

docs.title: SRv6 on Arista EOS
docs.text:
Arista EOS implements SRv6 with a uSID-first design: the forwarding model is built around micro-SIDs in the F3216 format (32-bit block, 16-bit uSIDs), starting with the uN node SID and adding static uA adjacency SIDs, IS-IS integration, counters, and hitless upgrade support over the 4.35 and 4.36 release trains. The authors of OpenAI's MRC AI-cluster transport collaborated with Arista to implement SRv6 in EOS on Broadcom Tomahawk 5 switches, and MRC runs in large-scale production — see AI/ML Networks.

Source scope

This page summarizes Arista's public EOS user manual (EOS 4.36.2F) and the titles/summaries of Arista's public SRv6 TOI (Technical Overview of Information) listings. Full TOI documents require an Arista login; check them and the release notes for your exact version before deploying.

docs.title: Feature Timeline
docs.text: Feature EOS release Source uN (End with uSID) Before 4.35.2F (base support referenced by the uA TOI) TOI listing Static SRv6 adjacency segments (uA) 4.35.2F TOI: "Support for SRv6 static adjacency segments (uA)" IS-IS SRv6 with micro-SID compression, Flex-Algo, and TI-LFA 4.36.1F TOI: "Support for SRv6 in IS-IS" Smart System Upgrade (SSU) with SRv6 uN 4.36.1F TOI: "SSU support for SRv6" Per-endpoint counters (packets/bytes per endpoint operation, e.g. uN) 4.36.2F TOI: "Support for SRv6 Counters"

docs.text:
The show srv6 capabilities example in the user manual reports:

Category Supported Not supported Endpoint behaviors End (uN when used with uSIDs), End.DT4, End.DT6 End.X, End.DX4, End.DX6 Flavors PSP, USD, Next-CSID USP Headend behaviors H.Encaps H.Encaps.Red, H.Insert, H.Insert.Red uSID formats F3216 —

Note

Static uA support (an End.X-type adjacency micro-SID) is documented separately in the uA TOI for EOS 4.35.2F and later, so treat the capability table as a snapshot of the manual's example rather than a complete feature list.

docs.text:
Family Models listed in the user manual 7060X6 DCS-7060X6 7280R3 / R4 DCS-7280R3, DCS-7280R4-32*, DCS-7280R4K-32*, DCS-7282R4* 7500R3 DCS-7500R3 7800R3 / R4 DCS-7800R3, DCS-7800R4-*, DCS-7800R4K-36PE-LC, DCS-7800R4M-36PE-LC, DCS-DL-7700R4K-*

On the R3/R4 (Jericho-family) platforms, SRv6 needs a TCAM profile with the feature srv usid f3216 feature; the 7060X6 is not listed for that requirement.

docs.title: Configuration Model
docs.text:
The manual organizes SRv6 under router srv6:

Command Purpose router srv6 → vrf default SRv6 configuration context micro-segment domain → block, usid length, gib range Defines the uSID block, uSID length, and Global ID Block range locator → prefix micro-segment domain <d> end usid <v> Allocates the node's uN from the domain igp algorithm flex-algo <name> Associates a locator with a Flex-Algo show srv6 capabilities / domain / locator / routes Verification ping srv6 sid … via segment-list …, traceroute srv6 sid … SRv6 OAM

See the user manual for complete configuration examples; exact syntax varies between EOS releases.

OAM gotcha

The manual notes that the target uN prefix (for example the /48) must be configured on a loopback for ping srv6 / traceroute srv6 to that uN to work.

docs.title: SRv6 with Cilium (eBPF)
docs.text:
Cilium is an open-source, eBPF-based networking solution for Kubernetes that brings SRv6 into the cloud-native world. Instead of relying on the kernel's routing stack, Cilium programs eBPF maps in the kernel data path — enabling SRv6 encapsulation and decapsulation at line rate without context switching.

Minimum version

SRv6 L3VPN support requires Cilium 1.13+ (alpha). Production-ready use is recommended on Cilium 1.15+.

docs.title: Why Cilium + SRv6?
docs.text:
Traditional SRv6 implementations (Cisco, Juniper, FRRouting) live on routers. Cilium extends the SRv6 fabric into the Kubernetes node — each worker node becomes an SRv6 endpoint with its own locator, SIDs, and BGP session.

graph TB
    subgraph K8s Cluster A
        P1[Pod] --> N1["K8s Node\n(Cilium agent\n+ eBPF SRv6)"]
    end
    subgraph SRv6 Fabric
        R1[PE Router] <-->|"BGP VPNv4/v6\nSRv6 SIDs"| N1
        R1 <-->|"IS-IS/OSPFv3"| R2[P Router]
        R2 <-->|"BGP VPNv4/v6\nSRv6 SIDs"| N2
    end
    subgraph K8s Cluster B
        N2["K8s Node\n(Cilium agent\n+ eBPF SRv6)"] --> P2[Pod]
    end
    style P1 fill:#1b5e2026,stroke:#1b5e20
    style P2 fill:#1b5e2026,stroke:#1b5e20

This makes each K8s node a first-class SRv6 PE — pod traffic is natively encapsulated into SRv6 by eBPF before it leaves the NIC, integrating seamlessly with a carrier-grade SRv6 underlay.

docs.title: Supported SRv6 Behaviors
docs.text: Behavior Role in Cilium Status H.Encaps Egress: encapsulate pod traffic into SRv6 1.13+ End.DT4 Ingress: decapsulate SRv6 → IPv4 VRF lookup 1.13+ End.DT6 Ingress: decapsulate SRv6 → IPv6 VRF lookup 1.13+ H.Encaps.Red Reduced encapsulation (no SRH when single SID) 1.15+

docs.title: How Cilium Implements SRv6 with eBPF
docs.text:
Cilium programs four eBPF maps per node that together implement the SRv6 data plane:

eBPF Map Key Value Purpose cilium_srv6_vrf Source IP + VRF ID SRv6 locator Maps pod traffic to a VRF cilium_srv6_policy Destination CIDR + VRF Egress SID Selects the SRv6 SID for encapsulation cilium_srv6_sid SRv6 SID VRF table ID Maps incoming SIDs to a local VRF for decapsulation cilium_srv6_state Flow state — Tracks active SRv6 flows for telemetry

At egress, the eBPF TC program looks up the destination in cilium_srv6_policy, prepends the SRv6 outer header (H.Encaps), and sends the packet into the underlay.

At ingress, the eBPF XDP program matches the destination SID against cilium_srv6_sid, strips the SRv6 header, and injects the inner packet into the correct VRF (End.DT4 / End.DT6).

docs.title: BGP Control Plane
docs.text:
Cilium uses an integrated BGP control plane (backed by GoBGP or FRRouting) to:

  • Advertise the node's SRv6 locator prefix to PE routers
  • Exchange VPNv4/VPNv6 routes with route targets for L3VPN
  • Receive remote SIDs and program them into cilium_srv6_policy

No external router daemon required — Cilium manages BGP sessions directly via CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy CRDs.

docs.title: One BGP Session — All VRFs
docs.text:
Common misconception

Cilium does not open one BGP session per VRF, nor does it use BGP EVPN (L2VPN AFI 25). It behaves exactly like a traditional PE router: one BGP session per peer, carrying routes for all VRFs simultaneously over the VPNv6 address family (AFI 2 / SAFI 128).

A single CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy neighbor entry covers every tenant/VRF on that node:

Cilium Node (worker-1)  ←──── 1 TCP session (port 179) ────→  PE Router
                                         │
                         BGP UPDATE messages contain:
                         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                         │ AFI 2 / SAFI 128 (VPNv6)               │
                         │                                         │
                         │  RD 65100:100 | RT 65000:100           │
                         │    prefix: 10.0.1.0/24                  │
                         │    next-hop SRv6 SID: fc00:0:10::dt6:100│ ← VRF Tenant-A
                         │                                         │
                         │  RD 65100:200 | RT 65000:200           │
                         │    prefix: 10.0.2.0/24                  │
                         │    next-hop SRv6 SID: fc00:0:10::dt6:200│ ← VRF Tenant-B
                         │                                         │
                         │  RD 65100:300 | RT 65000:300           │
                         │    prefix: 10.0.3.0/24                  │
                         │    next-hop SRv6 SID: fc00:0:10::dt6:300│ ← VRF Tenant-C
                         └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

The PE router uses the Route Target (RT) to import each prefix into the correct VRF — no separate BGP session needed.

docs.title: VPNv6 vs BGP EVPN — Key Differences
docs.text:
Both can carry L3 reachability for SRv6 tenants, but they are completely different address families:

BGP VPNv6 (Cilium) BGP EVPN Type 5 AFI / SAFI 2 / 128 25 / 70 NLRI type VPNv6 prefix + RD EVPN Route Type 5 (IP Prefix) Original purpose MPLS L3VPN (adapted for SRv6) L2VPN, extended to L3 via Type 5 Next-hop encoding SRv6 SID as BGP next-hop SRv6 SID in Tunnel Encap attribute VRF signaling Route Target extended community Route Target extended community MAC/L2 info None — L3 only Carries MAC+IP (Type 2) Valid for SRv6 L3VPN? Yes Yes (RFC 9252 §5) Cilium uses it? Yes No (implementation choice)

Both are valid for SRv6 L3VPN — but Cilium only speaks VPNv6

EVPN Type 5 (IP Prefix routes) over SRv6 is fully valid per RFC 9252 and widely deployed in carrier and DC fabrics. However, Cilium's BGP control plane does not implement AFI 25 / SAFI 70 (L2VPN EVPN). It only negotiates VPNv6 (AFI 2 / SAFI 128). If your SRv6 fabric uses EVPN Type 5 for L3VPN, Cilium cannot peer directly with those PE routers.

docs.title: Interoperability Gap: Cilium ↔ EVPN Fabrics
docs.text:
This is a real-world limitation. If your network already runs EVPN Type 5 over SRv6 (common in DC fabrics using SONiC, Juniper, or Cisco NCS), you have three options:

Option How Trade-off Route Reflector translation Deploy an RR (e.g. FRRouting) between Cilium and the PE. The RR peers with Cilium via VPNv6 and re-advertises towards the fabric via EVPN Type 5 Extra hop in control plane; RR becomes a dependency Dual address-family on the PE Configure the PE to peer with Cilium using VPNv6 and continue using EVPN with the rest of the fabric Requires PE support; routes must be redistributed between AFIs on the PE Wait for Cilium EVPN support EVPN is on the Cilium roadmap but not yet implemented for SRv6 No ETA as of Cilium 1.15 
graph LR
    C["Cilium Node
VPNv6 only
AFI 2/128"] -->|"VPNv6"| RR["Route Reflector
FRRouting
(bridge)"]
    RR -->|"EVPN Type 5
AFI 25/70"| PE["PE Router
EVPN fabric"]

docs.title: Enable SRv6 via Helm
docs.text:
helm install cilium cilium/cilium \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set bgpControlPlane.enabled=true \
  --set srv6.enabled=true \
  --set srv6.encapMode=srh        # or "reduced" for H.Encaps.Red

For Cilium 1.15+ with reduced encapsulation (recommended for production):

# values.yaml
bgpControlPlane:
  enabled: true

srv6:
  enabled: true
  encapMode: reduced    # uses H.Encaps.Red — no SRH when single SID

helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium -f values.yaml -n kube-system

docs.title: Step 1 — Assign a Locator to Each Node
docs.text:
Label each K8s node with its SRv6 locator prefix. Cilium allocates individual SIDs from this block for End.DT4 / End.DT6 behaviors.

kubectl label node worker-1 cilium.io/srv6-locator=fc00:0:10::/48
kubectl label node worker-2 cilium.io/srv6-locator=fc00:0:11::/48

docs.title: Step 2 — BGP Peering Policy
docs.text:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1
kind: CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy
metadata:
  name: srv6-peering
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      kubernetes.io/os: linux
  virtualRouters:
    - localASN: 65100
      exportPodCIDR: false          # pod CIDRs go via SRv6 L3VPN, not plain BGP
      neighbors:
        - peerAddress: "fc00:0:1::1/128"   # PE router SID/loopback
          peerASN: 65000
          families:
            - afi: ipv6
              safi: unicast
            - afi: ipv6
              safi: vpn-unicast     # VPNv6 for SRv6 L3VPN
      srv6:
        locatorPrefix: "fc00:0:10::/48"    # this node's SRv6 locator

docs.title: Step 3 — L3VPN (VRF) Mapping
docs.text:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1
kind: CiliumBGPAdvertisement
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-vpn
spec:
  advertisements:
    - advertisementType: "PodCIDR"
      service:
        addresses:
          - ClusterIP
      attributes:
        community:
          standard:
            - "65000:100"            # route target for Tenant A VRF

docs.title: Step 4 — Verify SRv6 State
docs.text:
# Check Cilium SRv6 is active
cilium status | grep -i srv6

# Inspect eBPF SRv6 maps
cilium bpf srv6 list

# Check BGP session state
cilium bgp peers

# Verify advertised/received SRv6 SIDs
cilium bgp routes advertised ipv6 vpn-unicast
cilium bgp routes received  ipv6 vpn-unicast

docs.title: Full Traffic Walk
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Pod as Pod A (10.0.1.5)
    participant eBPF as eBPF TC (egress)
    participant Fab as SRv6 Fabric
    participant eBPFr as eBPF XDP (ingress)
    participant PodB as Pod B (10.0.2.7)

    Pod->>eBPF: IPv4 packet → 10.0.2.7
    eBPF->>eBPF: lookup cilium_srv6_policy<br/>→ SID fc00:0:11::dt4
    eBPF->>Fab: SRv6 packet<br/>[fc00:0:11::dt4][IPv4: 10.0.2.7]
    Fab->>eBPFr: Deliver to worker-2<br/>DST = fc00:0:11::dt4
    eBPFr->>eBPFr: lookup cilium_srv6_sid<br/>→ VRF table 100
    eBPFr->>eBPFr: End.DT4: strip SRv6 header<br/>inject inner IPv4 into VRF 100
    eBPFr->>PodB: IPv4 packet → 10.0.2.7

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Cilium exports SRv6 telemetry via Hubble (Cilium's observability layer):

# Install Hubble CLI
hubble observe --type l3 --protocol SRv6

# Flow-level SRv6 visibility
hubble observe --namespace default \
  --output json | jq 'select(.destination.srv6_sid != null)'

Key Prometheus metrics exported:

Metric Description cilium_srv6_encap_total Total SRv6 encapsulations by VRF cilium_srv6_decap_total Total SRv6 decapsulations by behavior cilium_srv6_drop_total SRv6 drops (no policy match, invalid SID) cilium_bgp_session_state BGP session state per peer

docs.title: SRv6 on Cisco IOS-XE
docs.text: SRv6 on Cisco has long been an IOS-XR story (NCS, ASR 9000, Cisco 8000). That changed with IOS-XE 26.1: Cisco's enterprise/edge operating system now ships validated SRv6 uSID support, documented in the 2026 CVD Quantum-Safe SRv6 Fabric for Mission-Critical Networks. This brings SRv6 to the WAN-edge and branch platforms that historically terminated SD-WAN or DMVPN.

docs.title: Supported Platforms (validated in the CVD)
docs.text:
• Cisco 8000 Series Secure Routers (G2): 8161-G2 (compact edge), 8375-E-G2 / 8475-G2 (branch/campus edge), 8550-G2 / 8570-G2 (aggregation hubs)
  • Catalyst 8000 edge family (SR-TE/ePBR feature lineage)

docs.title: Feature Highlights
docs.text: Feature IOS-XE support uSID format F3216 only (format usid-f3216) — 32-bit block, 16-bit node, 16-bit function Headend encapsulation H.Encaps.Red (reduced) End behaviors uN, uA, uDT4, uDT6, uDT46, End.DTMC4 (multicast VRF decap) L3VPN SID allocation alloc-mode per-vrf only — per-prefix allocation is not supported IGP IS-IS with multi-topology IPv6, wide metrics SR-TE Per-Destination and Per-Flow policies, ODN/Automated Steering, ePBR + NBAR classification Flex-Algo Yes, with per-algorithm locators TI-LFA Yes, with node-protecting / SRLG-disjoint / linecard-disjoint tiebreakers Performance measurement Two-way active probes, delay advertisement into IS-IS, liveness detection Multicast BGP MVPN with SRv6 ingress replication (srv6-mcast ingress-replication partitioned)

docs.title: Basic Configuration
docs.text:
! SRv6 process: encapsulation source + F3216 locator
segment-routing srv6
 encapsulation
  source-address FC00::1
  traffic-class propagate
 locators
  locator MAIN
   prefix FCBB:DEAD:1::/48
   format usid-f3216

! IS-IS underlay — multi-topology IPv6 + locator advertisement
router isis 1
 net 49.0000.fc00.0001.00
 is-type level-2-only
 metric-style wide
 advertise link attributes
 distribute link-state
 !
 address-family ipv6
  multi-topology
  router-id Loopback0
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
   level-2
  fast-reroute ti-lfa level-2

! L3VPN over SRv6 (per-VRF Service SID)
router bgp 65001
 segment-routing srv6
  locator MAIN
 !
 address-family vpnv4
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
   alloc-mode per-vrf
  neighbor FC00::3 activate
  neighbor FC00::3 send-community extended

Ethernet interfaces must be point-to-point

IOS-XE treats Ethernet as broadcast by default, which creates IS-IS pseudonodes that silently break adjacency-SID allocation and SR-TE path computation. isis network point-to-point on every SRv6 core interface is non-negotiable.

Per-VRF allocation only

Unlike IOS-XR, IOS-XE supports only alloc-mode per-vrf for L3VPN Service SIDs — one uDT4/uDT6 per VRF, with the egress doing a full VRF lookup after decapsulation. Per-prefix mode does not exist.

docs.title: SRv6 on FRRouting (FRR)
docs.text: FRRouting is an open-source routing suite that provides SRv6 support through its IS-IS and BGP daemons.

docs.title: SRv6 Support Status
docs.text:
Feature Status FRR Version IS-IS SRv6 locator 8.4+ BGP SRv6 VPN 8.4+ SRv6 static SIDs 10.3+ SRv6 uSID (uA, headend behaviors, BGP uSID instructions) 10.4+ Multiple SRv6 locators / locator per VRF 10.5+ MPLS and SRv6 coexistence on the same L3VRF 10.5+ Global (default-VRF) IPv4/IPv6 unicast over SRv6 core (RFC 9252) 10.6+ EVPN with IPv6 VTEPs 10.6+ BGP-LS (RFC 9552) with SRv6 extensions (RFC 9514) 10.7+ Shared uDT46 SID for the global table 10.7+ SRv6 TE Policy In dev

Recent FRR releases have steadily closed the uSID gap: 10.3 (March 2025) added SRv6 static SIDs, 10.4 (July 2025) added uSID behaviors — uA, additional headend behaviors, BGP uSID instructions, and the seg6local uSID flavor — and 10.5 (November 2025) added multiple-locator support, per-VRF locator selection, and MPLS/SRv6 coexistence for migration scenarios.

FRR 10.6 (March 2026) extends SRv6 beyond VPNs: BGP can now carry global IPv4 and IPv6 unicast over an SRv6 core in the default VRF, the "Global IPv4/IPv6 over SRv6 Core" services of RFC 9252. The same release adds IPv6 VTEP support across the EVPN code, backward compatible with IPv4 VTEPs. Per the implementing pull request, the default-VRF service uses DT4/DT6 SIDs and requires the sr0 interface to install the DT routes because of a kernel limitation.

FRR 10.7 (July 2026) brings FRR into controller-driven SRv6 TE: it adds BGP-LS (RFC 9552) with the SRv6 extensions of RFC 9514 — SRv6 Capabilities and Locator TLVs, SRv6 SID NLRI for End, End.X and LAN End.X SIDs, and the Endpoint Behavior and SID Structure TLVs. Static SRv6 SIDs configured in zebra can be exported into BGP-LS so a TE controller sees them. The 10.7 changelog also adds a single uDT46 SID for the global table as an alternative to separate uDT4/uDT6 SIDs.

docs.title: Global table over SRv6 (10.6+)
docs.text:
router bgp 65001
 segment-routing srv6
  locator MAIN
 exit
 neighbor 2001:db8::2 remote-as 65001
 !
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  sid export auto
  neighbor 2001:db8::2 activate
  neighbor 2001:db8::2 encapsulation-srv6
 exit-address-family

sid export (default VRF only) allocates the global-table service SID; compare sid vpn export for L3VPN. encapsulation-srv6 makes BGP attach the Prefix-SID attribute toward that neighbor (encapsulation-srv6-relax sends routes with and without it). Command names are from the FRR 10.6 BGP user guide — check the docs for your release before deploying.

docs.title: Configuration Example
docs.text:
! Enable SRv6 in IS-IS
router isis CORE
 segment-routing srv6
  locator MAIN
 exit

! Define SRv6 locator
segment-routing
 srv6
  locators
   locator MAIN
    prefix fc00:0:1::/48 block-len 32 node-len 16 func-bits 16
   exit
  exit
 exit

docs.title: SRv6 on Juniper Junos
docs.text:
Juniper implements SRv6 in Junos OS (MX Series) and Junos OS Evolved (PTX and ACX7000 Series), with both full-length (classic) SIDs and micro-SIDs (uSID, the RFC 9800 NEXT-CSID flavor). This guide walks through a complete uSID deployment — locator, IS-IS, L3VPN and Internet services, Flex-Algo and TI-LFA — following the structure of Juniper's validated design for SRv6 core and edge, and shows the commands to verify each step.

Juniper Validated Design

The JVD for Service Provider SRv6 Core and Edge was qualified on Junos 24.4R2 and Junos Evolved 24.4R2 with MX480 (MPC7E, MPC10E), MX10004 (LC9600), MX2010 (MPC11E), MX304 and PTX10002-36QDD. It uses uSID only (F3216 format, blocks from 5f00::/16), Flex-Algo 0/128/129, TI-LFA with microloop avoidance, uDT46 L3VPN and uDX2 EVPN-VPWS.

docs.title: Platforms and Releases
docs.text:
Capability Junos OS (MX) Junos OS Evolved SRv6 in IS-IS, classic SIDs 20.3R1 (MX240/480/960/2000; MPC7E/8E/9E or newer) PTX10002-36QDD 24.2R2, PTX10008 24.4R1-S2 L3 services over SRv6 (BGP) 20.4R1 (MX and vMX); MX304 22.2R3; MX10004 22.3R1 PTX10002-36QDD 24.2R2; PTX10008 24.4R1-S2 uSID in IS-IS transport 23.4R1 (MX204 through MX10016) PTX10008 24.4R1-S2 uSID with L3VPN and IS-IS on ACX — ACX7024/7100/7509 23.2R1; ACX7024X/7332/7348 23.4R1 uSID with TI-LFA, microloop avoidance, Flex-Algo 23.4R1 ACX7024X/7348 24.2R1 SRv6 Flex-Algo Classic SIDs by 21.2R1 (inter-level leaking); uSID 23.4R1 ACX7024/7100/7509 23.1R1 SRv6 microloop avoidance (IS-IS) 21.1R1 PTX10002-36QDD 24.4R1

Release numbers are the "introduced" values from Juniper Feature Explorer; check it for your exact platform and line card. cRPD supports SRv6 in IS-IS and L3 services in BGP with limitations (no flavor or Flex-Algo options on End SIDs, no ARM64). There is no official SRv6 support statement for vJunos-router.

docs.title: Building Blocks
docs.text:
Junos object Hierarchy What it is Block routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 block The uSID block (default 32 bits, the only length on ACX), with global (GIB) and local (LIB) ID ranges Locator routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 locator The node's /48 (with micro-sid) or classic locator; can be bound to a Flex-Algo uN / End SID protocols isis source-packet-routing srv6 locator <name> micro-node-sid Advertised by IS-IS; without it the local locator is not even installed uA / End.X SID protocols isis interface <ifl> level 2 srv6-adjacency-segment Per-adjacency SID, protected or unprotected Service SID routing-instances <vrf> protocols bgp source-packet-routing srv6 locator <name> uDT4/uDT6/uDT46 (or End.DT4/6/46) per VRF

The default uSID length is 16 bits. In each block the GIB defaults to 0x0000–0xDFFF (static) and the LIB to 0xE000–0xFFFF (dynamic). With no flavor configured, micro-sid SIDs use PSP and USD.

docs.title: Step 1: Platform Prerequisites (MX)
docs.text:
set chassis network-services enhanced-ip
set routing-options resolution preserve-nexthop-hierarchy
set routing-options forwarding-table srv6-chain-merge

enhanced-ip is needed on MX only. The other two enable the chained, hierarchical next-hop structures that SRv6 services resolve through; the JVD sets them on every router.

docs.title: Step 2: uSID Block and Locator
docs.text:
The example uses the IANA SRv6 SID block 5f00::/16 (RFC 9602), block 5f00::/32 and node 1 = 5f00:0:1::/48 (F3216: 32-bit block, 16-bit node uSID, 16-bit function).

set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 block BLK0 5f00::/32
set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 block BLK0 local-micro-sid maximum-static-sids 2000
set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC0 5f00:0:1::/48
set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC0 micro-sid block-name BLK0

maximum-static-sids reserves part of the LIB for statically configured service SIDs. By default the static LIB range is empty, so any static micro-dt46-sid value would fail to commit. Changing GIB/LIB sizes later is disruptive (it requires restarting routing, and dynamic SIDs can change), so size it up front. Use the same block on every router; uSID compression only works between nodes that share a block.

Classic (full-length) SIDs instead of uSID 

set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 locator myloc 2001:db8:0:a0::/64
set protocols isis source-packet-routing srv6 locator myloc end-sid 2001:db8:0:a0:d01:: flavor usd
set protocols isis interface xe-0/0/0:0.0 level 2 srv6-adjacency-segment protected locator myloc end-x-sid 2001:db8:0:a0:1a01:: flavor psp
End and End.X SIDs must fall inside the locator prefix or the commit fails. Encapsulation defaults to a reduced SRH; set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 no-reduced-srh restores the full SRH (on ACX7000 this restarts the PFE).

docs.title: Step 3: IS-IS
docs.text:
set protocols isis interface et-0/0/0.0 point-to-point
set protocols isis interface et-0/0/0.0 level 2 srv6-adjacency-segment unprotected locator LOC0 micro-adjacency-sid
set protocols isis interface lo0.0 passive
set protocols isis source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC0 micro-node-sid
set protocols isis level 1 disable
set protocols isis level 2 wide-metrics-only
  • micro-node-sid advertises the locator and the uN SID (RFC 9352 SRv6 Locator TLV). The locator must be configured under IS-IS even if you only want SRv6 for L3VPN.
  • micro-adjacency-sid with no value allocates a dynamic uA from the LIB. The JVD uses unprotected uA SIDs and relies on TI-LFA to protect uN SIDs and prefixes.
  • IS-IS multi-topology (set protocols isis topologies ipv6-unicast) is not required. The JVD only uses it during migration, so IPv4 SR-MPLS and IPv6 SRv6 topologies can differ.

docs.title: Step 4: L3VPN over SRv6
docs.text:
On each PE, assign a service SID per VRF and enable SRv6 service signaling on the BGP families.

# VRF with a dynamic uDT46 SID (End.DT46 with NEXT-CSID)
set routing-instances CUST-A instance-type vrf
set routing-instances CUST-A interface ge-0/0/2.0
set routing-instances CUST-A route-distinguisher 192.0.2.1:100
set routing-instances CUST-A vrf-target target:65000:100
set routing-instances CUST-A protocols bgp source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC0 micro-dt46-sid
#   or a static value from the LIB static range:  ... micro-dt46-sid 0xfc30
#   or per address family:                         ... micro-dt4-sid / micro-dt6-sid
#   classic SIDs:                                  ... locator myloc end-dt4-sid / end-dt6-sid / end-dt46-sid <sid>

# IBGP to the route reflectors (IPv6 transport)
set protocols bgp group RR type internal
set protocols bgp group RR local-address 2001:db8:ff::11
set protocols bgp group RR family inet-vpn unicast extended-nexthop
set protocols bgp group RR family inet-vpn unicast advertise-srv6-service
set protocols bgp group RR family inet-vpn unicast accept-srv6-service
set protocols bgp group RR family inet6-vpn unicast advertise-srv6-service
set protocols bgp group RR family inet6-vpn unicast accept-srv6-service
set protocols bgp group RR family route-target nexthop-resolution no-resolution
set protocols bgp group RR neighbor 2001:db8:ff::1
set protocols bgp rfc8950-compliant
set protocols bgp multipath list-nexthop

How it resolves: with SRv6 services enabled, Junos ignores the BGP NEXT_HOP for resolution and resolves the route on the locator inside the SRv6 SID, which IS-IS has installed in inet6.3 as an SRV6-ISIS route. No resolution rib tweaks are needed. Two details matter in practice:

  • extended-nexthop and rfc8950-compliant make VPN-IPv4 routes carry IPv6 next hops in the standard (RFC 8950) encoding, which matters for interoperability with other vendors.
  • Route-target (RT-constraint) routes otherwise stay hidden, because the PE loopbacks exist only in inet6.0. nexthop-resolution no-resolution fixes this.

The per-VRF SID is advertised in the BGP Prefix-SID attribute (SRv6 L3 Service TLV) with the function bits transposed into the label field, as described in RFC 9252. Inter-AS Option C works over SRv6; Option B over SRv6 is not supported. For SIDs learned only via BGP (no IGP route to the remote locator), Junos 24.2R1+ on MX can use routing-options dynamic-tunnels <name> srv6.

docs.title: Internet (Global Table) over SRv6
docs.text:
set protocols bgp source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC0 micro-dt46-sid
set protocols bgp group RR family inet unicast extended-nexthop
set protocols bgp group RR family inet unicast advertise-srv6-service
set protocols bgp group RR family inet unicast accept-srv6-service
set protocols bgp group RR family inet6 unicast advertise-srv6-service
set protocols bgp group RR family inet6 unicast accept-srv6-service

Filter your SID block at the border

The JVD filters 5f00::/16 (and more-specifics) on eBGP sessions. If another AS can inject routes covering your SID space, it can attract SRv6-encapsulated VPN traffic. See Security.

docs.title: Step 5: Flex-Algo
docs.text:
A Flex-Algo needs a definition, IS-IS participation and its own locator. Services pick the algorithm through the locator their SID comes from.

# Algorithm 128 = low-latency
set routing-options flex-algorithm 128 definition metric-type delay-metric
set routing-options flex-algorithm 128 definition spf
set protocols isis source-packet-routing flex-algorithm 128

# Locator for algorithm 128, in its own /32 block
set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 block BLK128 5f00:a1::/32
set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC128 5f00:a1:1::/48
set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC128 algorithm 128
set routing-options source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC128 micro-sid block-name BLK128
set protocols isis source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC128 micro-node-sid
set protocols isis interface et-0/0/0.0 level 2 srv6-adjacency-segment unprotected locator LOC128 micro-adjacency-sid

# Option A: the whole VRF uses the low-latency locator
set routing-instances CUST-LL protocols bgp source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC128 micro-dt46-sid

# Option B: allocate a second SID in a VRF and select it per prefix by policy
set routing-instances CUST-A protocols bgp source-packet-routing srv6 locator LOC128 micro-dt46-sid non-default
set policy-options community VOICE members 65000:911
set policy-options policy-statement LL-PREFIXES term VOICE from community VOICE
set policy-options policy-statement LL-PREFIXES term VOICE then srv6 locator LOC128 micro-dt46-sid
set policy-options policy-statement LL-PREFIXES term VOICE then accept
set protocols bgp group RR export LL-PREFIXES

In option B the VRF advertises its default SID for most prefixes, and the export policy on the IBGP group swaps in the algorithm-128 SID for the matching ones, so remote PEs reach those prefixes over the low-latency topology.

Delay-based algorithms need link delay: enable delay-measurement on the IS-IS interfaces (TWAMP Light), and advertise it as an application-specific link attribute for Flex-Algo. IS-IS installs SIDs of non-zero algorithms in inet6color.0. On Junos, Flex-Algo participation applies to SR-MPLS and SRv6 together — you cannot define an algorithm for SRv6 only. See Flex-Algorithm.

docs.title: Step 6: TI-LFA and Microloop Avoidance
docs.text:
set protocols isis backup-spf-options use-post-convergence-lfa
set protocols isis backup-spf-options use-source-packet-routing
set protocols isis interface et-0/0/0.0 level 2 post-convergence-lfa
set protocols isis interface et-0/0/0.0 level 2 post-convergence-lfa node-protection cost 16777214
set protocols isis spf-options microloop-avoidance post-convergence-path delay 5000

Link protection is the default once post-convergence-lfa is on an interface. The JVD adds node protection with a very high cost, so the node-protecting path is preferred but a link-protecting backup is still used when no node-protecting path exists. uSID-based TI-LFA, microloop avoidance and Flex-Algo protection arrived in Junos 23.4R1. SRLG is not considered for SRv6 TI-LFA. The JVD measured worst-case link-failure convergence around 5 ms. See TI-LFA for the algorithm.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Command What to look for show isis overview SRv6: Enabled, the locator and algorithm, micro-node-SID … Flavor: PSP, USD, post-convergence backup and microloop avoidance state show isis adjacency extensive SRv6 unprotected END-X-SID … with its flavor, per adjacency show isis database <router> extensive \| find SRv6 SRv6 Locator TLV (MTID, algorithm), uN SID with block/node lengths, SRv6 MSDs, End.X SIDs show srv6 block BLK0 GIB/LIB ranges, static and dynamic SID counts show route table inet6.3 protocol isis Remote locators and SIDs as SRV6-ISIS routes with SRV6-Tunnel next hops show route table inet6.0 protocol srv6 Local service SIDs, e.g. a uDT46 SID pointing to table CUST-A.inet.0 show route receive-protocol bgp <rr> table CUST-A detail SRv6 SID: … Behavior: 63 BL:32 NL:16 FL:16 AL:0 TL:16 TO:48 (63 = End.DT4 with NEXT-CSID) show route table CUST-A.inet.0 <prefix> extensive SRV6-Tunnel: Reduced-SRH Encap-mode, the segment list and Protocol next hop: <remote locator> show isis backup coverage Percentage of nodes and prefixes protected, per topology show isis backup spf results Backup path per destination (add no-coverage to list unprotected ones) ping srv6 isis <sid> / traceroute srv6 isis <sid> SRv6 OAM reachability of a uN or End SID

show spring-traffic-engineering is for SR-TE policies, not for SRv6 locators and service SIDs.

docs.title: Limits and Gotchas
docs.text:
• SID depth (from the Junos SRv6 docs): MX encapsulates up to 6 SIDs and inserts up to 5; ACX7000 encapsulates 12 and inserts 10; PTX10002-36QDD and PTX10008 (Express 5) support 7. uSID packs up to six 16-bit uSIDs per 128-bit container, which leaves plenty of headroom for TE and TI-LFA.
  • Encap vs insert: ingress PEs always encapsulate, so egress SIDs must support USD; transit SRH insertion for TI-LFA needs a PSP-capable last SID.
  • Static plus IS-IS SIDs: configuring the same static uA or End.X SID under both the SRv6 manager and IS-IS fails commit (a duplicate uN is allowed; IS-IS wins).
  • IS-IS SRv6 does not support anycast locator prefixes, SRLG, End.X interface groups or Flex-Algo locator conflict resolution.
  • No next-hop-self knob: Junos IBGP needs an export policy with then next-hop self when you redistribute CE routes into plain IPv4/IPv6 BGP.

docs.title: SRv6 on Linux
docs.text: The Linux kernel has had native SRv6 since 4.10 (February 2017; seg6local endpoint behaviors since 4.14) and is one of the most complete open-source SRv6 data planes. Everything is configured with iproute2: seg6 routes act as headends (H.Encaps and friends), and seg6local routes bind local SIDs to endpoint behaviors (End, End.X, End.DT4, …). Routing daemons such as FRRouting program the same kernel objects, so what you learn here applies to FRR, SONiC hosts and container labs alike.

docs.title: Behavior Support by Kernel Version
docs.text: First mainline release containing each feature, checked against the kernel git history (latest release: 7.3, October 2026). Distribution and stable kernels may carry fixes earlier; features also need a matching iproute2.

docs.title: Headend behaviors (ip route ... encap seg6 mode ...)
docs.text: RFC 8986 behavior iproute2 mode Kernel Notes H.Encaps encap 4.10 IPv6 or IPv4 payload SRH insertion (not in RFC 8986) inline 4.10 Adds an SRH to an IPv6 packet in place H.Encaps.L2 l2encap 4.14 Ethernet payload H.Encaps.Red encap.red 6.0 iproute2 6.0 H.Encaps.L2.Red l2encap.red 6.0 iproute2 6.0 Per-route outer source (tunsrc) ... tunsrc <addr> 7.1 iproute2 7.1; overrides the per-namespace ip sr tunsrc

docs.title: Endpoint behaviors (ip -6 route ... encap seg6local action ...)
docs.text: Behavior Kernel Notes End 4.14 seg6local itself arrived in 4.14 End.X 4.14 Optional oif for link-local next hops from 6.17 End.T 4.14 table N End.DX2 4.14 oif <dev>; no VLAN variant (End.DX2V) End.DX4 / End.DX6 4.14 nh4 / nh6 End.DT6 4.14 (table), 5.11 (vrftable) VRF mode needs net.vrf.strict_mode=1 End.DT4 5.11 vrftable only; needs VRF strict mode End.DT46 5.14 vrftable; needs VRF strict mode End.B6 (SRH insertion) 4.14 srh segs ... End.B6.Encaps 4.14 srh segs ... End.BPF 4.18 Attach an eBPF program as the behavior PSP flavor 6.3 End only (flavors psp) NEXT-C-SID flavor (uSID) 6.1 (End), 6.6 (End.X) flavors next-csid lblen 32 nflen 16 (defaults 32/16) Per-SID counters 5.13 count; iproute2 5.14

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Feature Kernel Notes SRH processing, seg6_enabled sysctl 4.10 Per interface; see Troubleshooting HMAC TLV, seg6_require_hmac, ip sr hmac 4.10 Constant-time MAC compare from 6.17 ip sr tunsrc (per-namespace outer source) 4.10 Default :: = pick from the egress interface net.ipv6.seg6_flowlabel 4.18 Compute the outer flow label for encapsulated traffic Netfilter hooks on seg6/seg6local 5.15 Off by default; net.netfilter.nf_hooks_lwtunnel=1 Post-encapsulation lookup in a chosen FIB table 7.3 SEG6_IPTUNNEL_TABLE; iproute2 support not yet in a release

Not implemented in the kernel

End.DX2V, End.DT2U, End.DT2M, End.B6.Encaps.Red, the USP and USD flavors, REPLACE-C-SID and every RFC 9433 mobile behavior. End.BM, End.S, End.AS and End.AM exist as names in the UAPI and in iproute2, but the kernel has no implementation behind them. For EVPN (End.DT2U/DT2M), use FRRouting with a VXLAN data plane or a vendor router. For MUP behaviors, use an eBPF data plane such as Vinbero.

docs.title: iproute2 Recipes
docs.text: Every command on this page was tested on kernel 6.12 with iproute2 6.9. Behavior names follow RFC 8986; in iproute2 they are the action keyword of a seg6local route.

docs.title: Headend: steering traffic into SRv6 (seg6)
docs.text:
# H.Encaps: IPv4 prefix into an outer IPv6 header + SRH with two segments
ip route add 198.51.100.0/24 encap seg6 mode encap \
    segs fc00:0:3::1,fc00:0:4::a4 dev eth0

# H.Encaps.Red: same, but the first SID is only in the DA (SRH one entry shorter;
# with a single SID there is no SRH at all)
ip route add 198.51.101.0/24 encap seg6 mode encap.red \
    segs fc00:0:3::1,fc00:0:4::a4 dev eth0

# uSID: one container carrying uN(3) uN(4) uDT4 — no SRH needed
ip route add 198.51.102.0/24 encap seg6 mode encap \
    segs fcbb:bb00:300:400:e004:: dev eth0

# SRH insertion into an existing IPv6 packet (not an RFC 8986 behavior)
ip -6 route add 2001:db8:99::/48 encap seg6 mode inline segs fc00:0:3::1 dev eth0

# H.Encaps.L2 / H.Encaps.L2.Red: frames received for this route are carried as Ethernet payload
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::12/128 encap seg6 mode l2encap segs fc00:0:4::d2 dev eth1
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::13/128 encap seg6 mode l2encap.red segs fc00:0:3::1,fc00:0:4::d2 dev eth1

The outer source address comes from ip sr tunsrc set <addr> (one per network namespace); if it is unset, the kernel picks a source address of the outgoing interface. Kernel and iproute2 7.1 add a per-route tunsrc <addr> option that overrides it.

docs.title: Endpoint behaviors (seg6local)
docs.text:
# End (node SID), optionally with the PSP flavor (6.3+)
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::1/128 encap seg6local action End dev eth0
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::2/128 encap seg6local action End flavors psp dev eth0

# End.X (adjacency SID) toward a specific IPv6 next hop
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1:e001::/64 encap seg6local action End.X nh6 2001:db8:1::2 dev eth0

# End.T: next segment looked up in table 10
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::3/128 encap seg6local action End.T table 10 dev eth0

# End.DX4 / End.DX6: decapsulate and cross-connect to a next hop (per-CE VPN)
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::d4/128 encap seg6local action End.DX4 nh4 192.0.2.2 dev eth1
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::d6/128 encap seg6local action End.DX6 nh6 2001:db8:2::2 dev eth1

# End.DX2: decapsulate and send the inner Ethernet frame out of eth1
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::d2/128 encap seg6local action End.DX2 oif eth1 dev eth1

# End.B6 (SRH insertion) and End.B6.Encaps: binding SIDs for an SR policy
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::b6/128 encap seg6local action End.B6 srh segs fc00:0:3::1,fc00:0:4::1 dev eth0
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::b7/128 encap seg6local action End.B6.Encaps srh segs fc00:0:3::1,fc00:0:4::1 dev eth0

# Per-SID counters (read with: ip -s -6 route show fc00:0:1::c)
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::c/128 encap seg6local action End count dev eth0

docs.title: VRF decapsulation: End.DT4, End.DT6, End.DT46
docs.text:
The table-lookup behaviors deliver the inner packet into a VRF. Create the VRF first and enable strict mode; without it the kernel rejects any vrftable SID with Error: Strict mode for VRF is disabled.

ip link add vrf-red type vrf table 10
ip link set vrf-red up
sysctl -w net.vrf.strict_mode=1      # the sysctl appears once the vrf module is loaded

ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::a4/128  encap seg6local action End.DT4  vrftable 10 dev vrf-red
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::a6/128  encap seg6local action End.DT6  vrftable 10 dev vrf-red
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::a46/128 encap seg6local action End.DT46 vrftable 10 dev vrf-red

# legacy End.DT6 form without a VRF device: plain table lookup
ip -6 route add fc00:0:1::a7/128 encap seg6local action End.DT6 table 10 dev eth0

docs.title: Compressed SIDs: NEXT-C-SID (uSID)
docs.text:
# uN: End with the NEXT-C-SID flavor (6.1+), 32-bit block + 16-bit node uSID
ip -6 route add fcbb:bb00:100::/48 encap seg6local action End \
    flavors next-csid lblen 32 nflen 16 dev eth0

# uA: End.X with NEXT-C-SID (6.6+)
ip -6 route add fcbb:bb00:100:e001::/64 encap seg6local action End.X nh6 2001:db8:1::2 \
    flavors next-csid lblen 32 nflen 16 dev eth0

lblen is the locator-block length and nflen the node + function length (both in bits, multiples of 8). See uSID Compression for how the destination address is shifted at each hop.

docs.title: Lab: Two Routers in Network Namespaces
docs.text:
A self-contained L3VPN over SRv6 between two network namespaces, r1 and r2. Each has a customer VRF (table 100) with a dummy "LAN", an End.DT46 SID for the VRF, and an H.Encaps.Red route toward the other side. Static routes for the locators stand in for IS-IS. Run as root on any recent kernel:

srv6-lab.sh
#!/bin/sh
set -e
ip netns add r1
ip netns add r2
ip link add veth1 netns r1 type veth peer name veth2 netns r2

for r in r1 r2; do
  ip -n $r link set lo up
  ip -n $r link add vrf-cust type vrf table 100
  ip -n $r link set vrf-cust up
  ip -n $r link add cust0 type dummy
  ip -n $r link set cust0 master vrf-cust up
  ip netns exec $r sysctl -qw net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1
  ip netns exec $r sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
  ip netns exec $r sysctl -qw net.ipv6.conf.all.seg6_enabled=1
  ip netns exec $r sysctl -qw net.vrf.strict_mode=1
  ip netns exec $r sysctl -qw net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=0
  ip netns exec $r sysctl -qw net.ipv4.conf.vrf-cust.rp_filter=0
done
ip netns exec r1 sysctl -qw net.ipv6.conf.veth1.seg6_enabled=1
ip netns exec r2 sysctl -qw net.ipv6.conf.veth2.seg6_enabled=1

ip -n r1 link set veth1 up
ip -n r2 link set veth2 up
ip -n r1 -6 addr add 2001:db8:12::1/64 dev veth1 nodad
ip -n r2 -6 addr add 2001:db8:12::2/64 dev veth2 nodad
ip -n r1 addr add 10.1.1.1/24 dev cust0
ip -n r2 addr add 10.2.2.2/24 dev cust0

# Locators: r1 = fc00:0:1::/48, r2 = fc00:0:2::/48
ip -n r1 -6 route add fc00:0:2::/48 via 2001:db8:12::2
ip -n r2 -6 route add fc00:0:1::/48 via 2001:db8:12::1

# Service SIDs: End.DT46 into the customer VRF
ip -n r1 -6 route add fc00:0:1::d46/128 encap seg6local action End.DT46 vrftable 100 dev vrf-cust
ip -n r2 -6 route add fc00:0:2::d46/128 encap seg6local action End.DT46 vrftable 100 dev vrf-cust

# Headend: H.Encaps.Red from the VRF toward the remote End.DT46 SID
ip -n r1 route add 10.2.2.0/24 vrf vrf-cust encap seg6 mode encap.red segs fc00:0:2::d46 dev veth1
ip -n r2 route add 10.1.1.0/24 vrf vrf-cust encap seg6 mode encap.red segs fc00:0:1::d46 dev veth2

ip netns exec r1 ping -c 3 -I vrf-cust 10.2.2.2

Watch the encapsulated traffic on r2 while pinging. With a single SID and encap.red, there is no SRH: the outer header's next header is 4 (IPv4).

# ip netns exec r2 tcpdump -nvi veth2 'ip6[6] == 4'
IP6 (hlim 64, next-header IPIP (4) payload length: 84) 2001:db8:12::1 > fc00:0:2::d46:
    IP (tos 0x0, ttl 64, id 60488, offset 0, flags [DF], proto ICMP (1), length 84)
    10.1.1.1 > 10.2.2.2: ICMP echo request, id 49, seq 1, length 64

Switch r1 to mode encap and the SRH appears, with one segment and Segments Left 0:

# ip -n r1 route replace 10.2.2.0/24 vrf vrf-cust encap seg6 mode encap segs fc00:0:2::d46 dev veth1
# ip netns exec r2 tcpdump -nvi veth2 'ip6[6] == 43'
IP6 (hlim 64, next-header Routing (43) payload length: 108) 2001:db8:12::1 > fc00:0:2::d46:
    RT6 (len=2, type=4, segleft=0, last-entry=0, flags=0x0, tag=0, [0]fc00:0:2::d46)
    IP (tos 0x0, ttl 64, ...) 10.1.1.1 > 10.2.2.2: ICMP echo request, id 54, seq 1, length 64

Clean up with ip netns del r1; ip netns del r2. To grow this into a multi-hop topology with IS-IS and BGP, move to Containerlab with FRR.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause Fix Packets with an SRH are dropped on arrival seg6_enabled is 0. The kernel uses the lower of the all value and the receiving interface's value, so both must be 1 sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.seg6_enabled=1 and net.ipv6.conf.<if>.seg6_enabled=1 Transit node does not forward SRv6 traffic IPv6 forwarding disabled sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 End.DT4/End.DT46 decapsulates, but nothing reaches the VRF and no counter increments Reverse-path filtering on the VRF device. Distributions often set rp_filter (1 or 2) by default; new devices inherit it, and the effective value is the max of all and the device sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.<vrf>.rp_filter=0 (and all) — this was the one failure we hit building the lab above Error: Strict mode for VRF is disabled. when adding End.DT4/DT6/DT46 VRF strict mode off sysctl -w net.vrf.strict_mode=1 (after creating a VRF) Ping from the VRF fails with ip vrf exec in containers ip vrf exec needs cgroup BPF Use ping -I <vrf-device> instead Encapsulated packets leave with an unexpected source No tunsrc set ip sr tunsrc set <addr> Large packets disappear after encapsulation Encapsulation adds 40 bytes (plus 8 + 16 × n for an SRH) Raise the underlay MTU or lower the customer MTU SRH packets dropped on an HMAC-enabled interface seg6_require_hmac = 1 drops packets without a valid HMAC TLV Configure keys with ip sr hmac set on both ends, or use 0 (validate only if present) / -1 (ignore HMAC)

Useful commands:

ip -6 route show | grep seg6local           # local SIDs
ip route show vrf vrf-cust                  # encap routes in a VRF
ip -s -6 route show fc00:0:1::c             # per-SID counters (routes added with "count")
ip -6 route get fc00:0:2::d46               # which route/SID a destination hits
tcpdump -nvi eth0 'ip6 proto 43'            # packets whose first extension header is the SRH
tcpdump -nvi eth0 'ip6[6] == 4 or ip6[6] == 41'  # H.Encaps(.Red) with no SRH (IPv4 / IPv6 inside)
nstat -az | grep -i -E 'Ip6InNoRoutes|Ip6InDiscards|Ip6InHdrErrors'
sysctl -a 2>/dev/null | grep seg6           # seg6_enabled / seg6_require_hmac per interface

Filtering SRv6 in tcpdump

ip6 proto 43 only matches when the SRH directly follows the IPv6 header. Reduced encapsulation with one SID has no SRH at all, so match the payload type (ip6[6] == 4 for IPv4, 41 for IPv6) or the destination prefix (dst net fc00::/16).

docs.title: Not Yet Merged: Mobile User Plane (RFC 9433)
docs.text:
The kernel has no RFC 9433 Mobile User Plane behaviors in any release up to 7.3. Patches from Yuya Kusakabe are under review on netdev (status as of 20 October 2026):

Series Posted Status What it adds net-next "seg6: add SRv6 Mobile User Plane (RFC 9433) behaviors" (7 patches) and the matching iproute2-next series v1 3 May, v2 4 May 2026 Changes requested; superseded End.MAP, End.M.GTP4.E, End.M.GTP6.E, End.M.GTP6.D, End.M.GTP6.D.Di and H.M.GTP4.D RFC net-next "seg6: add support for the SRv6 End.MAP behavior" + selftest v1 10 July → v5 2 October 2026 RFC, not merged End.MAP only: rewrites the IPv6 DA to a configured mapped SID and forwards via the FIB, under a new seg6mobile lightweight-tunnel encap RFC iproute2-next "End.MAP behavior under seg6mobile encap" v5 2 October 2026 RFC, not applied iproute2 support plus a new uapi header seg6_mobile.h

After review of the all-in-one submission, the author split the work into per-behavior series, starting with End.MAP; the GTP-U interworking behaviors (End.M.GTP4.E and friends) would follow separately. An "RFC" posting cannot be merged as is, so End.MAP will not appear before a non-RFC version is accepted into net-next — at the earliest, the release after that. Until then, use an eBPF data plane such as Vinbero for MUP/GTP behaviors.

docs.title: SRv6 on Nokia SR OS
docs.text: Nokia SR OS supports SRv6 in two forms: classic (full-length SIDs per RFC 8986) and micro-segment SRv6 (uSID), which Nokia describes as an extension of the SRv6 network-programming model rather than a replacement. Both can run on the same router at the same time, and Nokia's application note states that uSIDs and classic SIDs can be combined in the same segment list — keeping most of the path compressed while still carrying a full-length service or function SID where needed.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text: Aspect Detail Source SID modes Classic SRv6 and micro-segment SRv6 concurrently on one platform; SIDs of each type must come from different SID blocks SR OS 26.7 user guide Mixing in a segment list uSID containers and classic SIDs can be used together in one segment list Application note Classic SID length Variable: 32-bit, 16-bit or 128-bit Application note uSID container 32-bit block carrying up to six 16-bit uSIDs; uSIDs are global (node) or local (adjacency, service, function) Application note uSID allocation global-sid-entries (default 16) splits the 16-bit space: 0x0000-0x3FFF global, 0x4000-0xFFFF local; block-length must be identical network-wide SR OS 26.7 user guide Maximum SID depth Up to 9 classic SIDs or 47 uSIDs (including primary path, LFA backup and service SID) Application note Coexistence Classic SRv6, uSID and MPLS/SR-MPLS enabled together on the same router, service or IP interface Application note

docs.title: Behaviors (SR OS 26.7)
docs.text: Mode Behaviors Micro-segment uN and uA (advertised by IS-IS); uDT4, uDT6, uDT46, uDX2, uDT2U, uDT2M (BGP services or static) Classic End and End.X (with PSP/USP/USD flavors), End.DT4, End.DT6, End.DT46, End.DX2

docs.title: Services and Traffic Engineering
docs.text:
Area Supported (classic and uSID) L3 services Base-router BGP routes, VPRN (IP-VPN), EVPN-IFL L2 services EVPN-VPLS and EVPN-VPWS with single-active or all-active multihoming Multicast Point-to-multipoint SRv6 policy tunnels for multicast replication (see Multicast) IGP IS-IS, including Flex-Algo TE Flex-Algo; SRv6 policies configured statically, via BGP SR-TE policy AF, or from a PCE over PCEP (RFC 9603) Protection LFA, remote LFA, TI-LFA (link, node, SRLG); SR OS originates and terminates repair tunnels with H.Insert.Red and can terminate H.Encaps.Red repair tunnels from other vendors Gateway Interworking between MPLS, SR-MPLS, SRv6 classic, SRv6 uSID, VXLAN and MPLS-over-UDP at transport and service layers

Multi-vendor TI-LFA

SR OS builds TI-LFA and remote-LFA repair tunnels with H.Insert.Red, while some other implementations use H.Encaps.Red. The SR OS guide describes a termination mode to accept encapsulated repair tunnels — check this when mixing vendors in one IGP domain. See TI-LFA.
