docs.title: RFC 9433 - Segment Routing over IPv6 for the Mobile User Plane
docs.text: Field Value Title Segment Routing over IPv6 for the Mobile User Plane Authors S. Matsushima, C. Filsfils, M. Kohno, P. Camarillo, D. Voyer, C. Perkins Date July 2023 Status Proposed Standard Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9433

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9433 defines how SRv6 can be used as the mobile user plane protocol in 3GPP networks, replacing GTP-U tunneling between mobile network functions. By encoding mobile session state directly into SRv6 SIDs, the architecture eliminates the need for GTP-U encapsulation between the UPF (User Plane Function) nodes, reducing per-packet overhead and simplifying the data plane.

The document specifies several new SRv6 endpoint behaviors purpose-built for mobile user plane interworking. These behaviors handle the translation between GTP-U and SRv6 at network boundaries and the pure SRv6 forwarding within the mobile transport. The SID structure carries mobile-specific arguments such as QFI (QoS Flow Identifier) and TEID (Tunnel Endpoint Identifier) information, enabling stateless translation at domain boundaries.

This approach allows operators to converge their mobile backhaul and transport networks onto a single SRv6 infrastructure, reducing operational complexity while enabling advanced capabilities like network slicing using SRv6 and Flex-Algo.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 3 Reference Architecture 5G user plane architecture with SRv6 replacing GTP-U 4 SRv6 SID for Mobile User Plane SID structure carrying mobile session context 5 SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors New behaviors for GTP-U interworking 6 Uplink and Downlink Scenarios Packet flow for both directions 7 IPv4 User Plane Support Handling IPv4 UE traffic over SRv6

docs.title: MUP Endpoint Behaviors
docs.text: Behavior Direction Function End.M.GTP6.D Downlink Decapsulates SRv6 and encapsulates into GTP-U toward the gNB (IPv6 payload) End.M.GTP6.Di Downlink Same as above but for IPv6 traffic with inner header insertion End.M.GTP6.E Uplink Decapsulates GTP-U from gNB and encapsulates into SRv6 End.M.GTP4.E Uplink Decapsulates GTP-U (IPv4 outer) and encapsulates into SRv6 H.M.GTP4.D Downlink Headend behavior: encodes GTP-U parameters into SRv6 SID args for IPv4 N3

docs.title: MUP SID Structure
docs.text:
The MUP SID encodes mobile session information directly in the SRv6 SID:

|<-------- Locator -------->|<-- Function -->|<--- Argument --->|
|   Block     |    Node     |    Behavior    |  TEID + QFI etc  |
Field Purpose Locator Identifies the UPF or mobile anchor node Function Identifies the MUP behavior (e.g., End.M.GTP6.D) Argument Carries TEID, QFI, and other GTP-U session parameters

docs.title: GTP-U to SRv6 Interworking
docs.text:
Scenario Source Translation Point Destination Uplink (N3) gNB sends GTP-U Ingress UPF: GTP-U to SRv6 Anchor UPF (SRv6 endpoint) Downlink (N3) Anchor UPF sends SRv6 Egress UPF: SRv6 to GTP-U gNB receives GTP-U N9 (inter-UPF) UPF sends SRv6 No translation needed UPF receives SRv6

Common Pitfalls

  • The MUP behaviors require the argument portion of the SID to be large enough to encode the TEID (32 bits) and QFI (6 bits). An undersized Locator:Function leaves insufficient room for arguments.
  • The interworking functions at domain boundaries must maintain awareness of the GTP-U tunnel state for proper TEID mapping, even though the SRv6 core is stateless.
  • IPv4 user plane traffic requires special handling (End.M.GTP4.E / H.M.GTP4.D) because of the different N3 encapsulation header format.
  • Deploying MUP without Flex-Algo for network slicing loses one of the key benefits -- the ability to map 5G network slices to distinct SRv6 topologies.
  • Not all SRv6 implementations support MUP behaviors. Verify platform support before planning a GTP-U replacement deployment.

docs.title: RFC 9487 - Export of Segment Routing over IPv6 Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX)
docs.text: Field Value Title Export of Segment Routing over IPv6 Information in IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Authors T. Graf, B. Claise, P. Francois Date November 2023 Status Informational Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9487

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9487 defines new IPFIX (IP Flow Information Export) Information Elements for exporting SRv6-related data from network nodes to collectors. As SRv6 deployments grow, operators need visibility into how SRv6 traffic is forwarded -- which SIDs are being used, what segment lists packets carry, and how traffic maps to SR Policies. This RFC provides the telemetry building blocks to answer those questions.

The document specifies 11 new IPFIX Information Elements that capture the essential SRv6 forwarding state observed at a metering point. These elements cover the active SID in the IPv6 destination address, the full segment list from the SRH, the Segments Left value, Section Tag, and flags. Together, they enable a collector to reconstruct the SRv6 forwarding path a packet is following.

These IPFIX elements are essential for SRv6 network operations, enabling use cases such as traffic engineering validation (confirming packets follow the intended SR Policy), SLA monitoring (measuring per-path latency and loss), capacity planning (understanding per-SID traffic volumes), and troubleshooting (identifying packets with unexpected segment lists).

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 3 Use Cases Traffic engineering verification, SLA monitoring, troubleshooting 4 New IPFIX Information Elements Definition of 11 SRv6-specific IEs 5 Encoding How SRv6 SIDs and segment lists are encoded in IPFIX records 6 Export Scenarios Where in the network SRv6 IPFIX export is most useful

docs.title: New IPFIX Information Elements
docs.text: IE Name IE ID Type Description srhFlags 502 unsigned8 Flags field from the SRH srhTag 503 unsigned16 Tag field from the SRH srhSegmentIPv6 504 ipv6Address An individual SRv6 SID from the segment list srhActiveSegmentIPv6 505 ipv6Address The currently active SID (from IPv6 DA) srhSegmentIPv6BasicList 506 basicList Ordered list of all SRv6 SIDs in the SRH srhSegmentsIPv6Left 507 unsigned8 Segments Left value from the SRH srhIPv6Section 508 unsigned8 Section of the SRH being reported srhIPv6ActiveSegmentType 509 unsigned8 Type of the active segment (e.g., transit, endpoint) srhSegmentIPv6ListSection 510 basicList Section of the segment list for large SRHs srhSegmentsIPv6SectionLeft 511 unsigned8 Segments Left relative to the reported section srhIPv6SRHLength 512 unsigned16 Total length of the SRH in bytes

docs.title: Export Use Cases
docs.text: Use Case Key IEs Used Benefit TE Verification srhSegmentIPv6BasicList, srhActiveSegmentIPv6 Confirm packets follow the programmed SR Policy path SLA Monitoring srhActiveSegmentIPv6 + timestamps Measure per-path latency and jitter Capacity Planning srhSegmentIPv6 + byte/packet counters Understand traffic volumes per SID and segment list Troubleshooting srhFlags, srhSegmentsIPv6Left, full segment list Identify unexpected forwarding behavior or misrouted packets Accounting srhActiveSegmentIPv6 + flow counters Per-service or per-tenant traffic accounting

docs.title: IPFIX Export Points in an SRv6 Network
docs.text:
Export Point What is Visible Typical Use Headend (ingress) Full SRH with complete segment list Verify SR Policy is applied correctly Transit node IPv6 DA (active SID); SRH if configured to inspect Monitor per-SID traffic load Endpoint (egress) Final SID processing, decapsulated inner packet End-to-end path validation

Common Pitfalls

  • Not all hardware supports deep SRH inspection for IPFIX export. Transit routers often only see the IPv6 destination address (active SID) and cannot export the full segment list without SRH parsing support.
  • The srhSegmentIPv6BasicList IE uses the IPFIX basicList structured data type (RFC 6313). Collectors must support structured data to parse this field correctly.
  • Large segment lists may exceed IPFIX template or record size limits. The srhSegmentIPv6ListSection and srhIPv6Section IEs provide a mechanism for sectioned export, but collector support varies.
  • SRv6 compressed SIDs (uSID, RFC 9800) appear as standard 128-bit IPv6 addresses in IPFIX. The collector needs additional context (the GIB prefix and C-SID length) to decompose containers into individual micro-SIDs.
  • IPFIX sampling configuration significantly affects telemetry accuracy for SRv6. Low sampling rates may miss short-lived or low-volume SRv6 flows entirely.

docs.title: RFC 9513 - OSPFv3 Extensions for SRv6
docs.text: Field Value Title OSPFv3 Extensions for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Authors Z. Li, Z. Hu, K. Talaulikar, P. Psenak Date December 2023 Status Proposed Standard Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9513

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9513 defines the OSPFv3 extensions required to support Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6). While IS-IS SRv6 extensions were defined in RFC 9352, many networks rely on OSPFv3 as their IPv6 link-state routing protocol, and this document provides the equivalent functionality for OSPF-based deployments.

The specification introduces new TLVs and sub-TLVs within OSPFv3 Extended LSAs to advertise SRv6 capabilities, SRv6 Locators, SRv6 End SIDs, and SRv6 Adjacency SIDs. It builds on the OSPFv3 Extended LSA framework defined in RFC 8362, which provides a flexible TLV-based encoding for OSPFv3 advertisements.

The extensions enable OSPFv3 to distribute all the information needed for SRv6 forwarding: node capabilities, locator prefixes, endpoint behaviors (SID functions), and adjacency SIDs for traffic engineering. Combined with Flex-Algo support (RFC 9350), these extensions allow OSPFv3 to fully participate in SRv6 network deployments.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 3 SRv6 Capabilities TLV Advertising node-level SRv6 support and flags 4 SRv6 Locator TLV Advertising SRv6 locator prefixes in the E-Router-LSA 5 SRv6 End SID sub-TLV Associating endpoint behaviors with locators 6 SRv6 Adjacency SID sub-TLV Advertising per-link SRv6 adjacency SIDs 7 SRv6 SID Structure sub-TLV Describing the LOC:FUNC:ARG bit-length structure of a SID

docs.title: New TLVs and Sub-TLVs
docs.text: TLV/Sub-TLV Type Carried In Purpose SRv6 Capabilities TLV Router Information LSA Advertise SRv6 support and capability flags SRv6 Locator TLV E-Router-LSA Advertise an SRv6 Locator prefix with algorithm and metric SRv6 End SID Sub-TLV SRv6 Locator TLV Bind an SRv6 endpoint behavior (e.g., End, End.X) to a SID SRv6 Adjacency SID Sub-TLV E-Router-LSA link entries Advertise per-adjacency SRv6 SIDs (End.X equivalent) SRv6 SID Structure Sub-TLV SRv6 End SID / Adj SID Describe the Locator Block, Locator Node, Function, and Argument bit lengths

docs.title: SRv6 Locator Advertisement
docs.text:
The SRv6 Locator TLV carries:

Field Description Route Type Intra-area or inter-area locator Algorithm 0 for SPF, 1 for Strict SPF, 128-255 for Flex-Algo Locator Prefix The IPv6 prefix representing the SRv6 Locator Metric Cost associated with reaching this locator Flags N-flag (node SID), A-flag (no-algorithm)

docs.title: SRv6 SID Structure Sub-TLV
docs.text: Field Bits Description Locator Block Length (LBL) Variable Length of the SRv6 SID Locator Block in bits Locator Node Length (LNL) Variable Length of the Locator Node identifier in bits Function Length (FL) Variable Length of the Function field in bits Argument Length (AL) Variable Length of the Argument field in bits

docs.title: OSPFv3 SRv6 vs IS-IS SRv6
docs.text:
Aspect OSPFv3 (RFC 9513) IS-IS (RFC 9352) LSA/LSP type E-Router-LSA (RFC 8362) Standard IS-IS LSP Capabilities SRv6 Capabilities TLV in RI LSA SRv6 Capabilities sub-TLV in Router Capability TLV Locator SRv6 Locator TLV in E-Router-LSA SRv6 Locator TLV (top-level) End SID Sub-TLV of SRv6 Locator TLV SRv6 End SID sub-TLV of Locator TLV Adjacency SID Sub-TLV of link in E-Router-LSA SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV in extended IS reachability Flex-Algo Algorithm field in Locator TLV Algorithm field in Locator TLV

Common Pitfalls

  • OSPFv3 SRv6 extensions require Extended LSAs (RFC 8362). Legacy OSPFv3 LSA types cannot carry the new TLVs. Ensure all routers support and are configured for Extended LSAs.
  • The SRv6 SID Structure sub-TLV is optional but strongly recommended. Without it, remote nodes must infer the LOC:FUNC:ARG boundaries, which may lead to interoperability issues.
  • OSPFv3 area boundaries affect SRv6 locator reachability. Inter-area locator advertisements require proper ABR configuration.
  • Do not confuse OSPFv3 SR extensions (RFC 8666, for SR-MPLS) with OSPFv3 SRv6 extensions (RFC 9513). They serve different data planes.
  • When deploying both IS-IS and OSPFv3 for SRv6, ensure consistent locator and SID advertisements to avoid forwarding inconsistencies.

docs.title: RFC 9514 - Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for SRv6
docs.text: Field Value Title Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) Extensions for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Authors G. Dawra, C. Filsfils, K. Talaulikar, M. Chen, D. Bernier, B. Decraene Date December 2023 Status Proposed Standard Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9514

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9514 defines extensions to the Border Gateway Protocol - Link State (BGP-LS) for carrying SRv6 information. BGP-LS (RFC 7752, updated by RFC 9552) is used to export link-state topology and traffic engineering information from IGP domains to external consumers such as SDN controllers and Path Computation Elements (PCEs). This RFC extends BGP-LS to include SRv6-specific attributes.

The extensions enable a centralized controller to learn the complete SRv6 topology of the network, including SRv6 capabilities, locators, End SIDs, adjacency SIDs (End.X), and the SID structure. With this information, a controller can compute SRv6 paths and program SR Policies without needing to participate in the IGP directly.

This is a critical building block for SDN-based SRv6 deployments where a PCE or SDN controller computes paths centrally and distributes them via PCEP or BGP SR Policy. The BGP-LS SRv6 extensions ensure the controller has a complete and accurate view of the SRv6 data plane.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 3 SRv6 Capabilities Node-level SRv6 support advertisement via BGP-LS 4 SRv6 Locator Prefix NLRI attribute carrying locator and algorithm 5 SRv6 End SID BGP-LS attribute TLV for SRv6 endpoint behaviors 6 SRv6 Adjacency SID (End.X) BGP-LS link attribute for per-adjacency SRv6 SIDs 7 SRv6 SID Structure TLV describing the LOC:FUNC:ARG bit layout

docs.title: BGP-LS SRv6 Attribute TLVs
docs.text: TLV Code Point BGP-LS Attribute Maps From (IGP) SRv6 Capabilities 1106 Node Attribute IS-IS / OSPFv3 SRv6 Capabilities SRv6 Locator 1162 Prefix Attribute IS-IS SRv6 Locator TLV / OSPFv3 SRv6 Locator TLV SRv6 End SID 1163 Prefix Attribute IS-IS SRv6 End SID sub-TLV / OSPFv3 SRv6 End SID sub-TLV SRv6 SID Structure 1164 Prefix/Link Attribute IS-IS / OSPFv3 SRv6 SID Structure sub-TLV SRv6 End.X SID 1106 Link Attribute IS-IS SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV / OSPFv3 SRv6 Adj SID sub-TLV

docs.title: BGP-LS to IGP Mapping
docs.text: BGP-LS Component IS-IS Source OSPFv3 Source Node NLRI + SRv6 Caps Router Capability TLV Router Information LSA Prefix NLRI + SRv6 Locator SRv6 Locator TLV SRv6 Locator TLV in E-Router-LSA Prefix NLRI + SRv6 End SID SRv6 End SID sub-TLV SRv6 End SID sub-TLV Link NLRI + SRv6 End.X SID SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV SRv6 Adjacency SID sub-TLV

docs.title: Use with SDN Controllers and PCE
docs.text:
+------------------+
|  SDN Controller  |     BGP-LS provides the SRv6 topology database
|  / PCE           |     to the controller, which then computes
+--------+---------+     paths and programs SR Policies via PCEP
         |                or BGP SR Policy.
    BGP-LS Session
         |
+--------+---------+
|   BGP-LS Speaker |     Collects IGP SRv6 data from IS-IS/OSPFv3
|   (Route Reflector)    and exports via BGP-LS to the controller.
+--------+---------+
         |
    IGP Domain (IS-IS or OSPFv3 with SRv6 extensions)
Component Role BGP-LS Speaker Collects SRv6 information from the IGP and exports it northbound SDN Controller / PCE Consumes the BGP-LS SRv6 topology to compute constrained paths PCEP / BGP SR Policy Southbound protocol to push computed SR Policies to headend routers

Common Pitfalls

  • BGP-LS SRv6 extensions only export information -- they do not program the data plane. A separate mechanism (PCEP, BGP SR Policy) is needed to install computed paths.
  • The BGP-LS speaker must participate in the IGP to learn SRv6 TLVs. If the IGP peering is misconfigured or the IGP does not carry SRv6 extensions, BGP-LS will have an incomplete view.
  • Ensure the BGP-LS speaker's IGP implementation supports the SRv6-specific TLVs from RFC 9352 (IS-IS) or RFC 9513 (OSPFv3). Older implementations may silently drop unknown TLVs.
  • The SRv6 SID Structure TLV is essential for the controller to correctly parse the LOC:FUNC:ARG boundaries. Missing SID Structure information can lead to incorrect path computation.
  • Multi-domain deployments require BGP-LS from each domain. The controller must stitch cross-domain topology views to compute end-to-end SRv6 paths.

docs.title: RFC 9524 - SR Replication Segment
docs.text: Field Value Title Segment Routing Replication for Multipoint Service Delivery Authors D. Voyer (Ed.), C. Filsfils, R. Parekh, H. Bidgoli, Z. Zhang Date February 2024 Status Proposed Standard Updated by RFC 9960 (Replication-ID structure) Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9524

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9524 adds a new segment type to the SR architecture: the Replication segment. A node that holds a Replication segment (the replication node) copies each packet it receives on that segment and sends one copy to each of a set of downstream nodes. The same construct works for SR-MPLS (a label) and SRv6 (a SID with the new End.Replicate behavior).

Unlike every other SRv6 behavior, End.Replicate is driven by local replication state rather than by the segment list. The replication node looks up the SID's FUNCT bits, finds its list of replication branches, and for each branch writes the downstream node's Replication-SID into the outer IPv6 destination address. Downstream nodes do not need to be adjacent: the locator of the downstream Replication-SID is enough to reach it over shortest path (default or Flex-Algo), or the replication node can add an H.Encaps.Red segment list to steer the copy over a TE path.

A single Replication segment whose downstream nodes are all the egress PEs is simply ingress replication. Stitching several Replication segments together (root → intermediate replication nodes → leaves) builds a P2MP tree; RFC 9524 deliberately leaves that stitching to a control plane, which RFC 9960 (SR P2MP Policy) defines.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 1.2 Use Cases Ingress replication for MVPN and EVPN BUM; trees built from stitched segments 2 Replication Segment Identifier <Replication-ID, Node-ID>, Replication-SID, downstream nodes, replication state 2.1 SR-MPLS Data Plane POP + per-branch PUSH of downstream Replication-SID 2.2 SRv6 Data Plane DA rewrite, optional H.Encaps.Red per branch, Hop Limit handling 2.2.1 End.Replicate Pseudocode for the replicate and/or decapsulate behavior 2.2.2 OAM Pinging a leaf Replication-SID through transit replication nodes 2.2.3 ICMPv6 Errors Same ICMPv6 restrictions as IPv6 multicast destinations App. A Illustration Worked SR-MPLS and SRv6 examples

docs.title: Node Roles and Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning Replication node Node that replicates packets based on a Replication segment Downstream nodes The set of nodes a Replication segment sends copies to Replication state (RS) List of branches, each a <downstream node, downstream Replication-SID> pair (optionally with a segment list) Root Ingress node of the P2MP service (also a replication node) Leaf Egress node; its Replication segment has a leaf indicator and an empty branch list Bud Node that is both a replication node and a leaf

docs.title: End.Replicate Processing (SRv6)
docs.text:
Step Action 1 Look up the FUNCT part of the DA to find the replication state; drop if none 2 Drop if Hop Limit ≤ 1, or below the optional per-segment Hop Limit Threshold (rate-limited log) 3 Decrement Hop Limit; optionally process SRH TLVs 4 For each branch: copy the packet, set DA = downstream Replication-SID, optionally apply H.Encaps/H.Encaps.Red with the branch's segment list, then forward via the IPv6 FIB 5 If the node is a Leaf or Bud: derive the packet-processing context (from the next SID in the SRH or from the Replication-SID itself), strip the outer header, and process the inner IPv4/IPv6/Ethernet payload

The SRH segment list is not advanced by a replication node — copies leave with the SRH unchanged. Any SIDs after the Replication-SID are context for leaf/bud nodes (for example, a service SID identifying the VPN).

Codepoint Value Registry End.Replicate 75 (0x004B) SRv6 Endpoint Behaviors

docs.title: Ingress Replication vs Tree
docs.text:
Model Replication segments Transit state Ingress replication One at the root; all leaves are downstream nodes None beyond normal unicast forwarding P2MP tree (RFC 9960) Root + intermediate replication nodes + leaves Replication state on each replication node; plain transit routers forward on the locator

Common Pitfalls

  • End.Replicate is stateful at replication nodes. It is not "replication encoded in the SRH" — the branch list lives on the node and is programmed locally or by a controller.
  • ICMPv6 errors (Time Exceeded, Parameter Problem) must not be generated for Replication-SIDs, so traceroute to a leaf Replication-SID does not work. Use ping to a leaf/bud Replication-SID instead (Section 2.2.2).
  • Set the root's Hop Limit high enough to reach the furthest leaf; copying the payload's Hop Limit may strand distant leaves. Non-replicating routers on the path can otherwise expire packets and storm the root with ICMPv6.
  • When a branch uses H.Encaps.Red to reach a non-adjacent downstream node, the extra IPv6 header must fit the path MTU.
  • If an HMAC TLV is used with a context SID in the SRH, the root must set the SRH D bit because the Replication-SID is not in the segment list.
  • Locally provisioned chains of Replication segments must not form loops; RFC 9524 itself has no loop detection.

docs.title: RFC 9602 - SRv6 Segment Identifiers in the IPv6 Addressing Architecture
docs.text: Field Value Title Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Segment Identifiers in the IPv6 Addressing Architecture Date October 2024 Status Proposed Standard Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9602

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9602 reserves 5f00::/16 from the IPv6 address space for SRv6 Segment Identifiers (SIDs), so SIDs can be recognized and filtered easily within an SR domain. The block is forwardable but not globally reachable. Operators may still use their own GUA prefixes as locators.

See SID Structure for the registry properties, allocation hierarchy, and boundary filtering examples.

docs.title: RFC 9603 - PCEP Extensions for SRv6
docs.text: Field Value Title Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) Extensions for IPv6 Segment Routing Authors C. Li (Ed.), P. Kaladharan, S. Sivabalan, M. Koldychev, Y. Zhu Date July 2024 Status Proposed Standard Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9603

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 8664 taught PCEP to carry SR-MPLS paths. RFC 9603 does the same for SRv6, so a PCE can compute SRv6 paths and a stateful PCE can initiate, update, and receive reports for SRv6 SR Policy candidate paths on a headend (PCC).

The extension is small and reuses the existing PCEP messages unchanged. It adds a new Path Setup Type (PST = 3), an SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV exchanged in the OPEN message, and new SRv6-ERO / SRv6-RRO subobjects that carry 128-bit SIDs, optionally with the node/adjacency they belong to (the NAI), the endpoint behavior, and the SID structure.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 3 Overview How SRv6 fits on top of RFC 8664 procedures 4.1 OPEN Object PST=3 and SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV (with optional SRv6 MSDs) 4.2 RP/SRP Object PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV with PST=3 is mandatory for SRv6 messages 4.3 SRv6-ERO SID, NAI, endpoint behavior, SID structure 4.4 SRv6-RRO Reports the SID list actually applied by the PCC 5 Procedures Capability exchange, ERO/RRO validation and error codes

docs.title: What It Adds
docs.text: Element Codepoint Purpose Path Setup Type PST = 3 "Path is set up using SRv6" SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV Type 27 Signals SRv6 support; PCC may add SRv6 MSD pairs and the N flag (can resolve NAI to SID) SRv6-ERO subobject Type 40 One SRv6 segment of the computed path SRv6-RRO subobject Type 40 One SRv6 segment of the path actually used

docs.title: SRv6-ERO Subobject
docs.text:
Field / Flag Meaning L Loose hop — PCC may expand or replace SIDs NT NAI type: 0 = none, 2 = IPv6 node ID, 4 = IPv6 adjacency, 6 = link-local adjacency S SID absent — PCC resolves it from the NAI F NAI absent T SID Structure present (LB, LN, Function, Argument lengths) V Verify the SID before use (RFC 9256 Section 5.1) Endpoint Behavior 16-bit RFC 8986 behavior code (0xFFFF if unknown)

An SRv6-ERO must carry a SID, an NAI, or both, and an ERO cannot mix SRv6-ERO with other subobject types.

docs.title: MSD Handling
docs.text:
A PCC may advertise its SRv6 Maximum SID Depths in the capability sub-TLV, but the PCE must consider the MSDs of every node on the path, not just the headend. If MSDs are available from IGP or BGP-LS, those take precedence, and the RFC recommends leaving them out of PCEP in that case. A PCC that receives a path exceeding its MSD returns a PCErr (Error-Type 10, value 40).

Common Pitfalls

  • Every SRv6 PCEP message must carry PST=3 in the RP or SRP object; sending an SRv6-ERO without it, or without having exchanged the capability, triggers a PCErr (Type 19, value 19).
  • Advertising PST=3 without the SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV closes the session.
  • Changing the PCC's advertised MSD requires tearing down and re-establishing the PCEP session.
  • The SID Structure is optional but useful: it lets the PCE validate SIDs against the operator's allocation plan.
  • RFC 9603 covers point-to-point SR Policies. Point-to-multipoint trees (RFC 9960) use a separate draft.

docs.title: RFC 9723 - BGP Colored Prefix Routing (CPR)
docs.text: Field Value Title BGP Colored Prefix Routing (CPR) for Services Based on Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Authors H. Wang, J. Dong, K. Talaulikar, T. Han, R. Chen Date May 2025 Status Informational Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9723

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9723 describes how to deliver intent-aware (color-aware) SRv6 services across multiple ASes without any new BGP extension. The trick is to put the intent into the locator: each PE splits its base locator into sub-locators, one per intent (low delay, high bandwidth, ...). These Colored Prefixes are advertised in plain BGP IPv6 unicast (AFI/SAFI 2/1) with a Color Extended Community.

Service SIDs are then allocated from the colored sub-locator that matches the service's intent — e.g., a low-latency VPN gets its End.DT4 SID from the low-delay locator. Service routes are advertised as usual (RFC 9252, Option C, next hop unchanged) and need no color of their own. Ingress PEs and border routers simply do longest-prefix match of the service SID against the colored prefix, and resolve that route onto an intra-domain path for the tuple (next hop, color) — an SRv6 Policy, SRv6 Flex-Algo, or even an SR-MPLS/RSVP-TE LSP in MPLS transit domains.

Because the packet's destination is always the service SID, no inter-domain transport label or SID is needed, keeping encapsulation small.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 2.1 Colored Prefix Allocation Split the base locator into per-intent sub-locators 2.2 Advertisement IPv6 unicast + Color Extended Community across ASes; color re-mapping at borders 2.3 Path Resolution Resolve on (next hop, color) to SRv6/SR-MPLS Policy, Flex-Algo, or RSVP-TE 2.4-2.5 Service Routes and Steering Service SIDs under colored locators; LPM steering 3 Encapsulation Packet walks over SRv6 and MPLS intra-domain paths 4 Operational Considerations Trust model, aggregation, fallback in legacy domains, 5f00::/16 filtering

docs.title: Example Allocation
docs.text: Prefix Intent Advertised with 2001:db8:aaaa:1::/64 Base locator No color 2001:db8:aaaa:1:0000::/68 Color 1 (e.g., low delay) Color Extended Community C1 2001:db8:aaaa:1:1000::/68 Color 2 (e.g., high bandwidth) Color Extended Community C2 ... up to 2001:db8:aaaa:1:f000::/68 16 intents total ...

docs.title: CPR vs Other Intent-Aware Approaches
docs.text:
Approach Signaling Intent carried in Border-node data plane CPR (RFC 9723) Existing IPv6 unicast SAFI + Color EC Service SID's locator Plain IPv6 forwarding (re-encapsulate per domain) BGP-CAR Separate SAFI Locator prefix Similar, with dedicated SAFI BGP-CT Classful Transport SAFI Additional transport SID SRv6 operation similar to label swap Inter-domain SR Policy Controller / BSID Segment list Policy stitching

Common Pitfalls

  • CPR assumes all participating ASes are one trusted domain (same operator or a formal trust model). Colored locators are ordinary IPv6 unicast routes, so boundary filters must keep them from leaking.
  • Disable aggregation for IPv6 unicast routes carrying a Color Extended Community; otherwise the base locator swallows the colored sub-locators.
  • If one intent uses different color values in different ASes, borders must rewrite the Color EC according to a consistent mapping policy. The same colored prefix appearing with two colors is a misconfiguration.
  • Domains that do not support CPR fall back to best-effort resolution — the service still works, but the intent is not honored in that AS.
  • With 5f00::/16 (RFC 9602) blocked by default at boundaries, explicitly permit the colored prefixes in use within the trusted domain.

docs.title: RFC 9800 - Compressed SRv6 Segment List Encoding
docs.text: Field Value Title Compressed SRv6 Segment List Encoding Authors C. Filsfils, Z. Ali, C. Previdi, F. Clad, et al. Date June 2025 Status Proposed Standard Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9800

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9800 defines the Compressed SRv6 Segment List Encoding, commonly known as micro-SID (uSID). This mechanism addresses one of the primary concerns with SRv6: the overhead of 128-bit SIDs in the Segment Routing Header. By packing multiple compressed SIDs (C-SIDs) into a single 128-bit container, the encoding dramatically reduces SRH overhead, making SRv6 competitive with SR-MPLS in terms of per-packet encapsulation cost.

The specification defines two SRv6 SID flavors: NEXT-C-SID and REPLACE-C-SID. Both flavors use a container structure where multiple short SID values (typically 16 or 32 bits) are packed into standard 128-bit SRv6 SID slots. The key operation is "shift-and-lookup": when a node processes its C-SID, it shifts the remaining C-SIDs within the container and performs a lookup on the next one, avoiding the need to decrement Segments Left for every micro-segment.

The compression is transparent to transit nodes, which see only a standard IPv6 destination address. This means uSID can be deployed incrementally -- only SR-capable endpoints need to support the compressed encoding, while the rest of the network forwards packets using standard IPv6.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 3 C-SID Container Format How compressed SIDs are packed into 128-bit slots 4 NEXT-C-SID Flavor Processing using the Next-Header chain for container advancement 5 REPLACE-C-SID Flavor Processing by replacing within the active container 6 C-SID Shift-and-Lookup Core forwarding operation for both flavors 7 Interworking Mixing compressed and uncompressed SIDs in the same SRH

docs.title: C-SID Container Format
docs.text:
A single 128-bit SRv6 SID slot is divided into a Global Identifier Block (GIB) and a sequence of C-SIDs:

|<---------- 128 bits ---------->|
| GIB (variable) | C-SID1 | C-SID2 | C-SID3 | ... | padding |
Component Typical Size Purpose GIB 32 bits Common block prefix shared by all uSIDs in the domain C-SID 16 bits (default) Compressed node/function identifier Container 128 bits One Segment List entry holding multiple C-SIDs

With a 32-bit GIB and 16-bit C-SIDs, a single 128-bit container holds up to 6 micro-segments.

docs.title: NEXT-C-SID vs REPLACE-C-SID
docs.text: Property NEXT-C-SID REPLACE-C-SID Container advancement Decrements Segments Left to move to the next 128-bit container Replaces C-SIDs within the current container entry SL decrement On container boundary only On container boundary only Shift operation Shift C-SIDs left within the active container Same shift operation Empty container detection Next C-SID position is all zeros Same Interworking Can coexist with uncompressed SIDs Can coexist with uncompressed SIDs

docs.title: Overhead Comparison
docs.text: Encoding 4-Segment Path 8-Segment Path 12-Segment Path Uncompressed SRv6 64 bytes (4 x 16B) 128 bytes (8 x 16B) 192 bytes (12 x 16B) uSID (16-bit C-SIDs) 16 bytes (1 container) 32 bytes (2 containers) 32 bytes (2 containers) SR-MPLS 16 bytes (4 x 4B) 32 bytes (8 x 4B) 48 bytes (12 x 4B)

docs.title: Shift-and-Lookup Operation
docs.text:
When a uSID-capable node receives a packet:

  1. Extract its own C-SID from the current position in the active container
  2. Shift remaining C-SIDs left by one C-SID length within the container
  3. If the next C-SID position is all zeros (end of container), decrement Segments Left and move to the next container entry
  4. Write the updated container value into the IPv6 Destination Address
  5. Perform an IPv6 FIB lookup on the new Destination Address

Common Pitfalls

  • All nodes in a uSID domain must share the same GIB prefix and C-SID length. Mismatched configurations cause forwarding failures.
  • The "End of Container" condition (all-zeros in the next C-SID position) must be handled correctly. A C-SID value of 0 is reserved and must not be assigned to any node.
  • Mixing NEXT-C-SID and REPLACE-C-SID flavors within the same segment list is not supported. Choose one flavor per deployment.
  • Compressed and uncompressed SIDs can coexist in the same SRH, but the transition boundaries must be configured correctly.
  • Operators accustomed to SRv6 packet captures will see fewer Segment List entries than expected because multiple hops are packed into each container.

docs.title: RFC 9819 - Argument Signaling for BGP Services in SRv6
docs.text: Field Value Title Argument Signaling for BGP Services in Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Authors K. Talaulikar, K. Raza, J. Rabadan, W. Lin Date July 2025 Status Proposed Standard Updates RFC 9252 Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9819

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Some SRv6 behaviors take an argument in the low-order bits of the SID. The case that matters for BGP services is End.DT2M (EVPN BUM flooding), whose argument Arg.FE2 tells the egress PE which local Ethernet Segment to exclude — the split-horizon (ESI filtering) needed for EVPN multihoming and E-Tree leaf filtering.

RFC 9252 split the signaling: the egress PE advertises the LOC:FUNC part of its End.DT2M SID in the Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag route (Type 3) and the argument in the Ethernet A-D per ES route (Type 1), and the ingress PE combined them with a bitwise OR. Interop testing showed this was ambiguous and only works if both routes use identical SID structures. RFC 9819 replaces the OR with an explicit procedure: the ingress PE inserts the argument at the offset given by the SID Structure (LBL + LNL + FL) of the Type 3 route.

The rules are written for End.DT2M but apply to any argument-carrying SRv6 behavior signaled in BGP, and they cover the compressed (NEXT-C-SID) End.DT2M flavors from RFC 9800 as well.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 2 Advertisement of SID and Arguments SID Structure sub-sub-TLV is mandatory; AL = 0 means "no argument accepted" 3.1 Ethernet A-D per ES route Carries the ESI filtering argument (or :: with AL = 0) 3.2 Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag route Carries only LOC:FUNC; AL announces the argument size 3.3 Ingress PE processing How to build the data-plane SID and what to do on inconsistent AL 4 Backward compatibility When the RFC 9252 bitwise-OR still works

docs.title: Signaling Rules
docs.text: Route SID field Argument Length (AL) Type 1 (A-D per ES), no ESI filtering :: (End.DT2M), structure still included 0 Type 1 (A-D per ES), ESI filtering Argument value placed at LBL+LNL+FL offset Argument size (SHOULD be a multiple of 8) Type 3 (IMET), no ESI filtering LOC:FUNC only 0 Type 3 (IMET), ESI filtering LOC:FUNC only Must equal the AL in the Type 1 route

docs.title: Ingress PE Decision
docs.text:
Condition Result Type 3 AL = 0 Use LOC:FUNC only; ignore any Type 1 argument Type 3 AL ≠ 0, no matching Type 1 SID or Type 1 AL = 0 No usable argument; use LOC:FUNC only Both AL ≠ 0 but different Configuration error — do not forward BUM from that ES to avoid loops; log it Both AL ≠ 0 and equal Insert the Type 1 argument at offset LBL+LNL+FL of the Type 3 SID

Example from the RFC: Type 3 2001:db8:1:fbd1:: (structure 32/16/16, AL 16) plus Type 1 argument aaaa gives the data-plane SID 2001:db8:1:fbd1:aaaa::. With a 32-bit function on another bridge domain, the same argument lands one hextet further right — something a plain OR could not express.

Common Pitfalls

  • Older RFC 9252-only implementations that OR the two SIDs interoperate only when both routes advertise the same SID structure. Mixed structures require RFC 9819 support on the ingress PE.
  • An egress PE must use the same AL for all local Ethernet Segments in a broadcast domain.
  • Do not "simplify" the Type 1 encoding by zeroing LBL/LNL/FL — it breaks backward compatibility with RFC 9252 receivers.
  • ESI filtering is not needed with the "Local Bias" method (RFC 8365), without multihoming, or without E-Tree leaf BUM traffic.

docs.title: RFC 9855 - TI-LFA
docs.text: Field Value Title Topology Independent Fast Reroute Using Segment Routing Authors A. Bashandy, S. Litkowski, C. Filsfils, P. Francois, B. Decraene, D. Voyer Date October 2025 Status Proposed Standard Working group RTGWG (draft-ietf-rtgwg-segment-routing-ti-lfa) Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9855

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9855 defines Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA), the fast-reroute mechanism for node and adjacency segments in Segment Routing networks. It builds on LFA (RFC 5286), Remote LFA (RFC 7490) and Directed LFA, and extends them to provide guaranteed coverage in any two-connected network running a link-state IGP — hence "topology independent". It protects against the failure of a single link, a single node or a single SRLG.

The defining choice is to repair onto the expected post-convergence path: the path the PLR will use once the IGP has converged without the failed resource. Because the repair path matches the final path, traffic does not move twice, and operators do not need to tune tie-breaks between many possible backups. The PLR encodes the repair path as a short repair list (RL) of node and adjacency segments; for SRv6, the list is added with an RFC 8986 headend behavior.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 2.1 Terminology P-space, extended P-space, Q-space, SPT_old/SPT_new, explicit path EP(P,Q) 3 Base Principle Pre-compute the post-convergence SPT and encode it as a loop-free segment list 4 P-space and Q-space over post-convergence paths Computing the extended P-space and Q-space along the post-convergence path, and scaling the Q-space computation 5 TI-LFA Repair Path Direct neighbor (5.1), PQ node (5.2), adjacent P and Q (5.3), distant P and Q (5.4) 6 Repair lists for SR segments What to do when the active segment is a node segment or an adjacency segment 7 Data-plane considerations MPLS label handling (7.1) and SRv6 (7.2) 8 TI-LFA and SR Algorithms Protecting Flex-Algo SIDs with the algorithm's own constraints 9 Adjacency segments in the repair list Using unprotected Adj-SIDs to avoid double FRR App. A Post-convergence path Why repairing onto it is better App. B Real topologies Repair-list size distribution on nine networks

docs.title: P-Space, Q-Space, and PQ Node
docs.text: Concept Definition P-space P(R,X) Routers reachable from R on pre-convergence shortest paths without any of those paths (including ECMP splits) crossing the protected resource X Extended P-space The union of the P-spaces of R's neighbors, excluding neighbors reached via X Q-space Q(D,X) Routers from which the destination is reached without any path (including ECMP splits) crossing X PQ node A node in both the (extended) P-space and the Q-space; the term comes from RFC 7490 P node / Q node Nodes in only one of the two spaces; a repair through them needs an explicit path between them

docs.title: Repair List Construction
docs.text:
Section Scenario Repair list Comparable to 5.1 A direct neighbor on the post-convergence path is in P and Q Empty (new outgoing interface only) Post-convergence LFA 5.2 A PQ node exists <Node-SID(PQ)> Remote LFA 5.3 P and Q nodes are adjacent <Node-SID(P), Adj-SID(P→Q)> Directed LFA 5.4 P and Q nodes are distant <Node-SID(P), explicit path to Q> —

When the packet's active segment is a node segment, it stays on the packet and the RL is added in front of it (§6.1). When it is an adjacency segment, the PLR repairs toward the far end of that adjacency (§6.2).

For SRv6 (§7.2) the computation is unchanged. Adjacency SIDs are globally routable, so the list is often shorter than on SR-MPLS. A transit PLR adds the RL with an RFC 8986 §5 headend behavior; a PLR that is also a segment endpoint for the packet first executes its endpoint behavior.

docs.title: Protection Types
docs.text: Protection Level What is Protected Computation Link Protection Single link failure Post-convergence SPF excluding the protected link Node Protection Failure of the neighbor on the primary link Post-convergence SPF excluding that neighbor and all its links SRLG Protection Links sharing fate with the primary link Post-convergence SPF excluding the configured set of links sharing a risk group with it

docs.title: TI-LFA vs Other FRR Mechanisms
docs.text: Mechanism Published coverage Requires SR Repairs onto post-convergence path Topology dependent LFA (RFC 5286) 67–99% per prefix on 11 SP cores (RFC 6571) No Not necessarily Yes Remote LFA (RFC 7490) 97.5–100% link protection on 14 topologies (RFC 7490) No (LDP tunnel) Not necessarily Yes TI-LFA Any two-connected network; >99% with ≤ 1 SID for link protection (App. B) Yes Yes No

docs.title: Microloops
docs.text:
TI-LFA is local to the PLR and does not prevent microloops elsewhere during convergence. The RFC notes that if the PLR converges early and stops using its TI-LFA path, especially one built per §5.2–5.4, microloops can appear. It recommends combining TI-LFA with microloop-avoidance techniques such as the local convergence delay of RFC 8333.

Common Pitfalls

  • TI-LFA requires Segment Routing to be enabled. Without SR, the repair segment list cannot be constructed.
  • Repair lists are limited by the PLR's maximum SID depth; some platforms skip a backup that needs more SIDs than they can impose.
  • Node protection is strictly stronger than link protection but may produce longer repair segment lists, and the node-protecting path is used even when only the link failed.
  • SRLG protection requires that SRLG membership be consistently configured across all nodes. Inconsistent SRLG definitions lead to inadequate protection.
  • The post-convergence path computation assumes all nodes reconverge to the same topology. Asymmetric link costs or misconfigured metrics can invalidate this assumption.
  • TI-LFA protects the data plane within 50ms, but the control plane still needs full IGP convergence. During the window between FRR activation and convergence, traffic follows the repair path, which may differ from the final converged path.

docs.title: RFC 9857 - BGP-LS Advertisement of SR Policies
docs.text: Field Value Title Advertisement of Segment Routing Policies Using BGP - Link State Authors S. Previdi, K. Talaulikar (Ed.), J. Dong, H. Gredler, J. Tantsura Date October 2025 Status Proposed Standard Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9857

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9514 lets a controller learn SRv6 topology (locators, SIDs) through BGP-LS. RFC 9857 adds the other half: the state of SR Policies instantiated on headends. Each SR Policy candidate path — whether configured locally, pushed via PCEP, or pushed via the BGP SR Policy SAFI — can be reported with its Binding SID, state, constraints, and segment lists, for both SR-MPLS and SRv6.

This matters when the headend does not speak PCEP (management-based PCE), when a parent PCE needs a global view from child PCEs, or when a service-placement system or NMS needs to see which policies exist and whether they are up. It closes the loop for the BGP SR Policy SAFI (RFC 9830): controllers push policies with BGP and read their operational state back with BGP-LS.

The BGP-LS producer can be the headend itself or a PCE relaying what its PCCs report.

docs.text:
Value Meaning 1 / 2 / 3 PCEP / BGP SR Policy / Configuration (CLI, YANG, NETCONF) — reported by the headend 10 / 20 / 30 Same origins, reported by a PCE acting as the BGP-LS producer

Common Pitfalls

  • The NLRI reports state at candidate-path granularity; composite candidate paths are out of scope.
  • Large policy counts produce many BGP-LS updates. Check whether the platform lets you filter which policies are exported.
  • The Local Node Descriptor identifies the headend, even when a PCE is the producer — do not mistake it for the BGP-LS speaker.
  • Other TE path types (e.g., RSVP-TE LSPs) are handled by a separate draft, not this RFC.

docs.title: RFC 9860 - MoFRR Based on TI-LFA
docs.text: Field Value Title Multicast-Only Fast Reroute (MoFRR) Based on Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA) Fast Reroute Authors Y. Liu, M. McBride, Z. Zhang, J. Xie, C. Lin Date October 2025 Status Informational Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9860

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
MoFRR (RFC 7431) protects PIM multicast by joining the same (S,G) on two upstream paths and switching to the standby stream on failure. Its weakness is how it picks the secondary upstream hop: it relies on classic LFA, so in many topologies no loop-free secondary exists and MoFRR simply cannot protect the flow.

RFC 9860 borrows the repair path that TI-LFA already computes for unicast — which has full topology coverage — and uses it to build the standby multicast tree. The catch is that PIM joins must be processed hop by hop to create state on every router, so they cannot just be tunneled along the repair segment list. Instead, the receiver-side router translates the repair segments into existing PIM RPF Vector attributes:

  • a Node SID / End SID (the P-node or PQ-node) becomes an RPF Vector (RFC 5496) carrying that node's address;
  • an Adjacency SID / End.X SID (P-node → Q-node link) becomes an Explicit RPF Vector (RFC 7891) carrying the far-end interface address.

The secondary join follows these vectors hop by hop, creating PIM state along the TI-LFA path. It works for both SR-MPLS and SRv6 IGP SIDs, and needs no new protocol extensions — only that every router on the backup join path supports RPF Vectors.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 2.1 LFA for MoFRR Why LFA-based secondary UMH fails in common topologies 2.2 TI-LFA for MoFRR Why a segment list cannot be used directly for PIM joins 3 Solution Mapping Node/Adjacency SIDs to RPF Vector and Explicit RPF Vector 4 Illustration Worked SR-MPLS and SRv6 example 5 Operations RPF Vector support requirements and debugging with mtrace

docs.title: SID-to-PIM Mapping
docs.text:
TI-LFA repair element PIM Join attribute Effect Node SID / SRv6 End SID of P (or PQ) node RPF Vector (Type 0) with node address Join is routed toward the P-node instead of the source Adj-SID / SRv6 End.X SID from P to Q Explicit RPF Vector (Type 4) with remote interface address P-node sends the join across that specific link (after last vector) No vector Normal RPF toward the source from the Q-node

When a single PQ-node exists, only one RPF Vector is needed.

Common Pitfalls

  • Every router on the backup join path must understand RPF Vectors. A router that does not must strip them — leaving them in can loop the join back.
  • Scope is a single IGP area; exit routers and inter-domain links are not protected.
  • Micro-loops during reconvergence are not addressed for PIM.
  • This protects PIM trees. It does not apply to SRv6-native replication (RFC 9524 / RFC 9960) or BIER.
  • It is Informational and optional: deployments must explicitly configure when secondary joins with vectors are sent.

docs.title: RFC 9960 - SR P2MP Policy
docs.text: Field Value Title Segment Routing Point-to-Multipoint Policy Authors R. Parekh (Ed.), D. Voyer (Ed.), C. Filsfils, H. Bidgoli, Z. Zhang Date April 2026 Status Proposed Standard Updates RFC 9524 Link datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9960

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
RFC 9960 is the architecture behind Tree-SID. It defines the SR P2MP Policy: a construct, identified by <Root, Tree-ID>, that names a root node and a set of leaf nodes and carries one or more candidate paths (CPs) with constraints and optimization objectives, reusing the candidate-path model and selection rules of RFC 9256.

A controller (typically a PCE) computes a P2MP tree instance (PTI) for each candidate path and instantiates it by programming RFC 9524 Replication segments on the root, the intermediate replication nodes, and the leaves. The Replication-SID at the root is the Tree-SID; the RFC recommends reusing the same value at every node of the instance to simplify troubleshooting. For SRv6, the Replication-SID is the FUNCT part of the SID, so even with a common Tree-SID value the locator differs per node.

It works for both SR-MPLS and SRv6, and it updates RFC 9524 by giving the Replication-ID a precise structure: <Root, Tree-ID, Instance-ID>.

docs.title: Key Sections
docs.text: Section Topic Description 2 SR P2MP Policy Identification, components, candidate paths and tree instances 3 Steering Local-policy steering at the root vs BSID/Tree-SID steering from upstream 4 P2MP Tree Instance Leaf Replication segments, shared Replication segments, forwarding 5 Controller Tree compute, SID management, instantiation order, protection App. A Illustration SR-MPLS and SRv6 examples with adjacent and non-adjacent replication

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
Identifier Size / Scope Purpose Tree-ID 32-bit, unique per root Identifies the SR P2MP Policy together with the root address Instance-ID 16-bit, unique per policy Identifies one PTI (e.g., old and new instance during make-before-break) Replication-ID <Root, Tree-ID, Instance-ID> Updated RFC 9524 identifier; full control-plane key adds Node-ID Tree-SID Replication-SID at the root Data-plane identifier of the PTI BSID Per policy Steers traffic into the policy when the root is not the domain ingress

Shared Replication segments (for example, one protecting the X→Y adjacency for many trees) use Root = ::/0.0.0.0 and Instance-ID = 0. The simple 32-bit Replication-ID of RFC 9524 maps to <::, Tree-ID, 0>.

docs.title: How a Tree Is Built
docs.text:
graph TD
    PCE[Controller / PCE] -.->|Replication segment| R[Root]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| M[Replication node]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| L1[Leaf 1]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| L2[Leaf 2]
    PCE -.->|Replication segment| L3[Leaf 3]
    R -->|copy, DA = M Replication-SID| M
    R -->|copy, DA = L1 Replication-SID| L1
    M -->|copy| L2
    M -->|copy| L3
Step Controller action 1 Learn topology and node P2MP capability 2 Compute a loop-free tree for the active CP (constraints from RFC 9256 SR Policy) 3 Assign Replication-SIDs (from SRLB for SR-MPLS, or reserved blocks) and the BSID 4 Program leaves and intermediate nodes first, then the root, then activate the instance 5 On topology change, recompute — optionally via make-before-break with a new Instance-ID

docs.title: SRv6-Specific Rules
docs.text: Rule Why Leaf nodes must have a Replication segment No penultimate-hop popping: the Tree-SID is in the IPv6 DA Multiple services on one PTI need a service-context SID as the last SID in the SRH Leaves derive the VPN/EVPN context from it Non-adjacent downstream nodes are reached via the Replication-SID's locator, or an optional segment list Same mechanics as RFC 9524 Section 2.2

docs.title: Protection
docs.text:
Type Mechanism Local Backup SR Policies per replication branch, or node-local LFA / TI-LFA plus micro-loop avoidance Path A backup CP whose PTIs are disjoint from the active CP's PTIs

Common Pitfalls

  • RFC 9960 defines the architecture, not the signaling. PCEP (draft-ietf-pce-sr-p2mp-policy) and BGP (draft-ietf-idr-sr-p2mp-policy) encodings are still Internet-Drafts, so vendor implementations may differ.
  • Only one PTI of a CP may be active at a time; two active instances deliver duplicate traffic to leaves.
  • Allocating Replication-SIDs from the SRGB is not recommended — trees are local state and can exhaust the global block.
  • A statically provisioned tree does not adapt to topology changes.
  • If the root's Replication segment fails to install, the controller should tear the instance down rather than leave a partial tree.

docs.title: BGP Overlay Services over SRv6
docs.text: SRv6 provides a clean, unified underlay for delivering L3VPN and L2VPN (EVPN) services using BGP — without MPLS, without LDP, without RSVP-TE. Just IPv6 + BGP.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph Overlay - BGP Control Plane
        BGP1[PE1 BGP] <-->|MP-BGP with SRv6 SIDs| BGP2[PE2 BGP]
    end

    subgraph Underlay - SRv6 Data Plane
        PE1[PE1] -->|SRv6 Transport| P1[P Node]
        P1 -->|SRv6 Transport| PE2[PE2]
    end

    CE1[CE1 - Customer] --- PE1
    CE2[CE2 - Customer] --- PE2

Key principle: BGP carries service information (VPN prefixes, EVPN routes) with SRv6 SIDs instead of MPLS labels. The SRv6 SID tells the remote PE exactly what to do with the packet (decap to which VRF, cross-connect to which interface, etc.).

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. PE1 learns customer prefix 10.1.0.0/24 from CE1 in VRF CUSTOMER-A
  2. PE1 advertises via MP-BGP VPNv4/VPNv6 with an SRv6 SID instead of a VPN label:
    • Prefix: 10.1.0.0/24
    • Next-Hop: PE1 IPv6 address
    • SRv6 Service SID: fcbb:bb01:0001::DT4 (End.DT4 behavior)
  3. PE2 receives the BGP update, installs the route
  4. When PE2 receives traffic for 10.1.0.0/24, it encapsulates with:
    • IPv6 DA = fcbb:bb01:0001::DT4
    • Inner packet = original IPv4
  5. PE1 receives, matches End.DT4 SID, decapsulates, looks up in VRF CUSTOMER-A

docs.title: SRv6 SID Allocation Modes
docs.text:
Mode Description SID per... Per-VRF One SID shared by all prefixes in a VRF VRF Per-CE One SID per CE neighbor CE Per-Prefix Unique SID for each prefix Prefix

Per-VRF is most common

Per-VRF allocation (End.DT4 / End.DT6) is the default and most scalable option. The SID says "decap and lookup in this VRF table."

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! VRF definition
vrf CUSTOMER-A
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  import route-target 100:1
  export route-target 100:1
 !
!

!! BGP with SRv6
router bgp 65000
 address-family vpnv4 unicast
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
  !
 !
 vrf CUSTOMER-A
  rd 100:1
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   segment-routing srv6
    locator MAIN
    alloc mode per-vrf
   !
  !
 !
!

set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A instance-type vrf
set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A route-distinguisher 100:1
set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A vrf-target target:100:1
set routing-instances CUSTOMER-A protocols bgp source-packet-routing srv6 locator myloc

docs.title: EVPN over SRv6
docs.text: EVPN (Ethernet VPN) provides L2 services (E-Line, E-LAN, E-Tree) and integrated L2/L3 services over SRv6 transport.

docs.title: EVPN Route Types with SRv6
docs.text: Route Type Name SRv6 Behavior Type 2 MAC/IP Advertisement End.DX2 or End.DT2 Type 3 Inclusive Multicast BUM traffic handling Type 5 IP Prefix Route End.DT4 / End.DT6 (IP-VRF)

docs.title: EVPN-VPWS (E-Line) with SRv6
docs.text:
Point-to-point L2 service using End.DX2 behavior:

CE1 ──[L2 Frame]──► PE1 ──[IPv6(DA=PE2::DX2)][SRH][L2 Frame]──► PE2 ──[L2 Frame]──► CE2

The End.DX2 SID tells PE2: "decapsulate and cross-connect this L2 frame to the specified attachment circuit."

docs.title: EVPN-VXLAN vs EVPN-SRv6
docs.text: Aspect EVPN-VXLAN EVPN-SRv6 Encapsulation VXLAN (UDP) SRv6 (IPv6 + SRH) Underlay IPv4 or IPv6 IPv6 native TE capability Limited Full SR Policy support Network programming None Rich (service chaining, slicing) MTU overhead 50 bytes 40 bytes (no SRH) to 56+ bytes (with SRH)

docs.title: BGP SRv6 Service TLV (RFC 9252)
docs.text:
RFC 9252 defines how SRv6 SID information is carried in BGP updates using the SRv6 Services TLVs within the BGP Prefix-SID attribute:

BGP Update Message:
  ├── NLRI: 10.1.0.0/24 (VPNv4)
  ├── Next-Hop: 2001:db8::1
  ├── Extended Community: RT 100:1
  └── BGP Prefix-SID Attribute:
      └── SRv6 L3 Service TLV:
          ├── SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb01:0001::DT4
          ├── SRv6 SID Behavior: End.DT4 (19)
          └── SRv6 SID Structure:
              ├── Locator Block Length: 32
              ├── Locator Node Length: 16
              ├── Function Length: 16
              └── Argument Length: 0

docs.title: SID Transposition
docs.text: To save space in BGP updates, the function part of the SID can be transposed into (encoded within) the VPN prefix itself, rather than carrying the full 128-bit SID. This is an optimization defined in RFC 9252.

!! Show VPNv4 routes with SRv6 SIDs
show bgp vpnv4 unicast vrf CUSTOMER-A

!! Show SRv6 SID details
show segment-routing srv6 sid

!! Show EVPN routes
show bgp l2vpn evpn

vtysh -c "show bgp ipv4 vpn"
vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn"
vtysh -c "show segment-routing srv6 locator"

docs.title: CLOS Fabrics & Load Balancing
docs.text: Modern data center networks use CLOS (Spine-Leaf) topologies with multiple equal-cost paths. SRv6 provides deterministic traffic placement across these paths, solving the fundamental limitations of traditional ECMP hashing.

docs.title: CLOS Topology Refresher
docs.text:
A CLOS fabric provides full bisectional bandwidth between any two leaf switches through multiple spine switches:

graph TB
    S1[Spine 1] --- L1[Leaf 1]
    S1 --- L2[Leaf 2]
    S1 --- L3[Leaf 3]
    S1 --- L4[Leaf 4]
    S2[Spine 2] --- L1
    S2 --- L2
    S2 --- L3
    S2 --- L4
    S3[Spine 3] --- L1
    S3 --- L2
    S3 --- L3
    S3 --- L4

docs.title: The ECMP Problem
docs.text:
Traditional ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) uses a hash of packet headers (5-tuple) to select a path. This works well for diverse traffic, but fails with:

  • Elephant flows — large, long-lived flows that saturate a single path
  • Synchronized workloads — AI/ML training where thousands of flows start and end simultaneously
  • Hash collisions — multiple flows hashing to the same spine, causing congestion while other spines are idle
  • Hash polarization — similar hash results at multiple layers of the fabric

docs.title: SRv6 Deterministic Path Placement
docs.text:
Instead of relying on hashing, SRv6 allows the source (host, NIC, or controller) to explicitly choose which spine each flow traverses:

Traditional ECMP:
  Packet → Hash(5-tuple) → Spine selection    (probabilistic)

SRv6 Path Placement:
  Packet → SRv6 SID(Spine-N) → Spine selection  (deterministic)

Each spine is assigned an SRv6 uSID. The source encapsulates the packet with the desired spine's SID, guaranteeing the path.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text: Aspect ECMP SRv6 Deterministic Path selection Hash-based (probabilistic) Explicit (deterministic) Elephant flow handling Poor (collisions) Optimal (controlled placement) Fabric utilization 60-80% typical Near 100% achievable Application awareness None Source can control path Flowlet support Limited Native via SID switching

docs.title: What are Flowlets?
docs.text:
A flowlet is a burst of packets within a flow, separated by idle gaps. Unlike flow-level load balancing (which pins an entire flow to one path), flowlet-based load balancing can reassign traffic to different paths between bursts without causing reordering.

Flow timeline:
  ████████──gap──████████──gap──████████──gap──████████
  Flowlet 1       Flowlet 2       Flowlet 3       Flowlet 4
  → Spine 1       → Spine 2       → Spine 3       → Spine 1

docs.title: GLB with SRv6
docs.text:
Global Load Balancing (GLB) uses SRv6 to steer flowlets across different spines:

  1. Monitor fabric link utilization or congestion signals
  2. Assign each new flowlet to the least-loaded spine via SRv6 SID
  3. Reroute between flowlet gaps — no packet reordering

This is especially powerful for AI training workloads where collective operations (AllReduce, AllGather) create predictable traffic bursts with natural gaps.

docs.title: BGP in CLOS + SRv6
docs.text: BGP is the standard routing protocol for CLOS fabrics (replacing OSPF/IS-IS in many DC deployments). With SRv6:

docs.title: eBGP Underlay
docs.text:
Each leaf-spine link runs an eBGP session (each switch has its own ASN or uses BGP unnumbered):

Leaf ASN 65001 ──eBGP── Spine ASN 65100
Leaf ASN 65002 ──eBGP── Spine ASN 65100

docs.title: SRv6 Locator Advertisement
docs.text: Each switch advertises its SRv6 locator via BGP, making SRv6 SIDs reachable across the fabric.

docs.title: Overlay Services
docs.text:
BGP EVPN over SRv6 provides:

  • L2 bridging across the fabric (VXLAN replacement)
  • L3 routing between VRFs
  • Distributed anycast gateway at every leaf

docs.title: SRv6 vs VXLAN in Data Centers
docs.text: Aspect VXLAN + ECMP SRv6 uSID Encapsulation UDP/VXLAN IPv6 + SRH (or just DA with uSID) Path control Hash-based only Deterministic or hash-based TE capability None Full SR Policy support Overhead 50 bytes 40 bytes (no SRH) or 56+ bytes (with SRH) Flowlet support Limited Native via SID update between bursts Standards RFC 7348 RFC 8986, RFC 9800

  3. draft-filsfils-srv6ops-srv6-ai-backend - SRv6 deterministic path placement for AI backend networks
  4. RFC 9800 - Compressed SRv6 Segment List Encoding - uSID compression enabling efficient spine selection

docs.title: EVPN Multihoming
docs.text:
EVPN multihoming (often shortened to EVPN-MH or EVPN multi-homing) lets a customer device — a switch, router, server or access node — attach to two or more PE routers over a single logical link, with the PEs coordinating through BGP instead of a proprietary MC-LAG control channel. It is defined in RFC 7432 (the EVPN base specification) and refined by RFC 8584 (DF election framework). RFC 9252 and RFC 9819 carry the same machinery over SRv6.

This page covers the generic mechanisms first — they are identical whether the core runs MPLS, VXLAN or SRv6 — and then the parts that change with an SRv6 data plane.

graph LR
    CE[CE<br/>LAG with 2 member links] ---|ES 1| PE1[PE1]
    CE ---|ES 1| PE2[PE2]
    PE1 <--> CORE((MPLS / SRv6 core))
    PE2 <--> CORE
    CORE <--> PE3[PE3 remote]
    PE3 --- RCE[Remote CE]

docs.title: Ethernet Segment and ESI
docs.text:
An Ethernet Segment (ES) is the set of links that connect one customer site to several PEs. From the CE's point of view it is usually a single LACP bundle; each PE sees one member link. Every PE attached to the segment configures the same Ethernet Segment Identifier (ESI).

The ESI is 10 octets: a 1-octet type followed by a 9-octet value (RFC 7432 §5). Two values are reserved: all zeros means "single-homed, no ES", and all FF (MAX-ESI) is reserved.

Type Value is built from Typical use 0 9 octets configured by the operator Most common; you pick a unique value per segment 1 CE LACP system MAC (6) + port key (2) + 0 Auto-derived from LACP when the CE runs LACP 2 IST root bridge MAC (6) + root bridge priority (2) + 0 CE is a bridged LAN running MSTP; the PE learns the values from BPDUs 3 System MAC (6) + local discriminator (3) Auto-generated by the PE from a MAC 4 Router ID (4) + local discriminator (4) + 0 Auto-generated from the PE/CE router ID 5 AS number (4) + local discriminator (4) + 0 Auto-generated from an ASN

Type 0 vs auto-derived ESIs

Type 0 is explicit and portable between vendors. Auto-derived types save configuration on large access networks, but check what your vendor actually derives from: RFC 7432 Type 1 uses the CE's LACP system MAC and port key, while Junos auto-derive lacp builds the ESI from the PE's own LACP system ID and admin key (which must then be identical on every PE). Either way, all PEs on an all-active LAG must present the same LACP system ID to the CE, or the CE will not bundle the links.

docs.title: EVPN Routes Used for Multihoming
docs.text: Route Name Multihoming role Type 4 Ethernet Segment Discovery of the other PEs on the same ES and DF election. Carries the ES-Import Route Target (auto-derived from the ESI value for types 1–3), so only PEs on that ES import it Type 1 Ethernet A-D per ES Advertises the redundancy mode (single-active flag in the ESI Label extended community) and the split-horizon label/argument; withdrawing it is the mass withdrawal signal Type 1 Ethernet A-D per EVI Advertised per service instance; lets remote PEs build aliasing (all-active) or backup paths (single-active) Type 2 MAC/IP Advertisement MAC and ARP/ND bindings; synced between PEs on the same ES Type 3 Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag BUM delivery; in SRv6 also carries the End.DT2M SID Type 5 IP Prefix (RFC 9136) Routed prefixes, used by EVPN L3 multihoming

docs.title: All-Active vs Single-Active
docs.text:
All-active Single-active Who forwards known unicast Every PE on the ES Only the DF for that VLAN/EVI CE side One LAG across the PEs Separate links or LAG with standby members; the non-DF blocks its port for that service Remote PE behavior ECMP to all PEs on the ES (aliasing) Primary path to the DF, pre-programmed backup path to the non-DF BUM toward the CE Only the DF sends Only the DF sends Loop prevention needed Split-horizon filtering (BUM received from the ES must not be sent back into it) Not for the CE (the non-DF does not forward) Typical use Data center leaf pairs, access aggregation, bandwidth Hand-offs to devices that cannot run a cross-chassis LAG, strict per-VLAN active/standby

A third mode, port-active (RFC 9786, June 2025), elects one PE per interface rather than per VLAN — a drop-in replacement for MC-LAG active/standby. The DF election for port-active can use any of the algorithms below.

docs.title: Designated Forwarder (DF) Election
docs.text:
When the CE floods a broadcast or unknown-unicast frame, every PE on the ES would deliver remote BUM copies back to it. The DF is the one PE per that sends BUM toward the CE; the others drop it.

PEs learn each other through Type 4 routes, wait for the DF election timer (3 seconds by default) so all routes arrive, then run the election.

Algorithm Defined in How it picks the DF Trade-off Modulo / service carving (default) RFC 7432 §8.5 Sort PE IPs ascending (index 0..N-1); DF for VLAN V is index V mod N Simple, but when a PE joins or leaves, almost every VLAN moves HRW (Highest Random Weight) RFC 8584 §3 Each PE computes a hash weight of (VLAN, ESI, PE address); highest wins, ties go to the lowest IP Only the VLANs of the failed/added PE move; even spread with sparse VLAN IDs Preference-based RFC 9785 (June 2025) Operator sets a 2-octet preference per PE per ES; highest (DF Alg 2) or lowest (DF Alg 3) wins; the D (Don't Preempt) bit makes it non-revertive Deterministic primary/backup per ES; the norm for single-active designs AC-influenced (AC-DF) RFC 8584 Any of the above, but a PE whose attachment circuit is down for that EVI is excluded Avoids electing a DF that cannot actually forward

RFC 8584 also introduced the DF Election extended community on the Type 4 route: a 5-bit algorithm field (0 = modulo, 1 = HRW, ⅔ = highest/lowest preference) and a capability bitmap (D, AC-DF, …). If the PEs on a segment disagree, they all fall back to modulo. Vendor support varies: Cisco IOS-XR and Junos expose modulo and preference-based election in configuration, so check the release notes before designing around HRW.

Modulo example: ES with PE1 (192.0.2.1) and PE2 (192.0.2.2), N = 2
  Ordered list: [PE1, PE2]
  VLAN 100 → 100 mod 2 = 0 → PE1 is DF
  VLAN 101 → 101 mod 2 = 1 → PE2 is DF
  If you only use even VLANs, PE1 is DF for everything — HRW avoids this.

docs.title: Aliasing and Backup Path
docs.text:
A MAC address behind a multihomed CE may only be learned (and advertised in a Type 2 route) by one of the PEs — the one whose LAG member the CE hashed that flow onto. Without help, remote PEs would send all traffic for that MAC to that single PE.

Aliasing fixes this: each PE advertises an Ethernet A-D per EVI route for the ES. A remote PE that sees a Type 2 route with a non-zero ESI looks up every PE that advertised A-D per EVI for that ESI and load-balances across all of them, even the ones that never learned the MAC.

In single-active mode the same routes provide a backup path: the remote PE installs the DF as primary and the other PE as a pre-programmed backup, ready for fast switchover.

docs.title: Mass Withdrawal
docs.text:
If PE1 loses its link to a CE with 10 000 MACs, withdrawing 10 000 Type 2 routes takes time. Instead, PE1 withdraws a single Ethernet A-D per ES route. Every remote PE immediately removes PE1 from the next-hop set of all MACs associated with that ESI — a prefix-independent convergence step — and the individual Type 2 withdrawals follow in the background.

sequenceDiagram
    participant CE
    participant PE1
    participant PE2
    participant PE3 as PE3 (remote)

    Note over CE,PE1: Link CE–PE1 fails
    PE1->>PE3: Withdraw Ethernet A-D per ES (ESI 1)
    PE3->>PE3: Remove PE1 from every MAC/IP with ESI 1
    Note over PE3: All flows now go to PE2 only
    PE1->>PE3: (later) Withdraw individual Type 2 routes

docs.title: Split-Horizon Filtering
docs.text:
In all-active mode, a BUM frame from the CE arrives at PE1, which floods it to every PE in the EVI — including PE2, which is attached to the same ES. If PE2 is the DF, it would send the frame straight back to the CE, creating a loop or duplicate. Split-horizon stops this: the receiving PE must know which ES the frame came from and skip that ES.

How the "came from" information is carried depends on the data plane:

Data plane Mechanism Defined in MPLS ESI label: each PE advertises a label in its A-D per ES route; the ingress PE pushes the egress PE's ESI label beneath the EVPN label on BUM sent to it. The egress PE sees the label and does not forward onto that ES RFC 7432 §8.3 VXLAN / NVO Local bias: no label space for an ESI label, so the egress PE uses the outer source IP to recognize a peer on the same ES; the ingress PE always floods locally to its own ESs regardless of DF state RFC 8365 §8.3.1 SRv6 ESI-filtering argument (Arg.FE2) carried in the argument bits of the egress PE's End.DT2M SID — the SRv6 equivalent of the ESI label. Local bias is also allowed RFC 8986 §4.12, RFC 9252 §6.1.1/§6.3, RFC 9819

RFC 9746 (March 2025) lets PEs signal which method they use, with a Split-Horizon Type field in the ESI Label extended community: MPLS defaults to ESI-label filtering, VXLAN to local bias, and SRv6 defaults to ESI filtering but supports both. Local bias only works with all-active redundancy.

docs.title: EVPN Multihoming over SRv6
docs.text:
SRv6 has no label stack to push an ESI label onto, so the egress PE's local ES identifier travels as an argument inside the SID itself:

  1. Each PE allocates an End.DT2M SID per bridge domain for BUM traffic and advertises its LOC:FUNC part in the Type 3 (IMET) route.
  2. For each local ES it allocates an Arg.FE2 value and advertises it in the Type 1 A-D per ES route (SRv6 L2 Service TLV).
  3. When PE1 floods BUM that it received from ES 1 to PE2, it combines PE2's End.DT2M LOC:FUNC with PE2's Arg.FE2 for ES 1 into the destination address.
  4. PE2 executes End.DT2M: it decapsulates and floods into the bridge domain, excluding the interfaces of the ES identified by the argument.
PE2 Type 3 route:  End.DT2M LOC:FUNC = fc00:0:2:e002::   SID structure 32/16/16, AL 16
PE2 Type 1 route:  Arg.FE2 for ES 1  = 0x00a1             AL 16
PE1 → PE2, BUM received from ES 1:
    argument inserted at offset 32+16+16 = 64 bits
    DA = fc00:0:2:e002:a1::
PE2: End.DT2M with argument 0x00a1 → flood to every AC in the bridge domain except ES 1

Why RFC 9819 exists

RFC 9252 said the ingress PE SHOULD bitwise-OR the Type 3 SID and the Type 1 argument. That only works when both routes use the same SID structure; interop testing found implementations disagreeing. RFC 9819 (July 2025) replaces the OR with an explicit rule: insert the argument at offset LBL + LNL + FL taken from the Type 3 route's SID Structure, and stop forwarding BUM from that ES if the two routes announce different argument lengths. If you mix vendors on an SRv6 EVPN all-active segment, check RFC 9819 support first.

Known unicast does not need split-horizon. Remote PEs use End.DT2U (bridge-table lookup) or End.DX2 (cross-connect, for EVPN-VPWS) SIDs from the Type 1 per-EVI and Type 2 routes, and aliasing simply becomes ECMP across the SRv6 SIDs of all PEs on the ES. With uSID these service SIDs are typically uDT2U/uDT2M micro-SIDs on the PE's locator.

The underlay contributes too: TI-LFA protects the core paths between PEs, while mass withdrawal and aliasing protect the attachment circuit — the two mechanisms are complementary.

docs.title: EVPN L3 Multihoming (Routed CE)
docs.text:
When the CE is a router and the service is an L3VPN, the same ES concepts apply to a routed hand-off. draft-ietf-bess-evpn-l3mh-proto specifies EVPN L3 multihoming:

  1. CE connects to PE1 and PE2 via an Ethernet Segment (same ESI on both PEs)
  2. PEs discover each other via Type 4 routes and elect a DF
  3. ARP/ND entries learned by one PE are synced to the other with Type 2 routes, so either PE can route to the CE immediately
  4. Prefixes are advertised to remote PEs as Type 5 (or VPNv4/VPNv6) routes with SRv6 End.DT4/End.DT6/End.DT46 service SIDs
  5. Remote PEs ECMP across both PEs; on PE or link failure, the Type 1 per-ES withdrawal triggers fast reconvergence
Aspect L2 multihoming (EVPN) L3 multihoming (EVPN L3MH) Service type L2VPN / bridging L3VPN / routing CE attachment Bridge domain VRF / routed interface MAC learning Required Only for ARP/ND sync Split-horizon Per ES (ESI label / Arg.FE2) Not needed for routed traffic Prefix advertisement Type 2 (MAC/IP) Type 5 (IP Prefix) + Type 2 (ARP/ND sync) SRv6 service SIDs End.DT2U, End.DT2M, End.DX2 End.DT4, End.DT6, End.DT46

Interoperability

EVPN L3 multihoming has been demonstrated in multi-vendor interoperability tests (EANTC) with Cisco and Nokia using both SRv6 and SR-MPLS underlays.

docs.title: EVPN Multihoming vs MC-LAG
docs.text: EVPN multihoming MC-LAG / MLAG Control plane Standard BGP (RFC 7432) Vendor-specific (ICCP, peer-link) Number of PEs 2 or more Usually exactly 2 Peer link between PEs Not required Usually required Multivendor PE pair Possible No Works across a routed core (MPLS, VXLAN, SRv6) Yes Typically same site only

docs.title: Configuration Examples
docs.text:
Both PEs on the segment get the same ESI and redundancy mode. The examples use the type 0 ESI 00:11:22:33:44:55:66:77:88:99 with preference-based DF election (PE1 preferred).

Cisco IOS-XRJunos 
!! PE1 (use weight 50 on PE2)
interface Bundle-Ether10
 lacp system mac 0011.2233.4455
!
evpn
 interface Bundle-Ether10
  ethernet-segment
   identifier type 0 11.22.33.44.55.66.77.88.99
   !! all-active is the default; alternatives:
   !! load-balancing-mode single-active | port-active
   service-carving preference-based
    weight 100
  !
 !
 !! SRv6: EVPN services take SIDs from this locator
 segment-routing srv6
  locator MAIN
 !
!

# PE1 (use preference value 50 on PE2)
set interfaces ae0 esi 00:11:22:33:44:55:66:77:88:99
set interfaces ae0 esi all-active
set interfaces ae0 esi df-election-type preference value 100
# identical LACP system ID on every PE of the segment
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp active
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp system-id 00:11:22:33:44:55

ESI notation

IOS-XR takes the 9-octet value after type 0; Junos takes all 10 octets, and a manually configured Junos ESI must start with 00 (type 0). The two lines above describe the same segment. IOS-XR locator precedence for EVPN SRv6 SIDs is per-service, then per-EVI (evi N segment-routing srv6 → locator), then the global evpn segment-routing srv6 locator.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
• ESI mismatch: a typo in one PE's ESI silently turns an all-active segment into two single-homed sites — the CE sees duplicate BUM and MAC flaps.
  • LACP system ID: for an all-active LAG, every PE must present the same LACP system ID and key to the CE.
  • Mixed DF algorithms: PEs that advertise different DF algorithms fall back to modulo; check the DF Election extended community on the Type 4 routes.
  • Core isolation: if a PE loses all core connectivity but keeps its CE link up, the CE keeps hashing traffic into a black hole. Most implementations bring the access interface down on core isolation — enable it.
  • SRv6 argument length: on SRv6, the End.DT2M argument length must match between Type 1 and Type 3 routes (RFC 9819); mismatches stop BUM from that segment.
