docs.title: SR Policy
docs.text: SR Policy is the framework for expressing traffic engineering intent in Segment Routing networks (RFC 9256). Instead of hop-by-hop RSVP-TE signaling, an SR Policy encodes the entire path as a segment list at the headend — no per-flow state on transit nodes.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
RSVP-TE provides path control but requires:

  • Per-tunnel state on every transit router — signaling messages, path maintenance, bandwidth reservations
  • Multiple protocols — RSVP for tunnels, IGP for routing, PCEP for computation
  • Scalability limits — thousands of tunnels degrade control plane performance
  • Slow convergence — path recomputation and re-signaling on failure

SR Policy eliminates distributed state by encoding the path in the packet header itself.

docs.title: SR Policy Architecture (RFC 9256)
docs.text:
An SR Policy is identified by a tuple of (headend, color, endpoint):

Component Description Example Headend Router originating the policy PE1 (2001:db8::1) Color Numeric intent identifier (community) 100 (low-latency) Endpoint Destination of the policy PE2 (2001:db8::2)

docs.title: Candidate Paths
docs.text:
Each SR Policy contains one or more candidate paths, ordered by preference. Only the highest-preference valid path is active.

SR Policy (headend=PE1, color=100, endpoint=PE2)
  ├── Candidate Path (preference 200, PCE-computed)
  │     └── Segment List: [P1::1, P3::1, PE2::1]
  ├── Candidate Path (preference 150, BGP SR Policy)
  │     └── Segment List: [P2::1, PE2::1]
  └── Candidate Path (preference 100, local config)
        └── Segment List: [PE2::1]

Each candidate path can contain multiple segment lists with weights for weighted ECMP load balancing.

docs.title: SR Policy Lifecycle
docs.text:
graph TD
    H[Headend Router] -->|1. Policy created| CP1[Candidate Path 1 - Pref 200]
    H -->|1. Policy created| CP2[Candidate Path 2 - Pref 100]
    CP1 -->|2. Validated| SL1[Segment List A - Weight 50]
    CP1 -->|2. Validated| SL2[Segment List B - Weight 50]
    CP2 -->|Standby| SL3[Segment List C]
    SL1 -->|3. Active - ECMP| FWD[Forwarding]
    SL2 -->|3. Active - ECMP| FWD

docs.title: Policy Instantiation Methods
docs.text:
SR Policies can be created through three mechanisms, each with a default preference:

Method Default Preference Source Use Case Local configuration 100 CLI / YANG Static TE, fallback paths BGP SR Policy (SAFI 73) 100-200 Controller / RR Multi-domain, centralized TE PCEP 200 SR-PCE Dynamic computation, bandwidth-aware

docs.title: Local Configuration
docs.text:
Explicit segment lists defined on the headend. Simple, static, and useful as a fallback.

Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
segment-routing
 traffic-eng
  policy LOW-LATENCY-TO-PE2
   color 100 end-point ipv6 2001:db8::2
   candidate-paths
    preference 100
     explicit segment-list VIA-P1-P3
    !
   !
  !
  segment-list VIA-P1-P3
   index 10 srv6 sid fc00:0:1::
   index 20 srv6 sid fc00:0:3::
   index 30 srv6 sid fc00:0:2::
  !
 !
!

set protocols source-packet-routing segment-list VIA-P1-P3 srv6 hop1 sid fc00:0:1::
set protocols source-packet-routing segment-list VIA-P1-P3 srv6 hop2 sid fc00:0:3::
set protocols source-packet-routing segment-list VIA-P1-P3 srv6 hop3 sid fc00:0:2::
set protocols source-packet-routing sr-policy LOW-LATENCY-TO-PE2 color 100
set protocols source-packet-routing sr-policy LOW-LATENCY-TO-PE2 end-point 2001:db8::2
set protocols source-packet-routing sr-policy LOW-LATENCY-TO-PE2 segment-list VIA-P1-P3

docs.title: BGP SR Policy (SAFI 73)
docs.text:
A controller or route reflector distributes SR Policies via BGP using the SR Policy SAFI. This enables centralized traffic engineering across multiple domains.

The BGP update carries:

  • Distinguisher + Policy Color + Endpoint as NLRI
  • Tunnel Encapsulation attribute with segment lists, preference, binding SID

docs.title: PCE-Initiated Policies
docs.text:
An SR-PCE (Path Computation Element) computes constrained paths using topology learned via BGP-LS (RFC 9514) and installs them on headends via PCEP.

graph LR
    BGP_LS[BGP-LS Topology] -->|RFC 9514| PCE[SR-PCE Controller]
    PCE -->|PCEP - Computed Path| PE1[Headend PE1]
    PE1 -->|SRv6 Segment List| P1[P1]
    P1 --> P3[P3]
    P3 --> PE2[Egress PE2]
Cisco IOS-XR 
!! PCE configuration on headend
segment-routing
 traffic-eng
  pcc
   source-address ipv6 2001:db8::1
   pce address ipv6 2001:db8:ffff::1
    precedence 10
   !
  !
 !
!

docs.title: On-Demand Nexthop (ODN)
docs.text: ODN dynamically creates SR Policies when a BGP prefix with a color community is received, without any pre-provisioned policy on the headend. This is the most operationally scalable approach.

docs.title: How ODN Works
docs.text:
1. Remote PE advertises a VPN prefix with a color extended community (e.g., color 100)
  2. Local PE receives the prefix and matches it against an ODN template for that color
  3. If no SR Policy exists for that (color, endpoint), the headend automatically creates one
  4. The policy is computed locally or delegated to PCE based on template configuration
graph LR
    CE1[CE1] --> PE1[PE1 - Headend]
    PE1 -->|ODN creates SR Policy| CORE((SRv6 Core))
    CORE --> PE2[PE2 - Egress]
    PE2 --> CE2[CE2]
    PE2 -.->|BGP: prefix + color 100| PE1

docs.title: ODN Configuration
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! ODN template for color 100 (low-latency)
segment-routing
 traffic-eng
  on-demand color 100
   dynamic
    metric type latency
   !
   srv6
    locator MAIN
   !
  !
 !
!

!! ODN with PCE delegation
segment-routing
 traffic-eng
  on-demand color 200
   dynamic
    pcep
    !
    metric type te
   !
  !
 !
!

set protocols source-packet-routing sr-preference-override color 100 routing-policy LOW-LATENCY
set policy-options policy-statement LOW-LATENCY term 1 then install-nexthop lsp-regex ".*"

docs.title: Binding SID (BSID)
docs.text: A Binding SID is a single SID that represents an entire SR Policy. Any packet arriving with a BSID as the active segment is steered into the associated policy's segment list.

docs.title: Key Properties
docs.text: Property Description Abstraction Hides the internal path — remote domains only see one SID Scalability Reduces segment list depth for multi-domain paths Stitching Chains policies across domains: [BSID-Domain1, BSID-Domain2] Dynamic BSID can be allocated dynamically and signaled via BGP or PCEP

docs.title: Multi-Domain BSID Chaining
docs.text:
Ingress segment list:  [BSID_AS1, BSID_AS2, PE-Remote::DT4]

At AS1 border:  BSID_AS1 expands to [P1::1, ASBR1::1]
At AS2 border:  BSID_AS2 expands to [P5::1, PE-Remote::1]
Cisco IOS-XR 
segment-routing
 traffic-eng
  policy TO-AS2
   binding-sid srv6 dynamic behavior ub6-insert-reduced
   color 500 end-point ipv6 2001:db8:2::1
   candidate-paths
    preference 100
     explicit segment-list VIA-ASBR
    !
   !
  !
 !
!

BSID and inter-domain TE

For a deep dive into Binding SID for multi-domain traffic engineering, see Inter-Domain SRv6. For BSID in the context of SR-MPLS/SRv6 migration, see Interworking & Migration.

docs.title: Color Steering
docs.text:
BGP color extended communities map service intent to SR Policies. When a VPN prefix carries a color, the headend PE automatically steers traffic into the matching SR Policy.

Color Intent Mechanism 100 Low latency Flex-Algo 128 or SR Policy with latency metric 200 High bandwidth Flex-Algo 129 or SR Policy with bandwidth constraint 300 Disjoint paths Pair of SR Policies with disjointness constraint 400 Cost-optimized Default IGP metric (best-cost path)

docs.title: How Color Steering Works
docs.text:
1. Customer VRF route is received via BGP with color:100 extended community
  2. Headend PE looks up SR Policy with (color=100, endpoint=BGP-next-hop)
  3. If found → traffic is steered into the policy
  4. If not found + ODN enabled → policy is created on demand

Color values are locally significant

Color values have no global meaning — operators define their own mapping between color values and intent. Consistent color assignment across the network is an operational requirement.

docs.title: Dynamic Path Computation
docs.text: SR Policies can be computed dynamically based on optimization objectives and constraints:

docs.title: Optimization Objectives
docs.text: Objective Description TE metric Minimize traffic engineering metric (admin-defined) Latency Minimize end-to-end delay Hop count Minimize number of nodes traversed IGP metric Minimize standard IGP cost

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Constraint Description Affinity (include/exclude) Links must match color/admin-group requirements SRLG Path must avoid specific shared risk link groups Bandwidth Path must have minimum available bandwidth Disjointness Two policies must not share links/nodes/SRLGs

docs.title: Reoptimization
docs.text:
Dynamic policies can be reoptimized when:

  • Topology changes (link up/down, metric change)
  • Periodic timer expires
  • Bandwidth threshold crossed
  • Manual trigger

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! Show all SR Policies
show segment-routing traffic-eng policy summary

!! Show specific policy details
show segment-routing traffic-eng policy color 100 endpoint ipv6 2001:db8::2

docs.title: SRH Mechanics & Packet Walk
docs.text:
Leer en español · 日本語で読む

Understanding how the Segment Routing Header (SRH) works at the packet level is essential for troubleshooting and designing SRv6 networks. This page walks through the mechanics step by step.

docs.title: Key Fields
docs.text:
Field Size Description Next Header 8 bits Type of the next header (e.g., 41 = IPv6, 4 = IPv4) Hdr Ext Len 8 bits Length of SRH in 8-octet units, not including first 8 octets Routing Type 8 bits Always 4 for SRH Segments Left (SL) 8 bits Index into the segment list pointing to the current active segment Last Entry 8 bits Index of the last element in the segment list (0-based) Flags 8 bits Currently unused (reserved) Tag 16 bits Packet grouping / marking Segment List 128 bits each Ordered list of SIDs in reverse order

Reverse order!

The segment list is encoded in reverse order: Segment List[0] is the last SID to be processed, and Segment List[n] is the first. The Segments Left pointer starts at n and decrements toward 0.

docs.title: Complete Packet Walk
docs.text:
Let's trace a packet through a 3-node SRv6 network:

Source (A) → Node B → Node C → Destination (D)

SRv6 SIDs:
  B::100  = End behavior on Node B
  C::200  = End.DT4 behavior on Node C (decap to IPv4)

docs.title: Step 1: Ingress (Source A)
docs.text:
Source A receives an IPv4 packet destined to 10.0.0.2 and needs to steer it through B then C.

Original packet:
  [IPv4: 10.0.0.1 → 10.0.0.2][Payload]

After SRv6 encapsulation:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Outer IPv6 Header                         │
  │   Source:      A::1                       │
  │   Destination: B::100  ← Active SID      │
  │   Next Header: 43 (Routing)               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ SRH                                       │
  │   Segments Left: 1                        │
  │   Last Entry:    1                        │
  │   Segment List[0]: C::200  (last SID)     │
  │   Segment List[1]: B::100  (first SID)    │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Inner IPv4 Header                         │
  │   10.0.0.1 → 10.0.0.2                    │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Payload                                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

DA = Active SID

The IPv6 Destination Address always equals the currently active SID (Segment List[Segments Left]).

docs.title: Step 2: Transit (Node B — End Behavior)
docs.text:
Node B receives the packet. The DA matches its local SID B::100 with End behavior:

  1. Decrement Segments Left: 1 → 0
  2. Copy Segment List[0] to IPv6 DA: DA = C::200
  3. Forward based on new DA
After Node B processing:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Outer IPv6 Header                         │
  │   Source:      A::1                       │
  │   Destination: C::200  ← Updated!        │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ SRH                                       │
  │   Segments Left: 0     ← Decremented!    │
  │   Last Entry:    1                        │
  │   Segment List[0]: C::200                 │
  │   Segment List[1]: B::100                 │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Inner IPv4: 10.0.0.1 → 10.0.0.2          │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Payload                                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Step 3: Egress (Node C — End.DT4 Behavior)
docs.text:
Node C receives the packet. The DA matches its local SID C::200 with End.DT4 behavior:

  1. SL = 0, so this is the last segment
  2. Decapsulate: remove outer IPv6 + SRH
  3. Lookup the inner IPv4 DA in the specified VRF table
  4. Forward the original IPv4 packet
After Node C processing:
  [IPv4: 10.0.0.1 → 10.0.0.2][Payload]  ← Original packet restored!

docs.title: Step 4: Delivery
docs.text: The original IPv4 packet is delivered to destination 10.0.0.2 as if SRv6 was never involved.

docs.title: Packet Walk Sequence Diagram
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Source A
    participant B as Node B (End)
    participant C as Node C (End.DT4)
    participant D as Destination

    A->>A: Receive IPv4 packet for 10.0.0.2
    A->>A: Encap: IPv6(DA=B::100) + SRH[C::200, B::100] + IPv4
    A->>B: Forward to B::100 (SL=1)

    B->>B: Match B::100 → End behavior
    B->>B: SL: 1→0, DA: B::100→C::200
    B->>C: Forward to C::200 (SL=0)

    C->>C: Match C::200 → End.DT4 behavior
    C->>C: Decapsulate, lookup IPv4 in VRF
    C->>D: Forward original IPv4 packet

docs.title: PSP, USP, and USD Flavors
docs.text:
SRv6 endpoints can support different processing flavors that optimize how the SRH is handled:

Flavor Full Name Description PSP Penultimate Segment Pop The penultimate node (SL=1) removes the SRH before forwarding to the last segment. Reduces overhead on the egress node. USP Ultimate Segment Pop The ultimate (last) node removes the SRH itself. USD Ultimate Segment Decap The ultimate node decapsulates the entire outer IPv6 header + SRH. Used with End.DT4/DT6.

PSP is the most common

PSP is widely deployed because it offloads SRH removal from the egress PE, improving efficiency. Most modern implementations advertise End with PSP or End with PSP-USP-USD.

docs.title: SRH with TLVs
docs.text:
The SRH can carry optional TLV (Type-Length-Value) objects after the segment list:

TLV Description HMAC TLV Cryptographic authentication of the SRH Padding TLV Alignment padding NSH Carrier TLV Carries NSH metadata for service chaining

docs.title: Reduced Encapsulation
docs.text:
H.Encaps.Red (Reduced Encapsulation, RFC 8986) optimizes the SRH by omitting the first SID of the path from the segment list, since the headend already places it in the IPv6 DA. This saves 16 bytes per packet, and with a single-SID path it removes the SRH entirely.

Path: SID-1 → SID-2 → SID-3   (segment list is stored in reverse order)

H.Encaps:      SRH [SID-3, SID-2, SID-1], SL=2, DA = SID-1
H.Encaps.Red:  SRH [SID-3, SID-2],        SL=2, DA = SID-1  ← SID-1 only in the DA

docs.title: Performance Measurement (SRPM)
docs.text: Segment Routing Performance Measurement (SRPM) provides real-time visibility into network path quality across SRv6 domains. By measuring delay, loss, and jitter on a per-path or per-flow basis, operators can enforce SLAs, optimize traffic engineering decisions, and detect degradation before it impacts services.

docs.title: Why Performance Measurement Matters
docs.text:
In SRv6 networks, traffic follows explicit segment lists through the fabric. Knowing how well each path performs is critical for:

  • SLA assurance -- Proving that contracted delay/loss targets are met
  • TE optimization -- Feeding real-time metrics into SR Policy path selection
  • Fault detection -- Identifying degraded links before they cause outages
  • Capacity planning -- Understanding utilization patterns per path

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text: Metric Description Typical Granularity One-way Delay Time for a packet to traverse a path from ingress to egress Per-path, per-color Round-trip Delay Total time for a probe and its reply Per-probe session Packet Loss Percentage of packets dropped along a path Per-interval (e.g., 10s) Jitter Variation in delay between consecutive packets Per-flow Throughput Effective data rate achieved on a path Per-interface or per-policy

docs.title: STAMP (RFC 8762)
docs.text:
Simple Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol is the modern standard for active probing in SRv6 networks. It replaces older TWAMP with a simpler, stateless design.

graph LR
    S[Sender PE] -->|"STAMP Probe (UDP)"| R[Reflector PE]
    R -->|"STAMP Reply + Timestamps"| S
    S --- M((PM Engine))
    M -->|"Delay, Loss, Jitter"| T[Telemetry Collector]

How it works:

  1. Sender generates UDP probe packets with timestamps embedded in the SRv6 path
  2. Reflector receives the probe, adds its own timestamps, and returns a reply
  3. PM Engine computes one-way delay, round-trip delay, and loss from timestamp differences
  4. Results are streamed to a telemetry collector for visualization and alerting

STAMP vs TWAMP

STAMP eliminates the control channel required by TWAMP, making it simpler to deploy at scale. The reflector is stateless -- it does not need to maintain session state, reducing overhead on transit nodes.

docs.title: Alternate-Marking (RFC 9341 / RFC 9342)
docs.text:
Alternate-marking is a passive measurement technique that avoids injecting probe traffic entirely. Instead, it marks production packets with alternating color bits and counts them at ingress and egress.

Phase Ingress Action Egress Action Block A (e.g., 10s) Mark packets with color 0 Count color-0 packets received Block B (next 10s) Mark packets with color 1 Count color-1 packets received

By comparing ingress and egress counters for each color block, the system calculates exact packet loss without any probe overhead.

When to use alternate-marking

Use alternate-marking when you need loss measurement on production traffic without adding probe overhead. It is especially useful for high-throughput paths where active probing would consume bandwidth.

docs.title: Color-Aware PM
docs.text:
SRv6 SR Policies can carry a color attribute that maps to an SLA class. Performance measurement sessions can be bound to specific colors, enabling per-SLA monitoring:

  • Color 10 -- Low-latency path (delay < 5ms)
  • Color 20 -- Best-effort path
  • Color 30 -- High-bandwidth path

This allows operators to measure whether each SLA class is meeting its target independently.

docs.title: Measurement Approaches Compared
docs.text: Approach Type Measures Overhead Accuracy STAMP Active probing Delay, loss, jitter Low (probe packets) High Alternate-Marking Passive (production traffic) Loss, delay None (uses existing traffic) Exact for loss IOAM (In-situ OAM) In-band Hop-by-hop delay, path trace Per-packet header overhead Very high TWAMP (legacy) Active probing Delay, loss, jitter Medium (stateful sessions) High

docs.title: PM with SR Policies
docs.text:
Performance measurement integrates directly with SR Policies. Each candidate path in an SR Policy can have PM enabled:

segment-routing
 traffic-eng
  policy POLICY-1
   color 10 end-point fc00:0:2::1
   candidate-paths
    preference 100
     explicit segment-list SL-LOW-LATENCY
    !
   performance-measurement
    liveness-detection
    delay-measurement
    loss-measurement
   !

Liveness detection

PM liveness probes can trigger fast path protection. If a probe fails, the SR Policy switches to an alternate candidate path within milliseconds, complementing TI-LFA for end-to-end protection.

docs.title: Anomaly Thresholds and Metric Fallback
docs.text:
When a PM session detects degradation, the router can advertise an anomaly and automatically raise the IS-IS metric on the affected interface to steer traffic away. The key to doing this without flapping is the hysteresis band — a pair of thresholds that separate the "enter anomaly" and "exit anomaly" conditions.

performance-measurement
 delay-profile interfaces default
  advertisement
   anomaly-loss
    upper-bound 30      ← anomaly declared when loss exceeds 30%
    lower-bound 20      ← anomaly cleared only when loss drops below 20%
   !
  !
 !

router isis 1
 interface GigabitEthernet0/2/0/1
  point-to-point
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   metric fallback anomaly loss increment 500
  !
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   metric fallback anomaly loss increment 500
  !
 !

How the hysteresis band works:

graph LR
    A["Loss < 20%<br/>(Normal)"] -->|"Loss rises above 30%"| B["Loss > 30%<br/>(Anomaly declared)"]
    B -->|"Metric += 500<br/>advertised in IS-IS"| C["Traffic rerouted"]
    C -->|"Loss drops below 20%"| D["Anomaly cleared<br/>Metric restored"]
    D --> A
    B -->|"Loss between 20–30%<br/>no state change"| B
    style B fill:#b71c1c26,stroke:#b71c1c
    style D fill:#1b5e2026,stroke:#1b5e20

The gap between upper-bound and lower-bound is the dead band (also called hysteresis zone). Loss oscillating in that range — say between 21% and 29% — does not trigger any state change, preventing metric flapping. Without hysteresis, a link hovering at exactly the threshold would cause the IS-IS metric to oscillate continuously.

Threshold Role Tuning guidance upper-bound Declares anomaly — triggers metric increment Set above your worst acceptable loss for the SLA class lower-bound Clears anomaly — restores original metric Set far enough below upper-bound to absorb normal measurement variance increment How much to raise the IS-IS metric Must exceed existing metric differences between paths to actually reroute traffic

Fine-tuning the band

A wider band (e.g., 20/40 instead of 20/30) reduces false positives at the cost of slower recovery detection. A narrower band (e.g., 25/30) reacts faster but risks flapping on lossy links with high variance. Start with a 10-point spread and adjust based on observed measurement jitter.

Relationship to SRPM

This mechanism is part of Cisco's SRPM anomaly advertisement feature. The performance-measurement block configures the PM thresholds; the metric fallback anomaly in IS-IS configures the reaction. Together they close the loop: PM detects the problem, IS-IS redistributes around it.

docs.title: SRv6 vs SR-MPLS
docs.text:
Leer en español · 日本語で読む

Both SRv6 and SR-MPLS implement Segment Routing, but they use different data planes. Here's a practical comparison.

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text:
Aspect SR-MPLS SRv6 Data Plane MPLS IPv6 Segment ID 20-bit label 128-bit IPv6 address SID Space ~1M labels Virtually unlimited Encapsulation MPLS label stack SRv6 SRH (IPv6 ext. header) Network Programming Limited Rich (End, End.X, End.DT4...) MTU Impact 4 bytes per label 40B IPv6 + 8B + 16B per SID Existing Infra Requires MPLS forwarding Uses native IPv6 Signaling None (same as SRv6) None Maturity Widely deployed Growing rapidly

SRv6 overhead is no longer what it was

The 16 bytes per SID figure applies to classic SRv6. With uSID (RFC 9800), up to 6 instructions fit in a single 16-byte container, putting SRv6 on par with or better than an MPLS label stack. See uSID / SRv6 Compression.

docs.title: When to Choose What
docs.text:
Choose SR-MPLS when...

  • You have existing MPLS infrastructure
  • MTU overhead is a concern
  • Your use case is primarily TE or VPN

Choose SRv6 when...

  • Building a new IPv6-native network
  • You need advanced network programmability
  • Simplification and future-proofing are priorities
  • You want to eliminate MPLS entirely

docs.title: TI-LFA (Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate)
docs.text:
Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate — TI-LFA, sometimes written TILFA or "TI LFA" — is the fast-reroute (FRR) mechanism of Segment Routing. Every router pre-computes, for each destination, a backup path that follows the route the network will use after the failure, and encodes it as a short segment list. When a link or neighbor fails, the router switches traffic onto that list in the data plane, without waiting for the IGP. It is standardized in RFC 9855 (October 2025, Proposed Standard) and works identically for SR-MPLS and SRv6.

TI-LFA builds on the older IP FRR ideas — LFA, Remote LFA and Directed LFA — and, in the RFC's words, extends them to "guaranteed coverage in any two-connected network". Segment Routing is what makes that possible: the repair router can steer a packet along any path with a couple of SIDs, so it never depends on a lucky neighbor.

docs.title: The Problem: The Convergence Window
docs.text:
When a link fails, the IGP must detect the failure, flood the change, run SPF and update the FIB on every affected router. Until that finishes — hundreds of milliseconds to seconds in a large network — packets toward the failed link are dropped or loop.

IP FRR closes that gap locally: the router next to the failure, the Point of Local Repair (PLR), has a backup next hop pre-installed in its FIB and switches to it as soon as it detects the failure (loss of light, BFD). The question is where that backup path comes from.

Mechanism How the backup is found Limitation LFA (RFC 5286) A neighbor whose own shortest path to the destination does not come back through the PLR Exists only if the topology happens to provide one. RFC 6571 measured per-prefix LFA coverage of 67–99% (median 94%) across 11 service-provider cores Remote LFA (RFC 7490) Tunnel (LDP) to a remote "PQ node" from which traffic flows to the destination unaided Still topology-dependent: RFC 7490 reports 97.5–100% link coverage on 14 topologies and much lower guaranteed node protection TI-LFA (RFC 9855) Segment list that reproduces the post-convergence path Needs Segment Routing and enough SID depth on the PLR; covers any two-connected topology

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning PLR Point of Local Repair — the router adjacent to the failure that switches traffic to the backup Protected resource (X) The link, node or SRLG the backup must avoid Post-convergence path The shortest path from the PLR to the destination once X is removed from the topology. TI-LFA repairs onto this path, so traffic does not move again when the IGP converges P-space P(R,X) Routers the PLR R can reach on its normal (pre-failure) shortest paths without any of those paths — including ECMP splits — crossing X Extended P-space The union of the P-spaces of the PLR's neighbors (except those reached via X). A router in the extended P-space can be reached by sending the packet out a specific neighbor first Q-space Q(D,X) Routers whose normal shortest path to the destination D does not cross X. A packet dropped off at a Q node gets to D on its own PQ node A node in both the (extended) P-space and the Q-space (RFC 7490 §1.1). A single segment to a PQ node is a complete repair Repair list (RL) The segments the PLR adds to the packet — generically <Node-SID(P), explicit path P→Q>

docs.title: Worked Example: Finding P, Q and the Repair List
docs.text:
Six routers, IS-IS metrics on the links. S is the PLR, protecting its link to N, for traffic to D.

graph LR
    S((S)) ---|10 · protected| N((N))
    N ---|10| D((D))
    S ---|10| A((A))
    A ---|10| B((B))
    B ---|40| C((C))
    C ---|10| D

Before the failure, S reaches D via N (cost 20). A also reaches D via S and N (cost 30), so A is not an LFA: by the RFC 5286 inequality, A is loop-free only if dist(A,D) < dist(A,S) + dist(S,D), i.e. 30 < 10 + 20, which is false. Classic LFA has nothing to offer here.

Step 1 — post-convergence path. Remove S–N and recompute: S → A → B → C → D, cost 70.

Step 2 — P-space of S (avoiding S–N).

Node Shortest path from S today Crosses S–N? In P-space? A S→A (10) No B S→A→B (20) No C S→N→D→C (30) Yes — D S→N→D (20) Yes —

Extended P-space adds what A can reach without S–N: B, but not C (A's shortest path to C, cost 40, goes back through S–N). Extended P-space = {A, B}.

Step 3 — Q-space of D (avoiding S–N).

Node Shortest path to D today Crosses S–N? In Q-space? C C→D (10) No B B→A→S→N→D (40), cheaper than B→C→D (50) Yes — A A→S→N→D (30) Yes —

Step 4 — intersect along the post-convergence path. P nodes on the path: A, B. Q nodes on the path: C. There is no PQ node, but the last P node (B) and the first Q node (C) are adjacent. RFC 9855 §5.3 gives the repair list:

RL = < Node-SID(B), Adj-SID(B→C) >

The adjacency SID is essential: if S only sent the packet to B, B would forward it on its own shortest path to D — back through A and S — and the packet would loop. The Adj-SID forces B to use the expensive B–C link, after which C's normal routing delivers it.

Variation: a PQ node exists

Lower the B–C metric to 10. Now B's own shortest path to D is B→C→D (20), so B is in the Q-space as well as the P-space. B is a PQ node and the repair list shrinks to a single segment: RL = < Node-SID(B) > — exactly what Remote LFA would have found, but without an LDP tunnel.

In SRv6 the same list becomes SRv6 SIDs: B's End (uN) SID followed by B's End.X (uA) SID toward C. With uSID both fit in one 128-bit container, so the PLR adds a single outer IPv6 header and no SRH:

Original packet at S:   IPv6(DA = D's service SID) | payload
Repaired at S:          IPv6(DA = fcbb:bb00:B:BC::) | IPv6(DA = D's service SID) | payload
                                    └uN(B) └uA(B→C)
At B:  uN shifts, uA forwards over B–C and, with PSP/USD, removes the outer header
At C:  plain IPv6 forwarding of the original packet to D

docs.title: Repair-list shapes (RFC 9855 Section 5)
docs.text:
Case RFC 9855 Repair list Comparable to A direct neighbor is on the post-convergence path and in P and Q §5.1 Empty — just a different outgoing interface Post-convergence LFA A PQ node exists §5.2 <Node-SID(PQ)> Remote LFA P and Q are adjacent §5.3 <Node-SID(P), Adj-SID(P→Q)> Directed LFA P and Q are distant §5.4 <Node-SID(P), …explicit path…> (implementation-specific optimization) —

How often each case occurs is measured in RFC 9855 Appendix B on nine real networks: for link and local-SRLG protection, one SID or fewer covers more than 99% of destinations; for node protection, two SIDs or fewer cover 99%. On SRv6, adjacency SIDs are globally routable, so the list is often even shorter than on SR-MPLS (§7.2).

docs.title: Link vs Node vs SRLG Protection
docs.text:
The algorithm is the same; what changes is the resource X removed from the topology before computing the post-convergence path, P-space and Q-space.

Protection Removes from the topology Repair-list effect Use when Link (default) The primary link S–N Shortest lists; the backup may still pass through N via another link Fiber cuts, optics failures Node N and all its links Can need one more SID than link protection; never uses N Router crashes, linecard resets, maintenance SRLG Every local link sharing an SRLG with S–N Avoids links in the same conduit, DWDM system or linecard Shared infrastructure failures

Two things are easy to miss:

  • A link-protecting backup can be useless for a node failure. If S has two parallel links to N, the link-protecting backup for one of them is simply the other — which dies too if N reboots. Node protection forces the list around N. If no node-protecting path exists, implementations fall back to link protection.
  • Node protection only protects transit through N. Traffic whose destination is N (or a service SID owned by N) cannot be rerouted around N; RFC 9855 §6.1 keeps an active node segment on the packet and adds the repair list in front of it. Protecting traffic to a failed egress PE is a separate problem (see draft-ietf-rtgwg-srv6-egress-protection and BGP PIC).

Vendors pick between the modes with tiebreakers. A node-protecting path is preferred only when you configure it. Check SRLG support per data plane: Junos ignores SRLG in SRv6 TI-LFA and does not support SRLG protection in IPv6 networks.

docs.title: How TI-LFA Works with SRv6
docs.text:
RFC 9855 §7.2 states that the computation is identical for SRv6; only the encoding differs:

  • At a transit PLR, the repair list is added with a headend behavior from RFC 8986 §5 — typically H.Encaps.Red, an outer IPv6 header whose DA is the first repair SID.
  • At a PLR that is itself a segment endpoint for the packet, it first executes its endpoint behavior and then protects the packet like a transit packet.
  • Repair SIDs advertised with the USD (and PSP) flavor let the last repair node remove the outer header and forward the original packet. That is why Cisco shows the P node's SID as uN (PSP/USD).

Implementations differ in how the repair is applied, so don't assume one behavior:

Platform Repair encoding shown in the FIB Cisco 8000 (IOS-XR) SRv6 H.Encaps.Red SID-list {…}; with full-length SIDs, a backup is installed only if it needs two SIDs or fewer Cisco NCS 5500/540 (IOS-XR) SRv6 H.Insert.Red SID-list {…} (SRH insertion) Cisco IOS-XE Segment List … mode:insert Junos Encapsulation (reduced SRH) at the ingress PE; SRH insertion at transit nodes with transit-srh-insert

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XR (SRv6)Cisco IOS-XEJunos 
segment-routing
 srv6
  locators
   locator MAIN
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fcbb:bb00:1::/48
!
router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  metric-style wide
  microloop avoidance segment-routing
  segment-routing srv6
   locator MAIN
 !
 interface HundredGigE0/0/0/1
  point-to-point
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   fast-reroute per-prefix
   fast-reroute per-prefix ti-lfa
   !! optional: prefer node-protecting, then SRLG-disjoint backups
   fast-reroute per-prefix tiebreaker node-protecting index 100
   fast-reroute per-prefix tiebreaker srlg-disjoint index 200

Link protection is the default. On current releases a lower index means a higher priority (range 1–255), and link protection always ranks below node or SRLG protection. Some older material, such as the 2016 SR TI-LFA TOI, describes the opposite ordering, so check the guide for your release. For SR-MPLS, configure the same fast-reroute commands under address-family ipv4 unicast with segment-routing mpls. To exclude a Flex-Algo from protection, use flex-algo 128 → fast-reroute disable.

!! SR-MPLS TI-LFA
router isis
 fast-reroute per-prefix level-2 all
 fast-reroute ti-lfa level-2
 fast-reroute tie-break level-2 node-protecting 100
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 isis network point-to-point
!
!! SRv6 TI-LFA (IOS XE 17.15.1a and later)
segment-routing srv6
 locators
  locator A
   prefix CAFE:0:601::/48
   format usid-f3216
!
router isis 1
 address-family ipv6
  multi-topology
  segment-routing srv6
   locator A
  fast-reroute per-prefix level-2 all
  fast-reroute ti-lfa level-2
 exit-address-family

Interface-level isis fast-reroute ti-lfa protection level-2 overrides the protocol default and ... disable excludes an interface. Default tiebreakers are linecard-disjoint, lowest-backup-metric and srlg-disjoint; node-protecting must be enabled explicitly. Cisco notes that IGP TI-LFA on IOS-XE "cannot guarantee 50 ms". See also Cisco IOS-XE.

# TI-LFA for SR-MPLS and SRv6 in IS-IS
set protocols isis backup-spf-options use-post-convergence-lfa
set protocols isis backup-spf-options use-post-convergence-lfa maximum-backup-paths 2
set protocols isis backup-spf-options use-source-packet-routing
set protocols isis interface et-0/0/1.0 level 2 post-convergence-lfa
# optional, per interface
set protocols isis interface et-0/0/1.0 level 2 post-convergence-lfa node-protection
set protocols isis interface et-0/0/1.0 level 2 post-convergence-lfa srlg-protection   # SR-MPLS/IPv4 only

# SRv6 microloop avoidance
set protocols isis spf-options microloop-avoidance post-convergence-path delay 5000

Link protection is the default once post-convergence-lfa is on an interface. maximum-labels (2–5, default 3) caps the MPLS repair stack and maximum-backup-paths (1–8, default 1) the number of backups. For SRv6, Junos encapsulates with a reduced SRH at the ingress PE and can insert an SRH at transit nodes with transit-srh-insert. Micro-SID support for SRv6 TI-LFA and microloop avoidance arrived in Junos 23.4R1 (MX). srlg-protection (MX/PTX, 20.2R1) does not apply to SRv6: SRv6 TI-LFA ignores SRLGs, and SRLG protection is not supported in IPv6 or multi-topology networks. See Juniper for the full SRv6 setup.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRCisco IOS-XEJunos 
show isis ipv6 fast-reroute fcbb:bb00:2::/48 detail
!! Backup path: TI-LFA (link), via fe80::..., HundredGigE0/0/0/1 Node3, Metric: 40
!!   P node: Node4.00 [...], SRv6 SID: fcbb:bb00:4:: uN (PSP/USD)

show route ipv6 fcbb:bb00:2::/48 detail
!!   ... Backup (TI-LFA)   Repair Node(s): ...
!!   SRv6 Headend: H.Encaps.Red, SID-list {fcbb:bb00:4::}

show cef ipv6 fcbb:bb00:2::/48 detail
show cef ipv6 fast-reroute-db

The protection type appears in parentheses: TI-LFA (link), (node), (srlg) or (node+srlg). On SR-MPLS, show isis fast-reroute <prefix> detail lists the P and Q nodes with their labels, and show cef shows the imposed label stack.

show isis fast-reroute ti-lfa tunnel          ! SR-MPLS repair tunnels
show ip cef 10.0.0.2 internal
show isis ipv6 fast-reroute summary            ! SRv6: protected prefixes and coverage
show isis ipv6 rib fcbb:bb00:2::/48            ! "repair path: via ... (DS,NP)"
show ipv6 cef fcbb:bb00:2::/48 internal        ! "Segment List ... mode:insert"
show isis ipv6 fast-reroute ti-lfa fwd-ids

show isis backup coverage            # % of nodes and prefixes protected per address family
show isis backup spf results         # backup computation per destination
show isis backup spf results no-coverage
show route 2001:db8::2 extensive     # primary and backup next hops

docs.title: TI-LFA and Micro-Loops
docs.text:
TI-LFA protects the moment of failure at the PLR. It does nothing for the micro-loops that can form elsewhere while routers update their FIBs at different times, or when the link comes back. RFC 9855 §1 calls the two mechanisms complementary and warns of one interaction: if the PLR converges early and releases its TI-LFA path before its neighbors have converged, the packets that were safely on the repair path can start looping — especially for repairs built from §5.2–5.4 (PQ or P/Q nodes rather than a direct neighbor).

The usual fix is to keep the TI-LFA path in place for a while after local convergence (RFC 8333-style local delay) or to steer traffic over a loop-free SR path until the network settles:

router isis CORE
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  microloop avoidance segment-routing
  microloop avoidance rib-update-delay 5000

On IOS-XR the delay range is documented as 1–60000 ms with a default of 5000. See Micro-Loop Avoidance for the full picture.

TI-LFA for multicast: RFC 9860

TI-LFA repair paths can also protect PIM trees. RFC 9860 (October 2025, Informational) uses the repair segment list to build the MoFRR standby tree: the P-node's End SID is translated into a PIM RPF Vector and the P→Q End.X SID into an Explicit RPF Vector, so the secondary join follows the repair path hop by hop. This gives MoFRR the same topology-independent coverage that TI-LFA gives unicast. See Multicast & Broadcast.

docs.title: TI-LFA vs Other FRR Mechanisms
docs.text:
Mechanism Coverage (published data) Extra state Repair follows post-convergence path Topology dependent LFA (RFC 5286) 67–99% per prefix (RFC 6571, 11 SP cores) None Not necessarily Yes Remote LFA (RFC 7490) 97.5–100% link protection (RFC 7490, 14 topologies) Targeted LDP sessions Not necessarily Yes TI-LFA (RFC 9855) Any two-connected network; >99% with ≤ 1 SID for link protection (RFC 9855 App. B) None beyond SR SIDs Yes No RSVP-TE FRR Full, per protected LSP Bypass/detour LSPs and RSVP state No No

No extra protocol state

TI-LFA needs no tunnels, no RSVP and no targeted LDP: the IGP computes the repair lists from the SIDs it already advertises. What it does need is enough SID depth on the PLR (some platforms install a backup only if it fits in two SIDs) and the protected SIDs advertised by every node on the repair path.

docs.title: uSID / SRv6 Compression
docs.text:
Leer en español · 日本語で読む

One of the early criticisms of SRv6 was overhead — each SID is 128 bits (16 bytes), and a segment list of 5 SIDs adds 80 bytes to every packet. Micro-SID (uSID) solves this by packing multiple segment instructions into a single 128-bit SID.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
With classic SRv6, each hop in the segment list costs 16 bytes:

Classic SRv6 (5 SIDs = 80 bytes overhead):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SRH: Segment List                             │
│   [0]: fc00:0:5::1  (16 bytes)               │
│   [1]: fc00:0:4::1  (16 bytes)               │
│   [2]: fc00:0:3::1  (16 bytes)               │
│   [3]: fc00:0:2::1  (16 bytes)               │
│   [4]: fc00:0:1::1  (16 bytes)               │
│                          Total: 80 bytes      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

For short packets or latency-sensitive traffic, this overhead is significant.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text: Component Size Description uSID Block 32 bits Common prefix for all uSIDs in the domain (e.g., fcbb:bbbb) uSID 16 bits each Individual micro-instruction identifying a node + behavior End-of-Container 16 bits (0000) Marks the end of active uSIDs in the container

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Processing a uSID container is a simple shift-and-lookup operation:

Step 1 - Ingress receives:
  DA = fcbb:bbbb:0001:0002:0003:0000:0000:0000
                  ^^^^
                  Active uSID → Node 1

Step 2 - Node 1 processes uSID 0001, shifts left:
  DA = fcbb:bbbb:0002:0003:0000:0000:0000:0000
                  ^^^^
                  Active uSID → Node 2

Step 3 - Node 2 processes uSID 0002, shifts left:
  DA = fcbb:bbbb:0003:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000
                  ^^^^
                  Active uSID → Node 3

Step 4 - Node 3 processes uSID 0003, shifts left:
  DA = fcbb:bbbb:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000
                  ^^^^
                  End-of-Container (0000) → Move to next SRH entry

docs.title: Overhead Comparison
docs.text:
Scenario Classic SRv6 uSID Savings 3 SIDs 48 bytes 16 bytes 67% 6 SIDs 96 bytes 16 bytes 83% 10 SIDs 160 bytes 32 bytes (2 containers) 80% 12 SIDs 192 bytes 32 bytes (2 containers) 83%

6 hops in 16 bytes

A single uSID container can encode up to 6 segment instructions in the same space that classic SRv6 uses for just 1 SID. This makes SRv6 competitive with or better than MPLS label stacks in terms of overhead.

docs.title: uSID vs G-SRv6
docs.text:
Two compression approaches emerged and are now unified under RFC 9800:

Aspect uSID (NEXT-C-SID) G-SRv6 (Replace-C-SID) Origin Cisco, Bell Canada China Mobile, Huawei Processing Shift-and-lookup Replace-and-lookup uSID size 16 or 32 bits 16 or 32 bits RFC RFC 9800 RFC 9800 Adoption Multiple global operators Multiple global operators

Both are now standardized in RFC 9800 (SRv6 SID Compression), ensuring interoperability.

  !

docs.title: What is SRv6?
docs.text:
Leer en español · 日本語で読む

Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) is a network architecture that leverages the IPv6 data plane to implement source routing and network programming capabilities. You will also see it called IPv6 Segment Routing or Segment Routing v6 — all three names refer to the same IETF technology.

docs.title: IPv6 Segment Routing, Segment Routing v6, SRv6: One Technology
docs.text:
Segment Routing (RFC 8402) is a source-routing architecture with two data planes:

Name you will see What it means SRv6, Segment Routing over IPv6, IPv6 Segment Routing, Segment Routing v6, SR v6 Segments are IPv6 addresses; the list travels in the destination address and, when needed, the Segment Routing Header (RFC 8754) SR-MPLS, Segment Routing MPLS Segments are MPLS labels on a label stack (RFC 8660)

The "v6" in "Segment Routing v6" names the IP version of the data plane, not a sixth release of Segment Routing. Control-plane features — IS-IS/OSPFv3 extensions, Flex-Algo, TI-LFA, SR Policy — are shared between the two, which is why vendor documentation often covers both under one "Segment Routing" guide. For a side-by-side comparison see SRv6 vs SR-MPLS.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SRv6 encodes a list of instructions (called segments) in the IPv6 packet header. Each segment is a 128-bit IPv6 address that represents a specific network instruction or behavior.

graph LR
    A[Source] -->|SRv6 Path| B[Node 1]
    B -->|Segment List| C[Node 2]
    C -->|End.DT4| D[Destination]

docs.title: Segments
docs.text:
A segment is an IPv6 address that encodes:

  • Locator: Identifies the node in the network
  • Function: Specifies the behavior to apply
  • Arguments: Optional parameters for the function

docs.title: Source Routing
docs.text: In SRv6, the source node (ingress) determines the entire path through the network by populating the segment list. Intermediate nodes simply process the active segment and forward the packet.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text: Feature Description Native IPv6 No overlay protocol needed, uses IPv6 natively Programmability Network behaviors defined via SRv6 functions Simplification Eliminates MPLS signaling protocols (LDP, RSVP) Scalability 128-bit SID space supports massive networks Security HMAC TLV support in SRH for authentication

docs.title: How It Works (Simplified)
docs.text:
1. Ingress node receives a packet and determines the SRv6 policy
  2. Encapsulates the packet with an outer IPv6 header + SRH
  3. Segment List is populated with the desired path
  4. Transit nodes forward based on the IPv6 destination address
  5. Endpoint nodes process the active SID and execute the associated behavior
  6. Egress node decapsulates and delivers the original packet

Simple SRv6 Packet Flow

Original:  [IPv4: 10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.0.2][Payload]

SRv6:      [IPv6: A::1 -> B::100]             <- Outer IPv6 (DA = active SID)
           [SRH: SL=1, [C::100, B::100]]       <- Segment List
           [IPv4: 10.0.0.1 -> 10.0.0.2]        <- Original Packet
           [Payload]

docs.title: SRv6 vs MPLS
docs.text: SRv6 fundamentally changes how networks are programmed compared to traditional MPLS. While MPLS uses 20-bit labels with signaling protocols (LDP, RSVP-TE), SRv6 uses 128-bit IPv6 addresses as segment identifiers, enabling a programmable network fabric without overlay complexity. See the detailed comparison in Interworking & Migration.

docs.title: 5G Transport with SRv6
docs.text: SRv6 (particularly uSID) is rapidly becoming the preferred transport technology for converged 5G xHaul networks — replacing legacy MPLS in backhaul, midhaul, and fronthaul segments.

docs.title: Why SRv6 for 5G?
docs.text: 5G Requirement SRv6 Solution Network Slicing SRv6 Flex-Algorithm enables per-slice path computation Low Latency SR Policies steer traffic on latency-optimized paths Scalability 128-bit SID space supports millions of endpoints Simplification No MPLS signaling (LDP, RSVP-TE) needed Convergence Single protocol for backhaul, midhaul, and fronthaul Automation Programmable SIDs enable intent-based networking

docs.text:
graph LR
    RU[Radio Unit] -->|Fronthaul| DU[Distributed Unit]
    DU -->|Midhaul| CU[Centralized Unit]
    CU -->|Backhaul| CORE[5G Core / UPF]

        DU

docs.title: SRv6 MUP (Mobile User Plane)
docs.text: One of the most significant innovations is SRv6 MUP (RFC 9433), pioneered by SoftBank. MUP replaces GTP-U tunnels with SRv6 segments, encoding mobile session information directly into SIDs.

docs.title: Before MUP (Traditional 5G)
docs.text: [IPv6][GTP-U][Inner IP][Payload]  ← Tunnel overhead

docs.title: With SRv6 MUP
docs.text:
[IPv6][SRH with MUP SIDs][Payload]  ← Native SRv6, no GTP-U

Benefits:

  • Eliminates GTP-U tunnel overhead
  • Enables end-to-end network slicing from RAN to core
  • Reduces cost and operational complexity
  • Enables seamless MEC (Multi-access Edge Computing) integration

  • Iliad (Italy) — announced greenfield SRv6 5G-ready network with no MPLS (source)

See Real-World Deployments for a full directory with links to original announcements.

SRv6 uSID meets 5G transport requirements

SRv6 uSID has been validated against eCPRI, O-RAN Alliance, ITU-T, and 3GPP standards for latency, jitter, synchronization, and convergence per service slice.

docs.title: AI/ML Training Networks with SRv6
docs.text: SRv6 is emerging as a critical technology for AI backend fabrics — the networks connecting thousands of GPUs in training clusters. Traditional ECMP routing fails catastrophically for AI workloads, and SRv6 provides the solution.

docs.title: The Problem: ECMP Hash Collisions
docs.text:
AI training workloads (like LLM training) use synchronized all-to-all communication patterns across thousands of GPUs. This creates massive elephant flows that cause:

  • Hash collisions in traditional ECMP — multiple flows land on the same path
  • Congestion on some links while parallel paths sit completely idle
  • Training slowdowns — the entire job is only as fast as the slowest GPU
  • Wasted bandwidth — up to 40-60% of fabric capacity underutilized
graph TB
    subgraph Traditional ECMP - The Problem
        G1[GPU 1] -->|Flow A| S1[Spine 1]
        G2[GPU 2] -->|Flow B| S1
        G3[GPU 3] -->|Flow C| S1
        G4[GPU 4] -.->|Idle| S2[Spine 2]
    end

    style S1 fill:#ef535026,stroke:#ef5350

docs.title: The Solution: SRv6 Deterministic Path Placement
docs.text:
With SRv6 uSID, the source (GPU host or controller) explicitly programs the exact path each flow takes through the fabric. No hashing, no collisions, no wasted capacity.

graph TB
    subgraph SRv6 Deterministic - The Solution
        G1[GPU 1] -->|SID→Spine1| S1[Spine 1]
        G2[GPU 2] -->|SID→Spine2| S2[Spine 2]
        G3[GPU 3] -->|SID→Spine3| S3[Spine 3]
        G4[GPU 4] -->|SID→Spine4| S4[Spine 4]
    end

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Each spine/path is assigned an SRv6 uSID
  2. The GPU host (or a controller) encapsulates traffic with an SRH containing the specific spine SID
  3. Traffic is deterministically placed on the chosen path — zero hash collisions
  4. Load balancing is done by the application or controller, not by the network

docs.title: Key Benefits for AI
docs.text: Benefit Description Zero hash collisions Every flow is explicitly placed on a specific path 100% fabric utilization No idle paths while others are congested Application-aware GPUs can control their own path selection No protocol overhead uSID fits in a single 128-bit IPv6 address Works with existing hardware Runs on standard Broadcom/Cisco Silicon One ASICs

docs.title: MRC: SRv6 Replaces Dynamic Routing at OpenAI
docs.text:
The strongest production validation of SRv6 for AI networking to date is MRC (Multipath Reliable Connection) — a multipath RDMA transport co-developed by OpenAI, Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom, and NVIDIA, published in May 2026 and released as an open OCP specification. MRC runs in production on OpenAI's and Microsoft's largest training clusters — including 100K+ GPU NVIDIA GB200 supercomputers used to train frontier models.

MRC's design goes further than deterministic path placement: it disables dynamic routing entirely. Switches run no BGP; data packets are source-routed along static paths using SRv6, and all failure handling moves to the transport layer at the edge.

docs.title: How MRC uses SRv6
docs.text:
• Static uSID forwarding: The fabric uses the uSID format with uN behavior — a 32-bit locator prefix followed by 16-bit uSIDs, one per switch on the path. Switch forwarding tables are configured at install time and essentially never change; the shift-and-forward operation runs at line rate on standard ASICs.
  • Entropy Values map to explicit paths: At queue-pair startup the NIC generates a set of 32-bit Entropy Values (EVs, typically 128-256), each algorithmically mapped to a unique SRv6 address — i.e., a specific physical path through a specific network plane. The sender rotates through its EV set, spraying every packet of a transfer across hundreds of SRv6-encoded paths, which load-balances the fabric without hash collisions or application involvement.
  • Multi-plane two-tier Clos: Instead of a three-tier 800G fabric, the 800G NIC is broken out by lane into 8 parallel 100G planes (or 4×200G), so ~131K NICs fit in just two switch tiers. Losing a single link costs ~0.4% of a node's capacity instead of 3%.
  • Microsecond-scale failure bypass: When a path loses a packet, MRC retires that EV and retransmits on another path — detecting and bypassing failures in tens of microseconds, versus seconds for routing-protocol convergence. Background probes resurrect paths once they recover. Link flaps between switch tiers become operationally ignorable.
  • Ground-truth telemetry: Because SRv6 makes probe paths explicit (no ECMP hash ambiguity, no dynamic routing underneath), the "Clustermapper" agents probe every link in the network every millisecond and know exactly which physical path each probe took — something switch-based telemetry cannot guarantee.
graph LR
    NIC[NIC<br/>EV set → SRv6 paths] -->|Plane 1 uSIDs| P1[T0 → T1 → T0]
    NIC -->|Plane 2 uSIDs| P2[T0 → T1 → T0]
    NIC -->|Plane N uSIDs| PN[T0 → T1 → T0]
    P1 --> DST[Destination NIC]
    P2 --> DST
    PN --> DST

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Aspect Before (RoCEv2 + ECMP + BGP) With MRC + static SRv6 Load balancing Per-flow ECMP hashing — collisions halve throughput Per-packet spraying across hundreds of explicit paths Failure recovery Routing convergence (seconds), lost GPU time EV retirement + selective retransmit (microseconds) Switch control plane BGP, large ECMP sets, hard to debug at scale Static tables, no dynamic routing to interact with transport Path visibility Hash-dependent, ambiguous Every packet and probe path is explicit

Validated results include ~96% of theoretical peak bandwidth (≈770 Gb/s application-level on 800G NICs), and NCCL collectives sustaining 92 GB/s at 42K-GPU scale. Hardware spans NVIDIA ConnectX-8, AMD Pollara, and Broadcom Thor Ultra NICs, with SRv6 forwarding on NVIDIA Spectrum-⅘ (Cumulus and SONiC), Broadcom Tomahawk 5, and Arista EOS switches.

SRv6 as the stability layer

MRC inverts the usual assumption that source routing and resilience are at odds: precisely because the SRv6 paths are static and explicit, the transport layer can reason about them, spray across them, and bypass failures faster than any routing protocol could converge.

The fastest-growing SRv6 use case

As of 2025-2026, AI networking is one of the fastest-growing areas of SRv6 adoption. The combination of SONiC (open-source NOS) + SRv6 uSID is emerging as a leading approach for AI backend fabrics.

docs.title: Cloud-Native SRv6 Backbone
docs.text:
Running SRv6 natively inside a public cloud eliminates the tunnel complexity of traditional SR-MPLS deployments. Instead of layering MPLS over GRE over the hyperscaler underlay, operators can build a single SRv6 domain that spans on-prem, cloud regions, availability zones, and even multiple clouds — using nothing but IPv6.

Reference deployment

Boost Mobile operates the first cloud-native 5G network in the United States, built entirely on Open RAN and hosted in AWS. Their transport backbone migrated from SR-MPLS with over 100,000 GRE tunnels to a unified SRv6 domain. The patterns described here are drawn from their production architecture.

docs.title: The Problem: SR-MPLS over GRE in the Cloud
docs.text:
A typical cloud-hosted mobile core uses a multi-tier topology:

  • Edge DCs (per market) — user data functions
  • Regional DCs — voice and regional services
  • National DCs — IMS/VoLTE, messaging, SBC interconnects
graph LR
    EDGE_A[Edge DC<br/>Market A] -->|GRE Tunnels| REG[Regional DC]
    EDGE_B[Edge DC<br/>Market B] -->|GRE Tunnels| REG
    REG -->|GRE Tunnels| NAT[National DC]
    ONPREM[On-Prem PE] -->|DX + GRE<br/>Inter-AS Opt A| EDGE_A
    ONPREM -->|DX + GRE<br/>Inter-AS Opt A| EDGE_B

In this model, vRouters interconnect via GRE tunnels carrying SR-MPLS, and on-prem connections use per-VRF BGP (Inter-AS Option A) over GRE across Direct Connect.

docs.title: Scaling limitations
docs.text: Challenge Impact Per-flow bandwidth cap Each GRE tunnel supports ~1.25 Gbps (single flow in AWS) Tunnel explosion Up to 8 GRE tunnels per VRF to reach ~10 Gbps; 100,000+ tunnels total Per-VRF Inter-AS complexity Every new VRF requires updates on all interconnects Policy fragmentation Community-based policies break across SR-MPLS domain boundaries

docs.title: The Solution: Native SRv6
docs.text:
Replacing the SR-MPLS/GRE stack with a single SRv6 domain eliminates these constraints:

graph LR
    VR1[vRouter<br/>Edge DC A] <-->|Native IPv6| VR2[vRouter<br/>Edge DC B]
    VR1 <-->|Native IPv6| VR3[vRouter<br/>Regional DC]
    VR2 <-->|Native IPv6| VR3
    VR3 <-->|Native IPv6| VR4[vRouter<br/>National DC]
    ONPREM[On-Prem] <-->|SRv6 over DX| VR1
    ONPREM <-->|SRv6 over DX| VR2

    subgraph Single SRv6 Domain
        VR1
        VR2
        VR3
        VR4
    end

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
• Single SRv6 domain — on-prem and cloud routers communicate natively using IPv6
  • No GRE or IGP in cloud — only IPv6 locator reachability is required
  • Direct vRouter-to-vRouter — no transit vRouters needed, only cloud-native IPv6 routing
  • Full path control — SRv6 steers services independent of the underlying infrastructure
  • Multi-cloud ready — add vRouters across AZs, regions, or clouds with minimal configuration

docs.title: Hierarchical SRv6 addressing
docs.text:
A well-designed addressing plan enables summarization and scales horizontally:

Level Prefix Purpose Global Block /24 Entire SRv6 address space Slice Blocks /32 Flex-Algo segmentation Domain Supersets /36 Regional boundaries (~4,000 routers per block); summarization between cloud and on-prem DC Sets /44 Per-DC addressing (256 sets per domain, 16 locators per set) Node Locators /48 One or more per vRouter

uSID alignment on 32-bit boundaries ensures single-SRH traversal.

docs.title: Underlay: summarization-driven reachability
docs.text:
• Superset aggregates (/36) are exchanged between cloud transit gateways and on-prem for end-to-end reachability
  • DC-specific prefixes (/44) are advertised through local interconnects for shortest-path routing
  • Once aggregate prefixes are configured, no further BGP reconfiguration is needed as the network grows

docs.title: Dynamic locator routing
docs.text:
vRouters advertise SRv6 locators via BGP, and a cloud-native route reflector (such as CTX Reflector) programs cloud route tables in real time:

  • SRv6 locators are advertised and withdrawn instantly — no static routes or overlay signaling
  • vRouter-to-vRouter communication works across AZs, regions, clouds, and on-prem
  • New slices or vRouters announce their locators automatically
  • ENI changes on redeployment are updated without manual intervention

docs.title: Solving ECMP Entropy in the Cloud
docs.text: One challenge in public cloud is that the underlay may ignore the IPv6 Flow Label for ECMP hashing — the standard SRv6 approach for entropy does not work.

docs.title: The solution: entropy in the source address
docs.text:
By copying the flow label into the least-significant bits of the SRv6 source address, each flow gets a unique source that the cloud underlay can hash on:

Standard SRv6:
  Source Address: [Locator]
  Flow Label:    [Hash]     ← Ignored by cloud ECMP

Cloud-optimized:
  Source Address: [Locator]:[Flow Label bits]  ← Cloud ECMP sees unique source per flow
  • Each flow gets a unique source address, enabling balanced ECMP across the cloud underlay
  • All generated source addresses remain within the SRv6 locator block — URPF and anti-spoofing validation passes
  • No hyperscaler changes needed

docs.title: Stack simplification
docs.text: Layer SR-MPLS (Before) SRv6 (After) Tunnel overlay GRE tunnels (100,000+) None — native IPv6 Service transport SR-MPLS over GRE SRv6 IGP in cloud Required Not required Inter-domain Per-VRF Inter-AS Opt A Single SRv6 domain Scaling model Add GRE tunnels per VRF Add vRouters with locator advertisement

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
Results from production (Boost Mobile)

  • Eliminated 100,000+ GRE tunnels
  • Single SRv6 domain spanning on-prem and AWS
  • Horizontal scale without BGP reconfiguration
  • Flow-level ECMP entropy without hyperscaler support
  • Multi-cloud ready architecture
  • The packet core runs on any IPv6 fabric

docs.title: Mission-Critical & Defense Networks
docs.text:
Mission-critical WANs — defense, public safety, critical infrastructure — have historically run on layered patchworks of MPLS/RSVP-TE overlays and controller-driven SD-WAN. In 2026 Cisco published a Validated Design (CVD) that replaces this stack with a quantum-safe SRv6 uSID fabric, targeting exactly these environments. This page summarizes the architecture and its design rules.

Primary source

This page is based on the Cisco CVD Quantum-Safe SRv6 Fabric for Mission-Critical Networks (August 2026), validated on Cisco 8000 Series Secure Routers running IOS-XE 26.1 — notable in itself, since Cisco SRv6 support had previously been an IOS-XR story. See Cisco IOS-XE for the platform details.

docs.title: Why SRv6 for Mission-Critical?
docs.text: Two requirements dominate this space, and both map directly onto SRv6 properties:

docs.title: 1. Survivability in DDIL environments
docs.text:
Tactical edges operate under DDIL conditions — Disconnected, Disrupted, Intermittent, Low-bandwidth. Links are cut, jammed, or fade with satellite handoffs, and reachability to a central controller cannot be assumed.

DDIL requirement SRv6 answer No controller dependency Path computation (CSPF) runs locally on the ingress head-end against the IGP link-state database — a cut-off site keeps steering traffic autonomously Narrow links can't afford signaling Source routing eliminates RSVP-TE refresh storms; the path travels in the packet header, so low-bandwidth SATCOM links carry payload, not protocol chatter Any available transport SRv6 runs over MACsec-secured private lines, GRE/IPsec over commercial internet, LTE/5G, or LEO satellite — the fabric is transport-agnostic Sub-50 ms failover without convergence TI-LFA pre-computes repair paths at each Point of Local Repair; failover happens locally, in hardware Detect degraded (not just dead) links Active performance measurement probes track per-link delay and steer around congestion or satellite fade before sessions drop

docs.title: 2. The quantum threat: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later
docs.text:
Adversaries intercept and archive encrypted traffic today, intending to decrypt it once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer can break the classical key exchange (RSA/DH/ECDH) with Shor's algorithm. For data with a 10+ year sensitivity horizon, classical IPsec is already insufficient — this is the HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later) threat, and it drives mandates like NSA CNSA 2.0 (full PQC compliance by 2030).

SRv6 itself provides no encryption (it never did) — the CVD's answer is to run the fabric over post-quantum-ready transport:

  • Private links: WAN MACsec (802.1AE) at line rate, with EAP-TLS authentication using ML-KEM (FIPS 203, formerly Kyber) key exchange over TLS 1.3
  • Untrusted transits: GRE over IPsec with IKEv2 hybrid key exchange (RFC 9370) combining classical ECDH with ML-KEM-1024 — the SA only establishes if both exchanges succeed
  • Transitional/multi-vendor: Post-Quantum Pre-Shared Keys (RFC 8784) mixed into IKEv2 key derivation
  • Management plane: ML-KEM key-exchange algorithms enforced in SSH

PQC keys are big — enable IKEv2 fragmentation

An ML-KEM-1024 public key is 1,568 bytes, so IKEv2 handshake messages exceed the 1500-byte MTU. Since most firewalls drop IP fragments, PQC IPsec deployments must enable application-layer IKEv2 fragmentation (RFC 7383) or tunnels silently fail to establish.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The design is a single IS-IS Level-2 domain carrying uSID (F3216) locators, with all services delivered as BGP overlays — no LDP, RSVP-TE, or BGP-LU anywhere:

graph LR
    FS[Field Site<br/>tactical edge] -->|MACsec E-Line| HUB1[DC Hub 1]
    FS -->|PQC GRE/IPsec<br/>over internet| HUB2[DC Hub 2]
    SPC[Processing Center<br/>dual routers] -->|MACsec| HUB1
    SPC -->|PQC IPsec| HUB2
    HUB1 --- RR[Route Reflector]
    HUB2 --- RR

Key building blocks, each covered in depth elsewhere on this site:

Layer Mechanism Notes Underlay IS-IS L2, multi-topology, wide metrics All Ethernet WAN links must be point-to-point — broadcast mode silently breaks adjacency-SID and SR-TE path computation Transport uSID F3216 (<32-bit block><16-bit node><16-bit function>) Stateless core; P routers do plain IPv6 longest-prefix-match on /48 locators Services BGP L3VPN over SRv6 with uDT4/uDT6 IOS-XE supports per-VRF SID allocation only — one Service SID per VRF, not per prefix Enclave isolation Red/black separation via VRFs bound to dedicated locators Classified (red) traffic never leaves trusted edge enclaves unencrypted; only ciphertext crosses the black transport Slicing Flex-Algo 128 (secure) + 129 (low-latency) Separate locator block per algorithm — see below Steering ODN + Automated Steering via BGP color; Per-Flow Policies ePBR/NBAR classification maps applications to forwarding classes, dispatched to per-color child policies Resiliency TI-LFA with node/SRLG/linecard-disjoint tiebreakers BFD-triggered, sub-50 ms, Flex-Algo-constraint-aware Telemetry Performance measurement probes at 3-second intervals Delay flooded into IS-IS; delay-metric policies re-optimize around congestion with zero packet loss Multicast BGP MVPN + ingress replication, End.DTMC4 Anycast RP + MSDP at the hubs; core stays multicast-stateless

docs.title: Design Rules Worth Stealing
docs.text:
The CVD codifies several rules that generalize beyond defense networks:

One locator block per Flex-Algo slice. Slice isolation is enforced through locator reachability, not a BGP attribute — BGP never signals "this route is Algo 128". Each slice gets its own 32-bit uSID block (e.g. FCBB:DEAA::/32 base, FCBB:DEAF::/32 secure, FCBB:DEAB::/32 low-latency), each VRF binds to the locator of its slice, and the IGP's per-algorithm SPF does the rest. A classified VRF bound to the Algo-128 locator cannot traverse an unencrypted link, because that link doesn't exist in the Algo-128 topology — even during TI-LFA failover, since the repair path is computed within the same algorithm's constraints.

Affinity-tag your cryptographic planes. Interfaces are tagged SECURED (MACsec/PQC-IPsec) or UNSECURED (plain internet) via IS-IS affinity maps. Both Flex-Algo definitions and SR-TE policies reference these affinities, so encryption becomes a routable constraint rather than an operational convention.

next-hop-unchanged at inter-domain boundaries. Default eBGP next-hop rewriting forces the ASBR to decapsulate, VRF-lookup, and re-encapsulate every packet — reintroducing state at the border and truncating end-to-end SR-TE (ODN policies would terminate at the ASBR instead of the real egress PE). Preserving the next-hop keeps ASBRs as pure control-plane reflectors and the data plane stateless end to end. See Inter-Domain SRv6.

Slicing vs. flow steering are different tools. Flex-Algo isolates entire prefixes/VRFs at the IGP level with no packet inspection; Per-Flow Policies differentiate applications to the same destination via edge classification. The order of operations: SR-TE policy match first, Flex-Algo routing-table fallback second.

Budget MTU for the full encapsulation stack. A tactical packet can carry Type-1 inline encryption (+~60 B), SRv6 encapsulation (+40 B), GRE (+24–44 B), IPsec (+~56–70 B), and MACsec (+32 B). The validated numbers: tunnel MTU 1400 (1300 over MACsec E-Lines, including clns mtu and IS-IS lsp-mtu), TCP MSS clamped to 1220/1200 at the LAN edge, and tunnel PMTUD enabled.

docs.title: Validated Case Study
docs.text: The CVD closes with "VeriVault", a fictional defense contractor migrating from an MPLS-TE + SD-WAN patchwork to the SRv6 fabric using three standardized site profiles (compact tactical field sites, dual-router processing centers, and redundant DC hubs with a dedicated route reflector). Migration is a phased parallel build: stand up the SRv6 fabric alongside the legacy WAN, cut over the DC hubs, bridge legacy and new domains via an NNI at the aggregation layer, then migrate spokes site by site. See Interworking & Migration for the general patterns.

docs.title: Network Slicing with SRv6
docs.text: Network slicing creates isolated logical networks over a shared physical infrastructure, each with its own topology, SIDs, QoS guarantees, and service-level objectives. SRv6 enables slicing natively through the combination of Flex-Algorithm, QoS policies, and SR Policy color steering — no additional overlay protocols required.

docs.title: What Is Network Slicing?
docs.text:
A network slice is an end-to-end logical partition that provides:

  • Topology isolation — each slice uses a different set of paths through the network
  • Resource guarantees — dedicated bandwidth, latency, or jitter targets per slice
  • Independent policies — each slice can have its own TE, protection, and routing constraints

docs.title: Slicing vs VPN vs Traffic Engineering
docs.text:
Concept Layer Isolation Type Mechanism VPN (VRF) L3 Routing table isolation Separate FIBs per customer Traffic Engineering Path Path selection SR Policy / RSVP-TE Network Slice Topology + Resources Topology + bandwidth + QoS Flex-Algo + QoS + Color

VPNs ride on slices

Network slicing and VPNs are complementary. A customer VPN can be mapped onto a specific slice (e.g., "Gold slice") to get both routing isolation and transport-level SLA guarantees.

docs.title: SRv6 Slicing Building Blocks
docs.text:
SRv6 network slicing combines three mechanisms:

graph TB
    subgraph Slice Architecture
        FA[Flex-Algorithm<br/>Topology Slicing] --> SLICE[Network Slice]
        QOS[QoS Policy<br/>Resource Slicing] --> SLICE
        COLOR[SR Policy + Color<br/>Service Steering] --> SLICE
    end
    SLICE --> S1[Slice 1: Low Latency]
    SLICE --> S2[Slice 2: High Bandwidth]
    SLICE --> S3[Slice 3: Best Effort]

docs.title: 1. Flex-Algorithm (Topology Slicing)
docs.text:
Each slice maps to a Flex-Algorithm (128-255), which computes an independent topology based on constraints like latency, affinity, or TE metric. Every node in the slice advertises a per-algorithm locator and SID.

Slice Flex-Algo Constraint Effect Low Latency 128 Minimize delay metric Uses only low-latency links High Bandwidth 129 Minimize TE metric + affinity Avoids congested links Best Effort 0 (default) Minimize IGP metric Uses all links

For full details, see Flex-Algorithm.

docs.title: 2. QoS (Resource Slicing)
docs.text:
Flex-Algorithm provides topology isolation, but bandwidth guarantees require QoS policies:

  • DSCP marking per slice — each slice gets a distinct DSCP value
  • Per-slice scheduling — strict priority, weighted fair queuing, or bandwidth reservation
  • Policers — rate limiting per slice to enforce SLA boundaries

For full details, see QoS.

docs.title: 3. SR Policy + Color (Service Steering)
docs.text:
BGP color extended communities map services into the correct slice:

  1. Service route is advertised with a color community (e.g., color 128 = low-latency slice)
  2. Headend PE matches the color to an SR Policy or Flex-Algo SID
  3. Traffic is steered into the slice automatically

For full details, see SR Policy.

docs.title: Use Case 1: 5G Network Slicing
docs.text:
3GPP defines standardized slice types that map directly to SRv6 Flex-Algorithm slices:

3GPP Slice Type SST Description SRv6 Mapping eMBB 1 Enhanced Mobile Broadband Flex-Algo 129 (bandwidth-optimized) URLLC 2 Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Flex-Algo 128 (latency-optimized) mMTC 3 Massive Machine-Type Comm. Flex-Algo 0 (best effort)

docs.title: End-to-End 5G Slice
docs.text:
graph LR
    RAN[RAN / gNB] -->|URLLC: Algo 128| TR1[Transport PE]
    RAN -->|eMBB: Algo 129| TR1
    TR1 -->|Slice-specific path| CORE((SRv6 Core))
    CORE --> UPF[UPF / Core PE]

The SRv6 MUP (Mobile User Plane) behaviors from RFC 9433 integrate with Flex-Algo slicing to provide end-to-end slice awareness from RAN to core.

For the full 5G transport architecture, see 5G Transport.

docs.title: Use Case 2: Enterprise Network Slicing
docs.text:
Enterprise operators use slicing to offer tiered services with guaranteed SLAs:

Tier Flex-Algo DSCP QoS Policy SLA Target Gold 128 EF (46) Strict priority, 30% BW guarantee <10ms latency, 99.999% Silver 129 AF31 (26) Weighted fair queue, 50% BW <50ms latency, 99.99% Bronze 0 BE (0) Best effort, remaining BW Best effort

docs.title: Configuration Example
docs.text:
Cisco IOS-XRJuniper 
!! Flex-Algorithm definitions
router isis CORE
 flex-algo 128
  metric-type delay
  advertise-definition
 !
 flex-algo 129
  affinity exclude-any CONGESTED
  advertise-definition
 !
!

!! Per-slice locators
segment-routing
 srv6
  locators
   locator GOLD
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fc00:128:1::/48
    algorithm 128
   !
   locator SILVER
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fc00:129:1::/48
    algorithm 129
   !
   locator BEST-EFFORT
    micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
    prefix fc00:0:1::/48
   !
  !
 !
!

!! Color steering for VPN → slice mapping
route-policy SET-GOLD-COLOR
 set extcommunity color 128
end-policy

router bgp 65000
 vrf GOLD-CUSTOMER
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   route-policy SET-GOLD-COLOR out
  !
 !
!

# Flex-Algo definition
set protocols isis flex-algorithm 128 metric-type min-delay
set protocols isis flex-algorithm 129 affinity exclude CONGESTED

# Per-slice locators
set routing-options segment-routing-v6 locator GOLD fc00:128:1::/48 algorithm 128
set routing-options segment-routing-v6 locator SILVER fc00:129:1::/48 algorithm 129
set routing-options segment-routing-v6 locator BEST-EFFORT fc00:0:1::/48

# Color steering
set policy-options community GOLD-COLOR color 128
set policy-options policy-statement GOLD-EXPORT term 1 then community add GOLD-COLOR

docs.title: Use Case 3: Data Center Slicing
docs.text:
In CLOS fabrics, Flex-Algorithm slicing isolates different traffic types:

Slice Purpose Constraint GPU Fabric AI/ML training traffic Low-latency links, RDMA-capable paths Storage NVMe-oF, iSCSI High-bandwidth, redundant paths Management SSH, SNMP, telemetry Best-effort, any path

Each slice gets its own Flex-Algo and locator, ensuring that GPU traffic never contends with storage replication on the same path.

For CLOS fabric design, see CLOS & Load Balancing. For AI/ML-specific networking, see AI/ML Networks.

docs.title: SID Allocation per Slice
docs.text:
Each slice requires a dedicated locator block. Plan allocations carefully:

Slice Algorithm Locator Block Nodes Best Effort 0 fc00:0::/32 All Low Latency 128 fc00:128::/32 All High Bandwidth 129 fc00:129::/32 All Custom 130 fc00:130::/32 Subset

docs.title: Monitoring and SLA Assurance
docs.text:
Per-slice monitoring is essential for SLA compliance:

  • SRPM (SR Performance Measurement) — per-slice delay/loss probes using slice-specific SIDs. See SRPM.
  • Telemetry — per-slice counters on interfaces and forwarding entries. See Telemetry.
  • IPFIX — per-slice flow records using RFC 9487 SRv6 Information Elements.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
Factor Limit Notes Flex-Algorithms 128 (128-255) Practical limit: 4-8 slices per network Locators per node Platform-dependent Typically 8-16 concurrent locators FIB impact N x nodes Each algorithm multiplies the IPv6 FIB by the number of participating nodes

FIB scaling

Each additional Flex-Algorithm adds a full set of locator routes to the FIB. With 1000 nodes and 4 algorithms, expect ~4000 locator entries. Plan hardware FIB capacity accordingly.

docs.title: Comparison: SRv6 Slicing vs Alternatives
docs.text: Aspect VRF-Only MPLS TE Tunnels FlexE SRv6 Flex-Algo Isolation Routing only Path only Physical (TDM) Topology + path Complexity Low High (RSVP state) Medium (hardware) Low-medium Scalability High Limited (~10K tunnels) Low (port-based) High SLA granularity Coarse (per VRF) Fine (per tunnel) Exact (hard isolation) Fine (per algorithm) Automation Limited Manual Manual Color steering + ODN Hardware Any Any FlexE-capable Any SRv6-capable
